# Linear algebra {#sec-linear-algebra}

Linear algebra is the study of vector spaces, the sets in which one can add and rescale, and of the maps between
them that respect those two operations. This chapter collects the part of it that geometry and field theory use on
every page, in six sections. Vector spaces defines spans, linear independence, bases and dimension, with
$\mathbb{R}^n$, spaces of matrices and spaces of functions as running examples. Linear maps and dual spaces treats
linear maps and their matrices, kernels and images, and the linear functionals that make up the dual space, with
the dual basis as the bridge between coordinates and functionals. Bilinear forms introduces the rule that assigns a
number to two vectors, with the Euclidean dot product and the Minkowski form of special relativity as the two
cases that matter most, and defines symmetry, non-degeneracy and signature. Multilinear maps and tensor products
generalises to maps of several arguments and to tensors of mixed type, their components and their contractions.
Determinants and trace builds the determinant from alternating forms, proves its rules for products, transposes and
inverses, and defines the trace and the partial trace. Eigenvalues and diagonalisation finds the directions that a map
only stretches, decides when they form a basis, reaches the Jordan form when they do not, and ends with singular values
and the polar decomposition.
Every definition, theorem and proposition is followed by ten examples of increasing complexity and ten exercises of
increasing difficulty, each exercise with a hidden solution worked by hand and in SageMath. The
reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the exact conventions for indices and
the summation convention are fixed in @sec-conventions.

## Vector spaces {#sec-vector-spaces}

A vector space is a set in which vectors can be added and rescaled. The six notions of this section, vector
spaces, linear combinations, spans, linear independence, bases and dimension, are the vocabulary in which every
later definition is phrased; the two propositions at its end record two dimension counts and the coordinates of one
vector in a skewed basis.

For more on this topic, see @axler2024linear [Ch. 1-2] and @lee2013introduction [App. B, pp. 617-622].

### Vector spaces

Everything in this chapter rests on two operations, adding two vectors and stretching one by a number, together with
the rules those operations obey. The definition below lists the rules once and for all; the picture to keep is that of
arrows in the plane, added tip to tail and rescaled along their own line. It also names the subsets that inherit the
structure, the subspaces, which is where most of the work will happen.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vector-space}
#### Vector space

A **real vector space** is a set $V$ with an addition $v + w$ and a multiplication $\lambda v$ by real numbers
(**scalars**) that obey the usual rules: addition is commutative and associative with a zero vector $0$ and
negatives, and $\lambda(v + w) = \lambda v + \lambda w$, $(\lambda + \mu) v = \lambda v + \mu v$, $(\lambda\mu) v =
\lambda(\mu v)$, $1 v = v$. Replacing $\mathbb{R}$ by $\mathbb{C}$ gives a **complex vector space**. A subset closed
under both operations is a **subspace**.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest vector spaces are worth naming before any interesting one, because they are the edge cases of every later
statement. The first example records the space with one element and the real line itself, and the subspaces the line
has.

::: {#exm-vs-trivial}
#### The zero space and the real line

The set $\{0\}$ with $0 + 0 = 0$ and $\lambda 0 = 0$ is a vector space, the **zero space**; every vector space contains
it as a subspace. The real line $\mathbb{R}$, with its own addition and multiplication, is a vector space whose only
subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathbb{R}$: a subspace containing some $a \neq 0$ contains every $\lambda a$, which is every
real number.
:::

In the plane the subspace test separates lines through the origin from the lines that miss it. The second example
shows the difference on two parallel lines; the shifted line is an affine subspace, a notion that returns with the
inhomogeneous equations of physics.

::: {#exm-vs-lines-plane}
#### Lines in the plane

The line $\{(x, y) : y = 2x\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$: if $y = 2x$ and $y' = 2x'$, then $y + y' = 2(x + x')$
and $\lambda y = 2(\lambda x)$. The parallel line $y = 2x + 1$ is not, since it misses $(0, 0)$. It is the set of
points $(0, 1) + w$ with $w$ on the first line, a translate of a subspace, which @lee2013introduction [App. B, p. 621]
calls an affine subspace.
:::

The coordinate spaces are the model for everything else, and they come next. The example below also shows the subspace
test at work in both directions, since a plane through the origin passes it while the unit sphere does not.

::: {#exm-vs-rn}
#### $\mathbb{R}^n$

$\mathbb{R}^n$, the set of columns $(x^1, \dots, x^n)$, with entrywise addition and scaling, is a vector space;
the plane $\{x^3 = 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$, while the sphere $S^2$ is not (the sum of two unit vectors
is not a unit vector).
:::

Complex columns behave in the same way with complex scalars, and the same set can be a vector space over two fields.
The example after this paragraph shows that the choice of scalars changes which subsets count as subspaces.

::: {#exm-vs-cn}
#### $\mathbb{C}^n$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and over $\mathbb{R}$

$\mathbb{C}^n$, with entrywise operations and complex scalars, is a complex vector space. Restricting the scalars to
real numbers makes it a real vector space as well [@lee2013introduction, Example B.7]. The real columns
$\mathbb{R}^n \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ form a subspace of the real space but not of the complex one: $i\,(1, 0, \dots, 0)
= (i, 0, \dots, 0)$ is not real [@axler2024linear, Exercise 1C.5].
:::

Vectors need not be columns. Square matrices add and rescale entrywise just as well, and applying the subspace test to
antisymmetric matrices on the one hand and to rotation matrices on the other separates a set of matrices that is a
vector space from one that is not.

::: {#exm-vs-matrices}
#### Matrices

The $n \times n$ real matrices form a vector space of dimension $n^2$ under entrywise operations; the
antisymmetric matrices $\mathbf A^\top = -\mathbf A$ form a subspace, closed also under the commutator $\mathbf A \mathbf B -
\mathbf B \mathbf A$. The rotation matrices do not: the sum of two rotations is not a rotation.
:::

The next instance has no finite list of coordinates at all. Functions on a set are added pointwise, so they form a
vector space that is usually infinite-dimensional, and the scalar fields of physics live in such a space; the
polynomials of bounded degree sit inside it as a finite-dimensional subspace.

::: {#exm-vs-functions}
#### Functions and fields

The real functions on a set $X$, with $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$ and $(\lambda f)(x) = \lambda f(x)$, form a vector
space, infinite-dimensional when $X$ is infinite; the polynomials of degree at most $2$ form a three-dimensional
subspace. A scalar field on spacetime (@sec-scalar-fields) is an element of such a function space.
:::

The first physical vector space is the solution set of a linear differential equation. For the harmonic oscillator
the subspace property is the superposition principle, and an external force destroys it.

::: {#exm-vs-oscillator}
#### Solutions of the harmonic oscillator

The functions $x(t)$ with $\ddot x + \omega^2 x = 0$ form a subspace of the functions of $t$: the equation is
unchanged when solutions are added or rescaled, which is the superposition principle. The solutions of the forced
equation $\ddot x + \omega^2 x = F\cos\Omega t$ with $F \neq 0$ do not; the difference of two of them solves the free
equation.
:::

In quantum mechanics the observables of a two-level system, such as a spin $\tfrac12$, are the Hermitian $2 \times 2$
matrices. They are a real vector space but not a complex one, which is the reason observables are expanded with real
coefficients.

::: {#exm-vs-hermitian}
#### Hermitian matrices

The Hermitian matrices $\mathbf H^\dagger = \mathbf H$ in the complex $2 \times 2$ matrices are closed under addition and under real
scaling, since $(\lambda \mathbf H)^\dagger = \lambda \mathbf H$ for real $\lambda$; they form a real vector space containing the Pauli
matrices $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$. They are not a complex subspace: $(i\sigma_1)^\dagger = -i\sigma_1$, so
$i\sigma_1$ is anti-Hermitian.
:::

Spacetime is a vector space, but the sets that physics singles out in it are often not subspaces. The light cone and
the future cone of Minkowski space fail the test in two different ways.

::: {#exm-vs-minkowski}
#### Cones in Minkowski space

Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^4$, with vectors $(t, x, y, z)$ and $\eta(v, v) = t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2$, is a vector
space. The null vectors $\eta(v, v) = 0$ are closed under scaling but not under addition: $(1, 1, 0, 0) + (1, -1, 0,
0) = (2, 0, 0, 0)$ has $\eta = 4$. The future cone $t \geq \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$ is closed under addition and under
positive scaling, but $-1$ maps it to the past cone: a cone, not a subspace.
:::

The last example is a warning that the rules, not the familiar operations, make a vector space. The positive reals
become a vector space once multiplication plays the part of addition and powers the part of scaling.

::: {#exm-vs-positive-reals}
#### An unusual vector space

On $V = (0, \infty)$ define $x \oplus y = xy$ and $\lambda \odot x = x^\lambda$. All the rules hold, with zero vector
$1$ and negative $1/x$. The map $x \mapsto \ln x$ turns $\oplus$ into $+$ and $\odot$ into
ordinary scaling, so this space is $\mathbb{R}$ in disguise.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The rules of the definition already imply the arithmetic one uses without thinking. The first exercise derives three
such facts, each in one line, so that later computations may use them freely [@axler2024linear, Sec. 1B].

::: {#exr-vs-zero-rules}
#### Consequences of the rules

Show from the rules of @def-vector-space that $0 v = 0$ and $\lambda 0 = 0$ for every vector $v$ and scalar
$\lambda$, and that $(-1) v = -v$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

From $(0 + 0) v = 0 v + 0 v$ we get $0 v = 0 v + 0 v$; adding the negative $-(0 v)$ to both sides gives $0 = 0 v$.
In the same way $\lambda 0 = \lambda (0 + 0) = \lambda 0 + \lambda 0$ gives $\lambda 0 = 0$. Finally $v + (-1) v = 1 v
+ (-1) v = (1 + (-1)) v = 0 v = 0$, so $(-1) v$ is a negative of $v$. Negatives are unique, since $w + v = 0 = w' + v$
gives $w = w + (v + w') = (w + v) + w' = w'$, so $(-1) v = -v$.

## SageMath

Check on a vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with symbolic entries and on the zero vector:

```{.python .sage}
a, b, c, lam = var("a b c lam")
v = vector(SR, [a, b, c])
z = vector(SR, [0, 0, 0])
print("0 v =", 0 * v, "; lam 0 =", lam * z)
print("v + (-1) v =", v + (-1) * v, "; (-1) v == -v:", (-1) * v == -v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
0 v = (0, 0, 0) ; lam 0 = (0, 0, 0)
v + (-1) v = (0, 0, 0) ; (-1) v == -v: True
```
::::
:::

The subspace test, closure under addition and under rescaling, is best learned on sets that fail it for different
reasons. Three subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$ follow, and the reader should identify a different culprit in each case: a
missing zero vector, or a sum that escapes the set. The exercise is adapted from @scott2023problems [Problem 2.3].

::: {#exr-vs-subspace-check}
#### Which subsets are subspaces?

Decide whether the plane $x + y + z = 0$, the plane $x + y + z = 1$ and the union of the two coordinate axes are
subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The plane $x + y + z = 0$ is a subspace: if $x + y + z = 0$ and $x' + y' + z' = 0$, then $(x + x') + (y + y') + (z +
z') = 0$ and $\lambda x + \lambda y + \lambda z = 0$, and $0$ lies in it. The plane $x + y + z = 1$ is not: it does not
contain $0$, and the sum of two of its points has coordinate sum $2$. The union of the axes is closed under scaling but
not under addition: $(1, 0, 0) + (0, 1, 0) = (1, 1, 0)$ lies on neither axis.

## SageMath

Sage tests each set on sample points: the sum and a multiple of two points of the first plane, and the sums that
escape the other two sets.

```{.python .sage}
P0 = lambda p: sum(p) == 0
P1 = lambda p: sum(p) == 1
axes = lambda p: list(p).count(0) >= 2
u, w = vector(QQ, [1, -1, 0]), vector(QQ, [2, 3, -5])
print("x+y+z=0: u + w and -7 u in the plane:", P0(u + w), P0(-7 * u))
p, q = vector(QQ, [1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 0])
print("x+y+z=1: contains 0:", P1(vector(QQ, [0, 0, 0])), "; p + q has coordinate sum", sum(p + q))
print("union of the x- and y-axes: p, q in it:", axes(p), axes(q), "; p + q in it:", axes(p + q))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
x+y+z=0: u + w and -7 u in the plane: True True
x+y+z=1: contains 0: False ; p + q has coordinate sum 2
union of the x- and y-axes: p, q in it: True True ; p + q in it: False
```
::::
:::

The same test can be run in Sage, which becomes useful as soon as the sets are too large to inspect by hand. This time
the matrices are symmetric rather than antisymmetric, their subspace has a dimension to be found, and the failure of
rotations to add up to a rotation is confirmed.

::: {#exr-vs-symmetric-matrices}
#### Symmetric matrices and rotations

Show with Sage that the symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices form a subspace of the $3 \times 3$ matrices, find its
dimension, and check that the sum of two rotation matrices is not a rotation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(\mathbf A + \mathbf B)^\top = \mathbf A^\top + \mathbf B^\top = \mathbf A + \mathbf B$ and $(\lambda \mathbf A)^\top = \lambda \mathbf A$, so sums and multiples of symmetric
matrices are symmetric, and the zero matrix is symmetric. A symmetric matrix is the combination $\sum_i A_{ii} \mathbf E_{ii} +
\sum_{i < j} A_{ij} (\mathbf E_{ij} + \mathbf E_{ji})$ of the $3 + 3 = 6$ matrices $\mathbf E_{ii}$ and $\mathbf E_{ij} + \mathbf E_{ji}$, which have their
non-zero entries in different places, so the subspace has dimension $6$. For rotations, let $\mathbf R_1$ be the rotation by
$90^\circ$ about the $z$-axis and $\mathbf R_2$ the one about the $x$-axis. The first column of $\mathbf R_1 + \mathbf R_2$ is $(1, 1, 0)$, of
length $\sqrt 2$, while every column of a rotation has length $1$; so $\mathbf R_1 + \mathbf R_2$ is not a rotation.

## SageMath

Sage checks closure on two symmetric matrices, computes the dimension of the span of the matrices $\mathbf E_{ij} + \mathbf E_{ji}$,
and tests $\mathbf R^\top \mathbf R = \mathbf I$ for $\mathbf R = \mathbf R_1 + \mathbf R_2$.

```{.python .sage}
M = MatrixSpace(QQ, 3, 3)
A = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2, 0], [2, 3, 1], [0, 1, 4]]); B = matrix(QQ, [[0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 2], [1, 2, 5]])
print("A, B symmetric:", A.is_symmetric(), B.is_symmetric(), "; A + B and 3A symmetric:", (A + B).is_symmetric(), (3 * A).is_symmetric())
# the subspace of symmetric matrices, as the span of E_ii and E_ij + E_ji
sym_space = span([vector(QQ, (m + m.transpose()).list()) for m in M.basis()], QQ)
print("dimension of the symmetric 3 x 3 matrices:", sym_space.dimension(), "= 3 * 4 / 2")
R1 = matrix(QQ, [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]]); R2 = matrix(QQ, [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]])
print("R1, R2 rotations (R^T R = 1):", R1.transpose() * R1 == 1, R2.transpose() * R2 == 1)
print("R1 + R2 is a rotation:", (R1 + R2).transpose() * (R1 + R2) == 1, " (so the rotations are not a subspace)")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A, B symmetric: True True ; A + B and 3A symmetric: True True
dimension of the symmetric 3 x 3 matrices: 6 = 3 * 4 / 2
R1, R2 rotations (R^T R = 1): True True
R1 + R2 is a rotation: False  (so the rotations are not a subspace)
```
::::
:::

Function spaces are checked in the same way, with pointwise operations in place of entrywise ones. The point of this
exercise is the difference between a bound on the degree, which gives a subspace, and an exact degree, which does not;
the same distinction appears whenever an expansion is truncated.

::: {#exr-vs-polynomials-axioms}
#### Polynomials of bounded degree

Show that the polynomials of degree at most $2$ form a subspace of the functions on $\mathbb{R}$, and that the
polynomials of degree exactly $2$ do not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(a + bx + cx^2) + (a' + b'x + c'x^2) = (a + a') + (b + b')x + (c + c')x^2$ and $\lambda(a + bx + cx^2) = \lambda a +
\lambda b x + \lambda c x^2$ have degree at most $2$, and the zero polynomial is included. The polynomials of
degree exactly $2$ miss the zero polynomial, and $x^2 + (-x^2 + x) = x$ has degree $1$: the set is closed under
neither operation, since also $0 \cdot x^2 = 0$ leaves it.

## SageMath

Sage adds two polynomials of degree at most $2$ and prints the degrees, then the counterexample for the exact degree.

```{.python .sage}
R.<x> = QQ[]
p, q = 3 - x + 2 * x^2, 1 + 5 * x - 7 * x^2
print("deg(p + q) =", (p + q).degree(), ", deg(-4 p) =", (-4 * p).degree())
print("x^2 and -x^2 + x have degree", (x^2).degree(), (-x^2 + x).degree(), "; their sum", x^2 + (-x^2 + x), "has degree", (x^2 - x^2 + x).degree())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
deg(p + q) = 2 , deg(-4 p) = 2
x^2 and -x^2 + x have degree 2 2 ; their sum x has degree 1
```
::::
:::

Conditions on functions are linear when they involve the function only through values, derivatives or integrals, with
no constant term. The exercise tests two such conditions, the second with a constant that may or may not vanish
[@axler2024linear, Exercises 1C.3-1C.4].

::: {#exr-vs-function-conditions}
#### Linear conditions on functions

Show that the differentiable functions $f$ on $(-4, 4)$ with $f'(-1) = 3 f(2)$ form a subspace, and that the
continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ with $\int_0^1 f = b$ form a subspace exactly when $b = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Derivatives and values are additive and homogeneous: if $f'(-1) = 3f(2)$ and $g'(-1) = 3g(2)$, then $(f + g)'(-1) =
f'(-1) + g'(-1) = 3(f + g)(2)$ and $(\lambda f)'(-1) = 3(\lambda f)(2)$; the zero function satisfies the condition.
For the integral, $\int (f + g) = \int f + \int g$ and $\int \lambda f = \lambda \int f$, so for $b = 0$ the set is
closed under both operations and contains $0$. For $b \neq 0$ it does not contain the zero function, whose integral
is $0$, so it is not a subspace.

## SageMath

Check on $f_1 = x - \tfrac53$ and $f_2 = x^2 - \tfrac{14}{3}$, which satisfy the first condition, and on $g = 2x$, with
$\int_0^1 g = 1$:

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
cond = lambda f: diff(f, x).subs(x=-1) - 3 * f.subs(x=2)        # zero exactly on the subset
f1, f2 = x - 5/3, x^2 - 14/3
print("f1, f2, 2 f1 - 7 f2 satisfy f'(-1) = 3 f(2):", [bool(cond(f) == 0) for f in (f1, f2, 2 * f1 - 7 * f2)])
g = 2 * x
print("integral of g:", integrate(g, x, 0, 1), "; integral of g + g:", integrate(g + g, x, 0, 1), "(so b = 1 is not closed under addition)")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f1, f2, 2 f1 - 7 f2 satisfy f'(-1) = 3 f(2): [True, True, True]
integral of g: 1 ; integral of g + g: 2 (so b = 1 is not closed under addition)
```
::::
:::

Whether a subset is a subspace depends on the scalars. The exercise asks for two subsets that pass the real test and
fail the complex one; the second is the space of spin observables of @exm-vs-hermitian [@axler2024linear, Exercise
1C.5].

::: {#exr-vs-real-not-complex}
#### Real but not complex subspaces

Show that $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a subspace of the complex vector space $\mathbb{C}^2$, and that the Hermitian $2
\times 2$ matrices are a subspace of the complex $2 \times 2$ matrices viewed as a real vector space but not viewed as
a complex one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbb{R}^2$ contains $(1, 0)$ but not $i\,(1, 0) = (i, 0)$, so it is not closed under complex scaling. For Hermitian
$\mathbf H, \mathbf K$ and real $\lambda$, $(\mathbf H + \mathbf K)^\dagger = \mathbf H^\dagger + \mathbf K^\dagger = \mathbf H + \mathbf K$ and $(\lambda \mathbf H)^\dagger = \lambda^*
\mathbf H^\dagger = \lambda \mathbf H$, so the Hermitian matrices form a real subspace. For complex $\lambda$ the same computation
gives $(\lambda \mathbf H)^\dagger = \lambda^* \mathbf H$, which differs from $\lambda \mathbf H$ when $\lambda$ is not real and $\mathbf H \neq \mathbf 0$;
for example $(i\sigma_1)^\dagger = -i\sigma_1$.

## SageMath

Check on the Pauli matrices over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$:

```{.python .sage}
s1 = matrix(QQbar, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]); s2 = matrix(QQbar, [[0, -I], [I, 0]]); s3 = matrix(QQbar, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])
herm = lambda H: H.conjugate_transpose() == H
i = QQbar(I)
print("sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 Hermitian:", herm(s1), herm(s2), herm(s3))
print("2 s1 - 5 s2 + s3 Hermitian:", herm(2 * s1 - 5 * s2 + s3), "; i s1 Hermitian:", herm(i * s1))
v = vector(QQbar, [1, 0])
print("i (1, 0) =", i * v, "; real:", all(c.imag() == 0 for c in i * v))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 Hermitian: True True True
2 s1 - 5 s2 + s3 Hermitian: True ; i s1 Hermitian: False
i (1, 0) = (I, 0) ; real: False
```
::::
:::

Two subspaces can be combined in two obvious ways, and only one of them always gives a subspace. The proof asked for
here is short in one direction and needs a well-chosen sum in the other [@axler2024linear, Exercises 1C.10 and 1C.12].

::: {#exr-vs-intersection-union}
#### Intersections and unions

Let $U$ and $W$ be subspaces of $V$. Prove that $U \cap W$ is a subspace, and that $U \cup W$ is a subspace only if
one of $U$, $W$ contains the other.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Both subspaces contain $0$, so $0 \in U \cap W$. If $u, u' \in U \cap W$, then $u + u'$ and $\lambda u$ lie in $U$
and in $W$, since each is closed, so they lie in $U \cap W$. For the union, suppose neither subspace contains the
other: pick $u \in U$ with $u \notin W$ and $w \in W$ with $w \notin U$. If $u + w$ were in $U$, then $w = (u + w) - u$
would be in $U$; if it were in $W$, then $u = (u + w) - w$ would be in $W$. Both are excluded, so $u + w \notin U \cup
W$ and the union is not closed under addition. Conversely, if $U \subseteq W$, the union is $W$, a subspace.

## SageMath

Check on the planes $U = \{z = 0\}$ and $W = \{x = 0\}$ of $\mathbb{Q}^3$:

```{.python .sage}
V = QQ^3
U = V.subspace([vector(QQ, [1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 0])])
W = V.subspace([vector(QQ, [0, 1, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, 1])])
print("U cap W is the line through", U.intersection(W).basis()[0], "; a subspace of dimension", U.intersection(W).dimension())
u, w = vector(QQ, [1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, 1])
print("u in U, w in W:", u in U, w in W, "; u + w =", u + w, "in U or W:", (u + w) in U or (u + w) in W)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
U cap W is the line through (0, 1, 0) ; a subspace of dimension 1
u in U, w in W: True True ; u + w = (1, 0, 1) in U or W: False
```
::::
:::

Every function on the line splits into an even and an odd part, and these parts live in two subspaces that meet only
in zero. The exercise proves the splitting, which returns as the parity decomposition of wave functions
[@axler2024linear, Exercise 1C.24].

::: {#exr-vs-even-odd}
#### Even and odd functions

Show that the even functions ($f(-x) = f(x)$) and the odd functions ($f(-x) = -f(x)$) on $\mathbb{R}$ are subspaces,
that their intersection is $\{0\}$, and that every function is uniquely the sum of an even and an odd one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The conditions $f(-x) = \pm f(x)$ are preserved by sums and multiples and hold for $0$, so both sets are subspaces. A
function in both has $f(x) = f(-x) = -f(x)$, so $f = 0$. Given $f$, put $f_e(x) = \tfrac12(f(x) + f(-x))$ and
$f_o(x) = \tfrac12(f(x) - f(-x))$; then $f_e$ is even, $f_o$ is odd and $f = f_e + f_o$. If also $f = g_e + g_o$, then
$f_e - g_e = g_o - f_o$ is both even and odd, hence $0$: the splitting is unique.

## SageMath

Check on $f(x) = e^x + x^3 + x^2$, whose even and odd parts are $\cosh x + x^2$ and $\sinh x + x^3$:

```{.python .sage}
x = var("x")
f = exp(x) + x^3 + x^2
fe, fo = (f + f.subs(x=-x)) / 2, (f - f.subs(x=-x)) / 2
print("even part:", fe.expand(), "; odd part:", fo.expand())
print("fe even, fo odd, fe + fo == f:", bool(fe.subs(x=-x) == fe), bool(fo.subs(x=-x) == -fo), bool(fe + fo == f))
print("fe - x^2 == cosh(x) = (e^x + e^-x)/2:", bool((fe - x^2 - (exp(x) + exp(-x)) / 2).simplify_full() == 0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
even part: x^2 + 1/2*e^(-x) + 1/2*e^x ; odd part: x^3 - 1/2*e^(-x) + 1/2*e^x
fe even, fo odd, fe + fo == f: True True True
fe - x^2 == cosh(x) = (e^x + e^-x)/2: True
```
::::
:::

The superposition principle of @exm-vs-oscillator can now be proved, together with its failure for the forced
oscillator. The exercise also shows the standard repair: the forced solutions form a translate of the free ones.

::: {#exr-vs-oscillator}
#### Free and forced oscillators

Show that the solutions of $\ddot x + \omega^2 x = 0$ form a subspace, that those of $\ddot x + \omega^2 x = F \cos
\Omega t$ with $F \neq 0$ do not, and that the difference of two forced solutions is a free solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Write $Lx = \ddot x + \omega^2 x$. Differentiation is additive and homogeneous, so $L(x + y) = Lx + Ly$ and
$L(\lambda x) = \lambda Lx$. If $Lx = Ly = 0$, then $L(x + y) = 0$ and $L(\lambda x) = 0$, and $L0 = 0$: the free
solutions form a subspace. If $Lx = Ly = F\cos\Omega t$, then $L(x + y) = 2F\cos\Omega t \neq F\cos\Omega t$, so the
forced solutions are not closed under addition, and $L(x - y) = 0$: their difference is a free solution. Hence every
forced solution is one particular forced solution plus a free one.

## SageMath

Check on $x_1 = \cos\omega t$, $x_2 = \sin\omega t$ and the particular forced solution $x_p = F\cos\Omega t / (\omega^2 -
\Omega^2)$:

```{.python .sage}
t, w, W, F, a, b = var("t omega Omega F a b")
L = lambda x: diff(x, t, 2) + w^2 * x
x1, x2 = cos(w * t), sin(w * t)
print("L(a x1 + b x2) =", L(a * x1 + b * x2).simplify_full())
xp = F * cos(W * t) / (w^2 - W^2)
print("L(xp) =", L(xp).simplify_full(), "; L(2 xp) =", L(2 * xp).simplify_full())
xq = xp + 3 * x1                     # another forced solution
print("L(xq) =", L(xq).simplify_full(), "; L(xq - xp) =", L(xq - xp).simplify_full())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
L(a x1 + b x2) = 0
L(xp) = F*cos(Omega*t) ; L(2 xp) = 2*F*cos(Omega*t)
L(xq) = F*cos(Omega*t) ; L(xq - xp) = 0
```
::::
:::

The last exercise returns to @exm-vs-positive-reals and puts the rules to work on unfamiliar operations. Its second
half shows a set with natural-looking operations that fails exactly one group of rules [@axler2024linear, Exercise
1B.6].

::: {#exr-vs-positive-reals}
#### Unusual operations

Show that $(0, \infty)$ with $x \oplus y = xy$ and $\lambda \odot x = x^\lambda$ satisfies every rule of
@def-vector-space. Then show that $\mathbb{R} \cup \{\infty, -\infty\}$, with $t + \infty = \infty$, $t + (-\infty) =
-\infty$, $\infty + (-\infty) = 0$, $\infty + \infty = \infty$ and $\lambda \infty = \pm\infty$ or $0$ according to
the sign of $\lambda$, is not a vector space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Multiplication of positive numbers is commutative and associative, the number $1$ satisfies $x \oplus 1 = x$, and $1/x$
satisfies $x \oplus 1/x = 1$. The scaling rules are the laws of exponents: $\lambda \odot (x \oplus y) = (xy)^\lambda =
x^\lambda y^\lambda$, $(\lambda + \mu) \odot x = x^{\lambda + \mu} = x^\lambda x^\mu$, $(\lambda\mu) \odot x =
x^{\lambda\mu} = (x^\mu)^\lambda$ and $1 \odot x = x$. For the extended line, associativity of addition fails:
$(\infty + \infty) + (-\infty) = \infty + (-\infty) = 0$, while $\infty + (\infty + (-\infty)) = \infty + 0 = \infty$.
A distributive rule fails too: $(2 + (-1))\infty = \infty$, but $2\infty + (-1)\infty = \infty + (-\infty) = 0$.

## SageMath

Check on $x = 2$, $y = \tfrac35$, $\lambda = \tfrac12$, $\mu = 3$ with exact algebraic numbers, and on the two failing
sums of the extended line:

```{.python .sage}
x, y, l, m = AA(2), AA(3/5), QQ(1/2), QQ(3)
add = lambda p, q: p * q
smul = lambda c, p: p^c
print("l(x + y) = lx + ly:", smul(l, add(x, y)) == add(smul(l, x), smul(l, y)))
print("(l + m)x = lx + mx:", smul(l + m, x) == add(smul(l, x), smul(m, x)), "; (lm)x = l(mx):", smul(l * m, x) == smul(l, smul(m, x)))
print("zero vector 1 and negative 1/x:", add(x, 1) == x, add(x, 1 / x) == 1)
def ext_add(p, q):                    # the addition of the extended line; "inf", "-inf" or a number
    if p == "inf" and q == "-inf" or p == "-inf" and q == "inf": return 0
    if "inf" in (p, q): return "inf"
    if "-inf" in (p, q): return "-inf"
    return p + q
print("(inf + inf) + (-inf) =", ext_add(ext_add("inf", "inf"), "-inf"), "; inf + (inf + (-inf)) =", ext_add("inf", ext_add("inf", "-inf")))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
l(x + y) = lx + ly: True
(l + m)x = lx + mx: True ; (lm)x = l(mx): True
zero vector 1 and negative 1/x: True True
(inf + inf) + (-inf) = 0 ; inf + (inf + (-inf)) = inf
```
::::
:::
::::

### Linear combinations

With addition and rescaling available, the simplest object one can build from a finite family of vectors is a weighted
sum of them. The definition that follows names this operation and fixes the index convention, upper indices on
coefficients and lower indices on vectors, on which every later formula relies.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-linear-combination}
#### Linear combination

A **linear combination** of vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ is a vector $\lambda^1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda^k v_k$ with real
coefficients $\lambda^i$. Repeated upper and lower indices are summed, $\lambda^i v_i$ (the summation convention of
@sec-conventions).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The degenerate cases come first: no coefficients at all, or a single vector. They show that the zero vector is a
combination of any family and that the combinations of one vector are its multiples.

::: {#exm-combination-trivial}
#### Trivial combinations

The combination $0 v_1 + \dots + 0 v_k = 0$ shows that $0$ is a linear combination of every family, and by convention
of the empty family as well [@lee2013introduction, App. B, p. 618]. The combinations of a single vector $v$ are its
multiples $\lambda v$; in $\mathbb{R}^2$, $(3, -1) = 3 \mathbf e_1 - \mathbf e_2$ is a combination of the two standard basis vectors.
:::

In coordinates a weighted sum is a sum of rescaled columns, and the standard basis vectors show that every column is
such a sum. The next example records one explicit combination of three-component columns; the same three vectors
return throughout the chapter as a running case.

::: {#exm-combination-r3}
#### In $\mathbb{R}^3$

$(1, 3, 1) = 1\cdot(1, 2, 0) + 1\cdot(0, 1, 1)$ is a linear combination of $(1, 2, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$; every vector
$(x, y, z)$ is the combination $x \mathbf e_1 + y \mathbf e_2 + z \mathbf e_3$ of the standard basis vectors.
:::

Polynomials combine in the same way, and one polynomial can be written in several families. The example rewrites a
square and a monomial in the shifted powers and in the first Legendre polynomials, which return with the hydrogen
atom.

::: {#exm-combination-polynomials}
#### Polynomials

$(x + 1)^2 = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot x + 1 \cdot x^2$ is a linear combination of the monomials. With the Legendre
polynomials $P_0 = 1$ and $P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1)$, the monomial $x^2 = \tfrac13 P_0 + \tfrac23 P_2$ is a linear
combination of $P_0$ and $P_2$.
:::

The same operation applied to the three generators of rotations produces every antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix. This
is the first appearance of the pattern "general element equals weighted sum of generators" that the notion of span
will make precise in the next section.

::: {#exm-combination-matrices}
#### Antisymmetric matrices

$a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$, with the three generators $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$ of rotations and real $a, b, c$, is a linear
combination; it is the general antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix.
:::

For a spin $\tfrac12$ the role of the generators is played by the Pauli matrices. Every Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrix
is a real combination of the identity and the three Pauli matrices, and the example works out one case.

::: {#exm-combination-pauli}
#### Pauli matrices

With $\sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0
\end{pmatrix}$ and $\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \\
1 + i & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf I + \sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \sigma_3$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf I, \sigma_1, \sigma_2,
\sigma_3$ with real coefficients.
:::

Functions can be combined with coefficients exactly as columns can. Trigonometric polynomials, finite sums of cosines
and sines with numerical coefficients, are the most important instance for physics, and they show that the candidate vectors may be
infinitely many as long as only finitely many coefficients are non-zero.

::: {#exm-combination-fourier}
#### Trigonometric modes

$a\cos\varphi + b\sin\varphi$ is a linear combination of the two functions $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$; a
trigonometric polynomial $\sum_n (a_n \cos n\varphi + b_n \sin n\varphi)$ is a linear combination of modes.
:::

The motion of a harmonic oscillator is the trigonometric example with time in place of the angle. Its coefficients carry
the initial data, so a linear combination here is a whole family of motions.

::: {#exm-combination-oscillator}
#### Oscillator motions

Every solution of $\ddot x + \omega^2 x = 0$ is the linear combination $x(t) = A\cos\omega t + B\sin\omega t$ of two
solutions, with $A = x(0)$ and $B = \dot x(0)/\omega$. Indeed, the difference $y$ of $x$ and this combination solves the
equation with $y(0) = \dot y(0) = 0$, and $E = \dot y^2 + \omega^2 y^2$ has $\dot E = 2\dot y(\ddot y + \omega^2 y) = 0$,
so $E$ stays $0$ and $y = 0$. The motion $\cos(\omega t +
\varphi_0) = \cos\varphi_0 \cos\omega t - \sin\varphi_0 \sin\omega t$ with a phase is one of them.
:::

Quantum states are combined with complex coefficients, in the complex vector space of @def-vector-space. For a spin
$\tfrac12$ the two states of definite $\sigma_3$ generate all the others.

::: {#exm-combination-spin}
#### Spin states

A spin-$\tfrac12$ state is a combination $\alpha\,{\uparrow} + \beta\,{\downarrow}$ of the states ${\uparrow} = (1, 0)$
and ${\downarrow} = (0, 1)$ of $\mathbb{C}^2$, with complex $\alpha, \beta$. The state of spin up along the
$x$-axis is ${+x} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}({\uparrow} + {\downarrow})$, and the state of spin up along the $y$-axis is
${+y} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}({\uparrow} + i\,{\downarrow})$.
:::

In the hydrogen atom the angular parts of the $2p$ orbitals are functions on the sphere. Chemists' real orbitals and
physicists' orbitals of definite angular momentum about the $z$-axis are linear combinations of each other.

::: {#exm-combination-hydrogen}
#### Orbitals of the hydrogen atom

On the sphere with polar angle $\theta$ and azimuth $\varphi$, the functions $\sin\theta\, e^{i\varphi}$ and
$\sin\theta\, e^{-i\varphi}$ (the $\varphi$-dependence of the $2p$ states with $m = \pm 1$) combine to the real
angular parts $\sin\theta\cos\varphi = \tfrac12(\sin\theta\, e^{i\varphi} + \sin\theta\, e^{-i\varphi})$ and
$\sin\theta\sin\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2i}(\sin\theta\, e^{i\varphi} - \sin\theta\, e^{-i\varphi})$, which are $x/r$ and
$y/r$.
:::

A linear combination has finitely many terms, and this limit matters. The last example shows a series of monomials
that is not a linear combination of them, however natural it looks.

::: {#exm-combination-infinite}
#### Infinite sums are not combinations

$e^x = \sum_{n \geq 0} x^n / n!$ is not a linear combination of the monomials $1, x, x^2, \dots$: a combination of
finitely many monomials is a polynomial of some degree $d$, whose $(d + 1)$-st derivative vanishes, while every
derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x \neq 0$. Infinite sums need a notion of convergence, which a vector space alone does not
provide.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is a direct computation of one combination. It also shows that the same vector can arise from two
different sets of coefficients, a point the section on linear independence makes precise.

::: {#exr-combination-evaluate}
#### Evaluating a combination

For $u = (1, 0, 2)$, $v = (0, 1, -1)$ and $w = (3, 3, 3)$, compute $2u - 3v + w$, and find a second combination of
$u, v, w$ with different coefficients that gives the same vector.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$2u - 3v + w = (2, 0, 4) - (0, 3, -3) + (3, 3, 3) = (5, 0, 10)$. This is $5u$, that is, the combination with
coefficients $(5, 0, 0)$ instead of $(2, -3, 1)$. Subtracting the two combinations gives $-3u - 3v + w = 0$, that is,
$w = 3u + 3v = (3, 3, 3)$: a combination with non-zero coefficients can vanish, and then coefficients are not unique.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates both combinations and the vanishing one.

```{.python .sage}
u, v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 0, 2]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, -1]), vector(QQ, [3, 3, 3])
print("2u - 3v + w =", 2 * u - 3 * v + w, "; 5u =", 5 * u)
print("3u + 3v - w =", 3 * u + 3 * v - w)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
2u - 3v + w = (5, 0, 10) ; 5u = (5, 0, 10)
3u + 3v - w = (0, 0, 0)
```
::::
:::

Given a target vector and a family, the coefficients are the unknowns of a linear system with as many equations as
there are coordinates. The exercise asks the reader to solve such a system by hand and then to recognise it in Sage as
a matrix equation whose columns are the given vectors.

::: {#exr-combination-solve}
#### Finding the coefficients

Write $w = (4, 7, 2)$ as a linear combination of $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$, $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ and $v_4 = (0, 0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The coefficients solve the linear system $\lambda^1 = 4$, $2\lambda^1 + \lambda^2 = 7$, $\lambda^2 + \lambda^4 = 2$,
read off coordinate by coordinate. The first equation gives $\lambda^1 = 4$, the second $\lambda^2 = 7 - 8 = -1$ and
the third $\lambda^4 = 2 + 1 = 3$, so $w = 4 v_1 - v_2 + 3 v_4$.

## SageMath

In Sage the system is the matrix with columns $v_1, v_2, v_4$, solved for the coefficient column.

```{.python .sage}
v1, v2, v4 = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, 1])
w = vector(QQ, [4, 7, 2])
C = matrix(QQ, [v1, v2, v4]).transpose()          # columns v1, v2, v4
lam = C.solve_right(w)
print("coefficients (lambda^1, lambda^2, lambda^4) =", lam)
print("check:", lam[0] * v1 + lam[1] * v2 + lam[2] * v4 == w)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
coefficients (lambda^1, lambda^2, lambda^4) = (4, -1, 3)
check: True
```
::::
:::

A system for the coefficients can also impose a condition on the target. Here the last coordinate of the target is
unknown, and it is fixed by asking that the system have a solution [@axler2024linear, Exercise 2A.5].

::: {#exr-combination-parameter}
#### A combination that fixes a parameter

Find the number $t$ for which $(5, 9, t)$ is a linear combination of $(3, 1, 4)$ and $(2, -3, 5)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

We need $a(3, 1, 4) + b(2, -3, 5) = (5, 9, t)$. The first two coordinates give $3a + 2b = 5$ and $a - 3b = 9$, so $a =
9 + 3b$ and $27 + 11b = 5$: $b = -2$, $a = 3$. These are the only possible coefficients, and the third coordinate is
then $t = 4a + 5b = 12 - 10 = 2$. For $t \neq 2$ there is no combination.

## SageMath

Sage solves the first two equations and evaluates the third coordinate.

```{.python .sage}
a, b = var("a b")
sol = solve([3 * a + 2 * b == 5, a - 3 * b == 9], a, b, solution_dict=True)[0]
print("a, b =", sol[a], sol[b], "; t = 4a + 5b =", 4 * sol[a] + 5 * sol[b])
print("check:", sol[a] * vector(QQ, [3, 1, 4]) + sol[b] * vector(QQ, [2, -3, 5]))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
a, b = 3 -2 ; t = 4a + 5b = 2
check: (5, 9, 2)
```
::::
:::

For functions the same question is not a system of equations but an identity to be recognised. Here the double-angle
and triple-angle formulas of trigonometry are reread as statements that a power of a cosine or sine is a weighted sum
of a few trigonometric modes.

::: {#exr-combination-fourier}
#### A trigonometric identity as a combination

Write $\cos^2\varphi$ as a linear combination of the functions $1$ and $\cos 2\varphi$, and $\sin^3\varphi$ as a
combination of $\sin\varphi$ and $\sin 3\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

From $\cos 2\varphi = 2\cos^2\varphi - 1$, $\cos^2\varphi = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac12 \cos 2\varphi$. From $\sin
3\varphi = 3\sin\varphi - 4\sin^3\varphi$, $\sin^3\varphi = \tfrac34 \sin\varphi - \tfrac14 \sin 3\varphi$. Every
polynomial in $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ is a linear combination of modes in this way.

## SageMath

Sage reduces the two powers to modes and checks the two identities.

```{.python .sage}
p = var("phi")
print("cos^2 =", (cos(p)^2).trig_reduce(), "; sin^3 =", (sin(p)^3).trig_reduce())
print("identities hold:", bool(cos(p)^2 == 1/2 + cos(2 * p) / 2), bool(sin(p)^3 == 3/4 * sin(p) - sin(3 * p) / 4))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
cos^2 = 1/2*cos(2*phi) + 1/2 ; sin^3 = -1/4*sin(3*phi) + 3/4*sin(phi)
identities hold: True True
```
::::
:::

For antisymmetric matrices the coefficients can be read off directly, because each generator occupies its own pair of
entries. The task is to extract the three coefficients of a given matrix while keeping track of the sign convention
$(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, which is easy to get backwards.

::: {#exr-combination-so3}
#### Reading off the coefficients of an antisymmetric matrix

Write the antisymmetric matrix with entries $X_{12} = -5$, $X_{13} = 2$, $X_{23} = -7$ as $a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

With $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, the generator $L_1$ has $(L_1)_{32} = -\epsilon_{132} = 1$, $L_2$ has $(L_2)_{13}
= -\epsilon_{213} = 1$ and $L_3$ has $(L_3)_{21} = -\epsilon_{321} = 1$, and each is zero in the other two of these
three places. So $a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$ has $X_{32} = a$, $X_{13} = b$, $X_{21} = c$, and here $(a, b, c) = (-X_{23},
X_{13}, -X_{12}) = (7, 2, 5)$.

## SageMath

Sage builds the generators, reads off the three entries and checks the combination.

```{.python .sage}
L1 = matrix(QQ, [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]])
L2 = matrix(QQ, [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [-1, 0, 0]])
L3 = matrix(QQ, [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]])
X = matrix(QQ, [[0, -5, 2], [5, 0, -7], [-2, 7, 0]])
print("X antisymmetric:", X.transpose() == -X)
a, b, c = X[2, 1], X[0, 2], X[1, 0]
print("coefficients (a, b, c) = (X_32, X_13, X_21) =", (a, b, c), "; a L1 + b L2 + c L3 == X:", a * L1 + b * L2 + c * L3 == X)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
X antisymmetric: True
coefficients (a, b, c) = (X_32, X_13, X_21) = (7, 2, 5) ; a L1 + b L2 + c L3 == X: True
```
::::
:::

The Legendre polynomials of @exm-combination-polynomials are the angular functions of the hydrogen atom along the
axis. The exercise rewrites two polynomials in them, working from the highest degree down.

::: {#exr-combination-legendre}
#### Polynomials in Legendre polynomials

With $P_0 = 1$, $P_1 = x$, $P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1)$ and $P_3 = \tfrac12(5x^3 - 3x)$, write $x^3$ as a combination
of $P_1, P_3$ and $1 + x + x^2$ as a combination of $P_0, P_1, P_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Only $P_3$ contains $x^3$, with coefficient $\tfrac52$, so $x^3 = \tfrac25 P_3 + r$ with $r = x^3 - (x^3 - \tfrac35 x) =
\tfrac35 x$: $x^3 = \tfrac25 P_3 + \tfrac35 P_1$. Likewise $x^2 = \tfrac23 P_2 + \tfrac13 P_0$, so $1 + x + x^2 =
\tfrac43 P_0 + P_1 + \tfrac23 P_2$.

## SageMath

Sage expands the two combinations and compares them with the targets.

```{.python .sage}
R.<x> = QQ[]
P0, P1, P2, P3 = R(1), x, (3 * x^2 - 1) / 2, (5 * x^3 - 3 * x) / 2
print("2/5 P3 + 3/5 P1 =", 2/5 * P3 + 3/5 * P1)
print("4/3 P0 + P1 + 2/3 P2 =", 4/3 * P0 + P1 + 2/3 * P2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
2/5 P3 + 3/5 P1 = x^3
4/3 P0 + P1 + 2/3 P2 = x^2 + x + 1
```
::::
:::

The coefficients of a Hermitian matrix in the Pauli family can be found by matching entries, as for the antisymmetric
matrices above. The exercise asks for the general formula and one numerical case, and shows that the coefficients come
out real.

::: {#exr-combination-pauli}
#### Hermitian matrices in the Pauli family

Show that the Hermitian matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b - ic \\ b + ic & d \end{pmatrix}$, with $a, b, c, d$ real, is $a_0
\mathbf I + a_1\sigma_1 + a_2\sigma_2 + a_3\sigma_3$ with real coefficients, and find them for $\mathbf H = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 + 2i
\\ 1 - 2i & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The combination $a_0 \mathbf I + a_1\sigma_1 + a_2\sigma_2 + a_3\sigma_3$ is $\begin{pmatrix} a_0 + a_3 & a_1 - i a_2 \\ a_1 +
i a_2 & a_0 - a_3 \end{pmatrix}$. Matching entries gives $a_0 = \tfrac12(a + d)$, $a_3 = \tfrac12(a - d)$, $a_1 = b$,
$a_2 = c$, all real. For $\mathbf H$: $a = 3$, $d = -1$, $b - ic = 1 + 2i$, so $(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3) = (1, 1, -2, 2)$.

## SageMath

Sage builds the combination with the coefficients found and compares it with $\mathbf H$.

```{.python .sage}
i = QQbar(I)
one = identity_matrix(QQbar, 2)
s1 = matrix(QQbar, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]); s2 = matrix(QQbar, [[0, -i], [i, 0]]); s3 = matrix(QQbar, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])
H = matrix(QQbar, [[3, 1 + 2 * i], [1 - 2 * i, -1]])
a = (H[0, 0] + H[1, 1]) / 2, H[0, 1].real(), -H[0, 1].imag(), (H[0, 0] - H[1, 1]) / 2
print("(a0, a1, a2, a3) =", a)
print("a0 1 + a1 s1 + a2 s2 + a3 s3 == H:", a[0] * one + a[1] * s1 + a[2] * s2 + a[3] * s3 == H)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(a0, a1, a2, a3) = (1, 1, -2, 2)
a0 1 + a1 s1 + a2 s2 + a3 s3 == H: True
```
::::
:::

For the oscillator the coefficients of a combination are fixed by initial conditions rather than by matching entries.
The exercise finds them, and rewrites a motion with a phase in the same two functions.

::: {#exr-combination-oscillator}
#### Coefficients from initial data

Find $A$ and $B$ such that $x(t) = A\cos\omega t + B\sin\omega t$ has $x(0) = x_0$ and $\dot x(0) = v_0$, and write
$3\cos(\omega t + \pi/3)$ as such a combination.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

At $t = 0$, $x(0) = A$ and $\dot x(0) = \omega B$, so $A = x_0$ and $B = v_0/\omega$. By the addition formula,
$3\cos(\omega t + \pi/3) = 3\cos\tfrac\pi3 \cos\omega t - 3\sin\tfrac\pi3 \sin\omega t = \tfrac32 \cos\omega t -
\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2} \sin\omega t$; its initial data are $x_0 = \tfrac32$ and $v_0 = -\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\omega$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the coefficients from the initial data of the phase-shifted motion and compares the two functions.

```{.python .sage}
t, w = var("t omega"); assume(w > 0)
x = 3 * cos(w * t + pi / 3)
A, B = x.subs(t=0), diff(x, t).subs(t=0) / w
print("A = x(0) =", A, "; B = v(0)/omega =", B)
print("x == A cos + B sin:", bool((x - A * cos(w * t) - B * sin(w * t)).expand_trig().simplify_full() == 0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A = x(0) = 3/2 ; B = v(0)/omega = -3/2*sqrt(3)
x == A cos + B sin: True
```
::::
:::

A change of the states one combines in is a change of the coefficients. The exercise rewrites the spin states of
@exm-combination-spin in the states of definite spin along the $x$-axis, with complex coefficients.

::: {#exr-combination-spin}
#### Spin states along another axis

With ${\pm x} = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}({\uparrow} \pm {\downarrow})$, write ${\uparrow}$, ${\downarrow}$ and $\tfrac15(3\,
{\uparrow} + 4i\,{\downarrow})$ as combinations of ${+x}$ and ${-x}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Adding and subtracting the two definitions gives ${+x} + {-x} = \sqrt2\,{\uparrow}$ and ${+x} - {-x} = \sqrt2\,
{\downarrow}$, so ${\uparrow} = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}({+x} + {-x})$ and ${\downarrow} = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}({+x} - {-x})$.
Substituting, $\tfrac15(3\,{\uparrow} + 4i\,{\downarrow}) = \tfrac{1}{5\sqrt2}\big((3 + 4i)\,{+x} + (3 - 4i)\,{-x}
\big)$.

## SageMath

Sage solves for the coefficients in $\mathbb{C}^2$ with the states as columns.

```{.python .sage}
i = QQbar(I); r = QQbar(2).sqrt()
up, dn = vector(QQbar, [1, 0]), vector(QQbar, [0, 1])
px, mx = (up + dn) / r, (up - dn) / r
X = matrix(QQbar, [px, mx]).transpose()
for name, s in [("up", up), ("down", dn), ("(3 up + 4i down)/5", (3 * up + 4 * i * dn) / 5)]:
    c = X.solve_right(s)
    print(name, ": coefficients of +x, -x times sqrt(2):", [(ci * r).radical_expression() for ci in c])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
up : coefficients of +x, -x times sqrt(2): [1, 1]
down : coefficients of +x, -x times sqrt(2): [1, -1]
(3 up + 4i down)/5 : coefficients of +x, -x times sqrt(2): [4/5*I + 3/5, -4/5*I + 3/5]
```
::::
:::

The last exercise shows that combinations of combinations are again combinations, and that their coefficients
multiply as matrices. This is the computation behind every change of generators in the rest of the chapter.

::: {#exr-combination-composition}
#### Combinations of combinations

Let $w_j = a^i{}_j v_i$ for $j = 1, \dots, m$ be combinations of $v_1, \dots, v_k$. Prove that every combination
$\mu^j w_j$ is a combination of the $v_i$, with coefficients $\lambda^i = a^i{}_j \mu^j$, the product of the matrix
$(a^i{}_j)$ with the column $\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the distributive rules of @def-vector-space, $\mu^j w_j = \mu^j (a^i{}_j v_i) = (a^i{}_j \mu^j) v_i$, where the
sums over $i$ and $j$ may be exchanged because addition is commutative and associative. The coefficient of $v_i$ is
$\lambda^i = \sum_j a^i{}_j \mu^j$, the $i$-th entry of the matrix product $a\mu$.

## SageMath

Check on three vectors $v_i$ of $\mathbb{Q}^3$, two combinations $w_j$ and the coefficients $\mu = (2, -1)$:

```{.python .sage}
v = [vector(QQ, [1, 2, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1]), vector(QQ, [3, 0, -1])]
a = matrix(QQ, [[1, 4], [-2, 0], [5, 1]])            # w_j = sum_i a[i, j] v_i
w = [sum(a[i, j] * v[i] for i in range(3)) for j in range(2)]
mu = vector(QQ, [2, -1])
lam = a * mu
print("mu^j w_j =", mu[0] * w[0] + mu[1] * w[1], "; (a mu)^i v_i =", sum(lam[i] * v[i] for i in range(3)), "; a mu =", lam)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
mu^j w_j = (25, -8, -13) ; (a mu)^i v_i = (25, -8, -13) ; a mu = (-2, -4, 9)
```
::::
:::
::::

### Spans

Taking all weighted sums of a family at once produces a set, and this set is itself a subspace, the smallest one
containing the family. The following definition gives it a name; the picture is a line or a plane through the origin
swept out by the vectors drawn in it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-span}
#### Span

The **span** of $v_1, \dots, v_k$ is the set of all their linear combinations. It is a subspace, the smallest one
containing them.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest spans are those of the zero vector and of the empty family. They anchor the conventions, and the span
of a single non-zero vector already shows the geometric picture of a line through the origin.

::: {#exm-span-zero}
#### Spans of no vector and of one vector

The span of the zero vector is $\{0\}$, and so, by convention, is the span of the empty family
[@lee2013introduction, App. B, p. 618]. The span of one vector $v \neq 0$ is the set of its multiples $\lambda v$, the
line through the origin in the direction of $v$.
:::

In the plane two vectors span either a line or everything, depending on whether they are aligned. The example shows
both outcomes on three small families.

::: {#exm-span-line}
#### Spans in the plane

In $\mathbb{R}^2$, the span of $(1, 2)$ is the line $y = 2x$. Adding $(2, 4) = 2\,(1, 2)$ does not change it. Adding
$(0, 1)$ instead gives all of $\mathbb{R}^2$, since $(x, y) = x\,(1, 2) + (y - 2x)\,(0, 1)$.
:::

Two vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$ that are not aligned sweep out a plane, which the figure draws. The example records
which plane the running vectors $v_1$ and $v_2$ generate and observes that adding their sum to the family changes
nothing, a first hint of the notion of dependence.

::: {#exm-span-plane}
#### A plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$

The span of $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$ and $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ is a plane through the origin, the plane $2x - y + z = 0$;
$v_3 = (1, 3, 1) = v_1 + v_2$ lies in it, so adding $v_3$ does not enlarge the span, while $(1, 1, 1)$ lies off it (@fig-span-plane).

![The plane spanned by $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$ and $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$, with $v_3 = v_1 + v_2$ in it and $(1, 1, 1)$ off it.
The dashed segment joins $(1, 1, 1)$ to the nearest point of the plane.](figures/span_plane.svg){#fig-span-plane width=60%}

{{< interactive span_plane 520 >}}
:::

Function spaces have spans too, and the polynomials are the first example. The span of the first few monomials is a
space of bounded degree, and the span of all of them still contains only polynomials.

::: {#exm-span-polynomials}
#### Polynomials

The span of $1, x, x^2$ is the space of polynomials of degree at most $2$. The span of the whole infinite family $1,
x, x^2, \dots$, the set of all finite combinations, is the space of all polynomials; it does not contain $e^x$
(@exm-combination-infinite).
:::

The matrix example of the previous section can now be rephrased: the whole space of antisymmetric $3 \times 3$
matrices is the span of three matrices. This is how such a space of matrices is usually presented, by a finite list of
generators whose weighted sums exhaust it.

::: {#exm-span-pauli}
#### Antisymmetric matrices

Every antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix is a linear combination $a L_1 + b L_2 + c L_3$ of the three generators
$L_a$ of @exm-combination-matrices, so the antisymmetric matrices are the span of $L_1, L_2, L_3$.
:::

For a spin $\tfrac12$ the same presentation uses the Pauli matrices. Their real span with the identity gives the
observables, and the real span of $i\sigma_a$ gives the anti-Hermitian matrices with zero diagonal sum.

::: {#exm-span-su2}
#### Pauli matrices and their real span

By @exr-combination-pauli the real span of $\mathbf I, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ is the space of Hermitian $2 \times 2$
matrices. The real span of $i\sigma_1, i\sigma_2, i\sigma_3$ is the space of anti-Hermitian matrices with $X_{11} +
X_{22} = 0$.
:::

For functions the span of finitely many modes is finite-dimensional, while the span of all of them is not. Both cases
are shown on the circle, and they prepare the count of modes carried out in the section on dimension.

::: {#exm-span-functions}
#### Trigonometric modes

The span of $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ in the functions on the circle is the two-dimensional space of first
modes $a\cos\varphi + b\sin\varphi$; the span of all $\cos n\varphi$, $\sin n\varphi$ is the
infinite-dimensional space of trigonometric polynomials.
:::

The solution space of a linear equation is usually described as a span. For the harmonic oscillator two different
families span it, one real and one complex.

::: {#exm-span-oscillator}
#### The oscillator's solutions

By @exm-combination-oscillator the solutions of $\ddot x + \omega^2 x = 0$ form the span of $\cos\omega t$ and
$\sin\omega t$. Over $\mathbb{C}$ the same space is the span of $e^{i\omega t}$ and $e^{-i\omega t}$.
:::

Spans in Minkowski space need not consist of vectors of the same kind as the generators. Two null vectors span a plane
that also contains timelike and spacelike vectors.

::: {#exm-span-minkowski}
#### A plane spanned by light rays

In Minkowski space with $\eta(v, v) = t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2$, the null vectors $n_\pm = (1, \pm1, 0, 0)$ span the
$(t, x)$-plane: $(t, x, 0, 0) = \tfrac12(t + x)\,n_+ + \tfrac12(t - x)\,n_-$. This plane contains the timelike vector
$\tfrac12(n_+ + n_-) = (1, 0, 0, 0)$ and the spacelike vector $\tfrac12(n_+ - n_-) = (0, 1, 0, 0)$.
:::

A span is always a subspace, but a set built from subspaces need not be. The last example shows that the union of two
lines is not a span, while the span of the union is a plane.

::: {#exm-span-union}
#### A union of lines is not a span

The union of the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a subspace (@exr-vs-subspace-check), so it is not
the span of anything. The span of the union is all of $\mathbb{R}^2$: it is the set of sums of a point on one axis and
a point on the other.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Deciding whether a vector lies in a span is again a linear system, now one that may have no solution at all. The
exercise asks for two such decisions and for the Cartesian equation of the plane, which provides a second,
coordinate-free way of answering the same question.

::: {#exr-span-membership}
#### Membership in a span

Decide whether $(2, 5, 1)$ and $(1, 1, 1)$ lie in the span of $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$ and $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$, and find
the equation of the plane they span.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(2, 5, 1) = 2 v_1 + 1 v_2$ lies in the span; $(1, 1, 1) = a v_1 + b v_2$ would need $a = 1$, $2a + b = 1$, $b = 1$,
which is contradictory. A combination $a v_1 + b v_2 = (a, 2a + b, b)$ has $x = a$, $z = b$ and $y = 2x + z$, so the
plane is $2x - y + z = 0$; conversely every solution $(x, 2x + z, z)$ of this equation is $x v_1 + z v_2$.

## SageMath

Sage tests membership and finds a normal vector $n$ of the plane as the kernel of the matrix with rows $v_1, v_2$.

```{.python .sage}
V = QQ ^ 3
v1, v2 = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1])
W = V.span([v1, v2])
for w in [vector(QQ, [2, 5, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 1, 1])]:
    print(w, "in span(v1, v2):", w in W, (" with coordinates " + str(W.coordinates(w))) if w in W else "")
n = matrix(QQ, [v1, v2]).right_kernel().basis()[0]
print("the plane span(v1, v2) is the solution set of n . x = 0 with n =", n, "; check n . v1 = n . v2 = 0:", n * v1 == 0 and n * v2 == 0)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(2, 5, 1) in span(v1, v2): True  with coordinates [2, 5]
(1, 1, 1) in span(v1, v2): False
the plane span(v1, v2) is the solution set of n . x = 0 with n = (1, -1/2, 1/2) ; check n . v1 = n . v2 = 0: True
```
::::
:::

A subspace given by an equation can be presented as a span in many ways. The exercise asks for a deliberately
redundant presentation, four distinct vectors spanning a plane [@axler2024linear, Exercise 2A.1].

::: {#exr-span-four-vectors}
#### Four vectors spanning a plane

Find four distinct vectors whose span is the plane $x + y + z = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A point of the plane is $(x, y, -x - y) = x\,(1, 0, -1) + y\,(0, 1, -1)$, so the plane is the span of $(1, 0, -1)$ and
$(0, 1, -1)$. Adding vectors of the plane does not enlarge a span that already contains them, so $(1, 0, -1)$, $(0, 1,
-1)$, $(1, -1, 0)$ and $(2, -1, -1)$, which all satisfy $x + y + z = 0$, also span the plane.

## SageMath

Sage compares the span of the four vectors with the kernel of the row $(1, 1, 1)$.

```{.python .sage}
fam = [vector(QQ, v) for v in [(1, 0, -1), (0, 1, -1), (1, -1, 0), (2, -1, -1)]]
P = matrix(QQ, [[1, 1, 1]]).right_kernel()
print("all in the plane:", all(v in P for v in fam), "; span of the four == plane:", (QQ^3).span(fam) == P)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
all in the plane: True ; span of the four == plane: True
```
::::
:::

The geometric vocabulary of lines and planes through the origin should be matched with the algebraic notion just
defined. The reader is asked to describe the span of one, two and three vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and to prove that a
dependent third vector leaves the span unchanged.

::: {#exr-span-line-plane}
#### Spans of one, two and three vectors

Describe the span of one non-zero vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$, of two vectors neither of which is a multiple of the
other, and of three vectors one of which is a combination of the other two.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

One vector spans the line through the origin in its direction. Two non-proportional vectors span the plane
through the origin containing both. If $v_3 = a v_1 + b v_2$, then $\lambda^1 v_1 + \lambda^2 v_2 + \lambda^3 v_3 =
(\lambda^1 + a\lambda^3) v_1 + (\lambda^2 + b\lambda^3) v_2$, so the span of the three is the same plane as the
span of the first two.

## SageMath

Check on $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$, $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ and $v_3 = 2v_1 - 3v_2$:

```{.python .sage}
V = QQ^3
v1, v2 = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1]); v3 = 2 * v1 - 3 * v2
print("span(v1) contains (2, 4, 0) and not v2:", vector(QQ, [2, 4, 0]) in V.span([v1]), v2 in V.span([v1]))
print("span(v1, v2, v3) == span(v1, v2):", V.span([v1, v2, v3]) == V.span([v1, v2]), "; == Q^3:", V.span([v1, v2, v3]) == V)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
span(v1) contains (2, 4, 0) and not v2: True False
span(v1, v2, v3) == span(v1, v2): True ; == Q^3: False
```
::::
:::

Two different families can generate the same subspace, and proving this means expressing each family in terms of the
other. The polynomial exercise practises this with the shifted powers $(x + 1)^k$ against the plain powers $x^k$, and
also exhibits a vector that lies outside a span.

::: {#exr-span-polynomials}
#### Spans of polynomials

Show that $(x + 1)^2$ lies in the span of $1, x, x^2$, that $x^3$ does not, and that the span of $1, x, x^2$ equals
the span of $1, x + 1, (x + 1)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(x + 1)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2$. A combination $a + bx + cx^2$ has degree at most $2$, so $x^3$ is not one. The three
functions $1, x + 1, (x + 1)^2$ are combinations of $1, x, x^2$, and conversely $x = (x + 1) - 1$ and $x^2 = (x +
1)^2 - 2(x + 1) + 1$, so each span contains the other's generators and the spans coincide.

## SageMath

Sage represents a polynomial of degree at most $3$ by its column of four coefficients and compares the spans in
$\mathbb{Q}^4$.

```{.python .sage}
R.<x> = QQ[]
col = lambda p: vector(QQ, p.padded_list(4))
V = QQ^4
S1 = V.span([col(R(1)), col(x), col(x^2)]); S2 = V.span([col(R(1)), col(x + 1), col((x + 1)^2)])
print("(x + 1)^2 in span(1, x, x^2):", col((x + 1)^2) in S1, "; x^3 in it:", col(x^3) in S1)
print("span(1, x, x^2) == span(1, x + 1, (x + 1)^2):", S1 == S2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(x + 1)^2 in span(1, x, x^2): True ; x^3 in it: False
span(1, x, x^2) == span(1, x + 1, (x + 1)^2): True
```
::::
:::

The definition claims two things about a span, that it is a subspace and that it is the smallest one containing the
generators. The exercise asks for both proofs [@scott2023problems, Problem 2.6].

::: {#exr-span-is-subspace}
#### The span is the smallest subspace

Prove that the span of $v_1, \dots, v_k$ is a subspace of $V$, and that every subspace containing $v_1, \dots, v_k$
contains their span.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The span contains $0 = 0 v_1 + \dots + 0 v_k$. If $a = \alpha^i v_i$ and $b = \beta^i v_i$, then $a + b = (\alpha^i +
\beta^i) v_i$ and $\lambda a = (\lambda\alpha^i) v_i$ are again combinations, so the span is closed under both
operations. If a subspace $U$ contains every $v_i$, it contains every $\lambda^i v_i$ by closure under scaling, and
then every sum $\lambda^1 v_1 + \dots + \lambda^k v_k$ by closure under addition, applied $k - 1$ times. So the span
lies in $U$.

## SageMath

Check on $v_1 = (1, 2, 0)$, $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$: a sum and a multiple of two combinations stay in the span, and the
span lies in the subspace $2x - y + z = 0$ that contains both vectors.

```{.python .sage}
V = QQ^3
v1, v2 = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1])
W = V.span([v1, v2])
a, b = 3 * v1 - v2, -v1 + 4 * v2
print("a + b and -5/2 a in span:", a + b in W, -5/2 * a in W)
U = matrix(QQ, [[2, -1, 1]]).right_kernel()
print("v1, v2 in U:", v1 in U and v2 in U, "; span(v1, v2) is a subspace of U:", W.is_subspace(U))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
a + b and -5/2 a in span: True True
v1, v2 in U: True ; span(v1, v2) is a subspace of U: True
```
::::
:::

Replacing the generators by sums or differences of them does not change their span, provided the replacement can be
undone. The exercise proves this for partial sums and for successive differences [@axler2024linear, Exercises 2A.2
and 2A.3].

::: {#exr-span-partial-sums}
#### Partial sums and differences

Let $w_k = v_1 + \dots + v_k$ for $k = 1, \dots, m$. Show that $v_1, \dots, v_m$ and $w_1, \dots, w_m$ have the same
span. Show also that $v_1 - v_2$, $v_2 - v_3$, $v_3 - v_4$, $v_4$ have the same span as $v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Each $w_k$ is a combination of the $v_i$, and conversely $v_1 = w_1$ and $v_k = w_k - w_{k - 1}$ for $k \geq 2$. So
each family lies in the span of the other, and by @exr-span-is-subspace each span contains the other: they are equal.
For the second family, the new vectors are combinations of the old, and conversely $v_4 = v_4$, $v_3 = (v_3 - v_4) +
v_4$, $v_2 = (v_2 - v_3) + v_3$ and $v_1 = (v_1 - v_2) + v_2$, each a combination of the new vectors by the previous
step.

## SageMath

Check on four vectors of $\mathbb{Q}^5$:

```{.python .sage}
V = QQ^5
v = [vector(QQ, r) for r in [(1, 0, 2, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1, 0, 0), (3, 0, 0, 1, 1), (1, 1, 1, 1, 1)]]
w = [sum(v[:k + 1]) for k in range(4)]
d = [v[0] - v[1], v[1] - v[2], v[2] - v[3], v[3]]
print("span(w) == span(v):", V.span(w) == V.span(v), "; span(differences) == span(v):", V.span(d) == V.span(v))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
span(w) == span(v): True ; span(differences) == span(v): True
```
::::
:::

The real span of $i\sigma_1, i\sigma_2, i\sigma_3$ was described in @exm-span-su2. The exercise proves the description
by matching the entries of a general anti-Hermitian matrix with zero diagonal sum.

::: {#exr-span-su2}
#### The span of $i\sigma_1, i\sigma_2, i\sigma_3$

Show that the real span of $i\sigma_1, i\sigma_2, i\sigma_3$ is the set of anti-Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices $\mathbf X$
($\mathbf X^\dagger = -\mathbf X$) with $X_{11} + X_{22} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The combination $a\,i\sigma_1 + b\,i\sigma_2 + c\,i\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} ic & b + ia \\ -b + ia & -ic
\end{pmatrix}$ is anti-Hermitian with zero diagonal sum. Conversely, $\mathbf X^\dagger = -\mathbf X$ forces the diagonal entries to be
imaginary and $X_{21} = -X_{12}^*$; with $X_{11} + X_{22} = 0$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} i\alpha & \beta \\
-\beta^* & -i\alpha \end{pmatrix}$ with $\alpha$ real. Writing $\beta = b + ia$ and $c = \alpha$ gives $\mathbf X = a\,i\sigma_1
+ b\,i\sigma_2 + c\,i\sigma_3$.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbf X = \begin{pmatrix} 2i & 3 - i \\ -3 - i & -2i \end{pmatrix}$, whose coefficients should be $(a, b, c) =
(-1, 3, 2)$:

```{.python .sage}
i = QQbar(I)
s = [matrix(QQbar, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]), matrix(QQbar, [[0, -i], [i, 0]]), matrix(QQbar, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])]
X = matrix(QQbar, [[2 * i, 3 - i], [-3 - i, -2 * i]])
print("X anti-Hermitian:", X.conjugate_transpose() == -X, "; X_11 + X_22 =", X[0, 0] + X[1, 1])
a, b, c = X[0, 1].imag(), X[0, 1].real(), X[0, 0].imag()
print("(a, b, c) =", (a, b, c), "; a i s1 + b i s2 + c i s3 == X:", a * i * s[0] + b * i * s[1] + c * i * s[2] == X)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
X anti-Hermitian: True ; X_11 + X_22 = 0
(a, b, c) = (-1, 3, 2) ; a i s1 + b i s2 + c i s3 == X: True
```
::::
:::

Two families that are combinations of each other have the same span. The exercise applies this to the real and the
complex exponential solutions of the oscillator, as claimed in @exm-span-oscillator.

::: {#exr-span-oscillator}
#### Real and complex solutions

Show that, over $\mathbb{C}$, the span of $\cos\omega t$ and $\sin\omega t$ equals the span of $e^{i\omega t}$ and
$e^{-i\omega t}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By Euler's formula $e^{\pm i\omega t} = \cos\omega t \pm i\sin\omega t$, so the exponentials lie in the span of the
cosine and the sine. Conversely $\cos\omega t = \tfrac12(e^{i\omega t} + e^{-i\omega t})$ and $\sin\omega t =
\tfrac1{2i}(e^{i\omega t} - e^{-i\omega t})$. Each family lies in the span of the other, so by @exr-span-is-subspace
the two spans are equal.

## SageMath

Sage checks the four expressions symbolically.

```{.python .sage}
t, w = var("t omega")
ep, em = exp(I * w * t), exp(-I * w * t)
diffs = [ep - (cos(w * t) + I * sin(w * t)), em - (cos(w * t) - I * sin(w * t)),
         cos(w * t) - (ep + em) / 2, sin(w * t) - (ep - em) / (2 * I)]
print("differences after rewriting in exponentials:", [d.exponentialize().simplify_full() for d in diffs])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
differences after rewriting in exponentials: [0, 0, 0, 0]
```
::::
:::

The span of a union of two subspaces is the natural replacement for the union, which is not a subspace in general.
The exercise identifies it with the set of sums [@lee2013introduction, App. B, p. 621], and combines it with
@exr-vs-intersection-union.

::: {#exr-span-union-sum}
#### The span of a union is a sum

For subspaces $U, W$ of $V$ let $U + W = \{u + w : u \in U, w \in W\}$. Show that $U + W$ is a subspace, that it is the
span of the vectors of $U \cup W$ (the set of all combinations of finitely many of them), and find $U + W$ and $U \cup
W$ for the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$0 = 0 + 0 \in U + W$, $(u + w) + (u' + w') = (u + u') + (w + w')$ and $\lambda(u + w) = \lambda u + \lambda w$, so
$U + W$ is a subspace. It contains $U$ and $W$ (take $w = 0$ or $u = 0$), hence every combination of vectors of $U \cup
W$. Conversely a combination of vectors of $U \cup W$ splits into the terms from $U$, which add to some $u \in U$, and
those from $W$, which add to some $w \in W$; so it lies in $U + W$. For the two axes, $U + W = \{(x, 0) + (0, y)\} =
\mathbb{R}^2$, while $U \cup W$ is the cross formed by the axes, which is not a subspace.

## SageMath

Sage forms the sum of the two axes as subspaces of $\mathbb{Q}^2$ and tests a point of the sum against the union.

```{.python .sage}
V = QQ^2
U, W = V.span([vector(QQ, [1, 0])]), V.span([vector(QQ, [0, 1])])
p = vector(QQ, [3, -2])
print("U + W == Q^2:", U + W == V, "; (3, -2) in U + W:", p in U + W, "; in U or in W:", p in U or p in W)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
U + W == Q^2: True ; (3, -2) in U + W: True ; in U or in W: False
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines spans with the Minkowski form of @exm-vs-minkowski. It asks which vectors of a plane
spanned by two light rays are timelike, spacelike or null.

::: {#exr-span-minkowski}
#### The plane of two light rays

Let $n_1 = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ and $n_2 = (1, 0, 1, 0)$ in Minkowski space, with $\eta(v, v) = t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2$.
Compute $\eta(v, v)$ for $v = a n_1 + b n_2$ and decide which vectors of the span are null, timelike and spacelike.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$v = (a + b, a, b, 0)$, so $\eta(v, v) = (a + b)^2 - a^2 - b^2 = 2ab$. The null vectors of the span are those with $ab
= 0$, the two lines through $n_1$ and $n_2$. The timelike ones have $ab > 0$, for example $n_1 + n_2 = (2, 1, 1, 0)$
with $\eta = 2$, and the spacelike ones have $ab < 0$, for example $n_1 - n_2 = (0, 1, -1, 0)$ with $\eta = -2$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\eta(v, v)$ with $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ for symbolic $a, b$ and two cases.

```{.python .sage}
a, b = var("a b")
eta = diagonal_matrix([1, -1, -1, -1])
n1, n2 = vector([1, 1, 0, 0]), vector([1, 0, 1, 0])
q = lambda v: v * eta * v
print("eta(v, v) =", q(a * n1 + b * n2).expand(), "; eta(n1 + n2) =", q(n1 + n2), "; eta(n1 - n2) =", q(n1 - n2))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
eta(v, v) = 2*a*b ; eta(n1 + n2) = 2 ; eta(n1 - n2) = -2
```
::::
:::
::::

### Linear independence

A span can be generated by many families, some of them wasteful. The notion defined next singles out the economical
ones, those in which no vector is a weighted sum of the others, through a single condition on the combinations that
vanish.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-linear-independence}
#### Linear independence

Vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ are **linearly independent** if the only linear combination equal to zero is the one
with all coefficients zero: $\lambda^i v_i = 0$ implies $\lambda^1 = \dots = \lambda^k = 0$. Otherwise they are
**linearly dependent**, and one of them is a combination of the others.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The quickest dependences are the trivial ones, and they are worth recognising on sight. A family containing the zero
vector, or the same vector twice, always has a vanishing combination with a non-zero coefficient.

::: {#exm-independent-zero}
#### Zero and repeated vectors

Any family containing $0$ is dependent, since $1 \cdot 0 = 0$ is a vanishing combination with a non-zero
coefficient. A family that lists the same vector twice, $(v, v)$, is dependent, since $v - v = 0$
[@lee2013introduction, App. B, p. 618]. In particular a single vector is independent exactly when it is not $0$.
:::

In the plane, the independence of two vectors is a pair of equations in two unknown coefficients. The next example
checks it for the pair $f_1, f_2$ on which the figure of the next section is built, and contrasts it with a pair of
proportional vectors.

::: {#exm-independent-basis-change}
#### Two vectors in the plane

$f_1 = (2, 1)$ and $f_2 = (1, 2)$ are independent, since $\lambda f_1 + \mu f_2 = (2\lambda + \mu, \lambda + 2\mu)$
vanishes only for $\lambda = \mu = 0$: from $2\lambda + \mu = 0$ and $\lambda + 2\mu = 0$,
$3\lambda = 2(2\lambda + \mu) - (\lambda + 2\mu) = 0$ and likewise $3\mu = 0$. The vectors $(2, 1)$ and $(4, 2)$ are
dependent, since $2 \cdot (2, 1) - (4, 2) = 0$.
:::

The two triples of running vectors of three-dimensional space illustrate both cases. The first triple admits no
vanishing combination, while the second satisfies $v_1 + v_2 - v_3 = 0$, the very relation that explained why the
third vector added nothing to the span.

::: {#exm-independent-r3}
#### In $\mathbb{R}^3$

$(1, 2, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(0, 0, 1)$ are independent; $(1, 2, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 3, 1)$ are dependent, with
the relation $v_1 + v_2 - v_3 = 0$.
:::

Polynomials give the first infinite independent family. The argument is that a non-zero polynomial has only finitely
many roots, so it cannot vanish at every point.

::: {#exm-independent-monomials}
#### Monomials

The monomials $1, x, \dots, x^n$ are independent functions on $\mathbb{R}$: a vanishing combination $\lambda^0 +
\lambda^1 x + \dots + \lambda^n x^n$ is a polynomial with infinitely many roots, hence the zero polynomial, so all its
coefficients vanish. Since $n$ is arbitrary, no finite family spans all polynomials.
:::

For functions a vanishing combination must vanish at every point, so evaluating at a few well-chosen points is the
standard route to independence. Dependence, by contrast, is a trigonometric identity, and $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$ is the
classic one.

::: {#exm-independent-functions}
#### Functions

$1$, $\cos\varphi$, $\sin\varphi$ are independent functions on the circle (evaluate a vanishing combination at
$\varphi = 0, \pi/2, \pi$); $\cos^2\varphi$, $\sin^2\varphi$ and $1$ are dependent, since $\cos^2 + \sin^2 - 1 = 0$.
:::

Exponentials with different rates are the solutions of linear equations with constant coefficients, and their
independence is what makes the general solution well defined. The example states the fact for three rates.

::: {#exm-independent-exponentials}
#### Exponentials

$e^{x}$, $e^{2x}$, $e^{3x}$ are independent: dividing a vanishing combination $a e^x + b e^{2x} + c e^{3x}$ by
$e^{3x}$ and letting $x \to \infty$ gives $c = 0$, and then $b = 0$ and $a = 0$ in the same way. In general,
exponentials with distinct rates are independent.
:::

The Pauli matrices and the identity are independent, which is why the coefficients of @exr-combination-pauli were
unique. The example records the fact for spin $\tfrac12$.

::: {#exm-independent-pauli}
#### Pauli matrices

$\mathbf I, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ are independent in the complex $2 \times 2$ matrices: $a_0 \mathbf I + a_1\sigma_1 +
a_2\sigma_2 + a_3\sigma_3$ has diagonal $a_0 \pm a_3$ and off-diagonal entries $a_1 \mp i a_2$, which all vanish only
when every $a_\mu = 0$.
:::

The oscillator's two basic motions are independent, and a third motion is always a combination of them. The example
shows both facts with a phase-shifted cosine.

::: {#exm-independent-oscillator}
#### Oscillator motions

$\cos\omega t$ and $\sin\omega t$ are independent: $a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t = 0$ at $t = 0$ gives $a = 0$, and at
$\omega t = \pi/2$ gives $b = 0$. The three motions $\cos\omega t$, $\sin\omega t$, $\cos(\omega t + \varphi_0)$ are
dependent, by the relation $\cos(\omega t + \varphi_0) - \cos\varphi_0\cos\omega t + \sin\varphi_0\sin\omega t = 0$.
:::

Three vectors can fail to be independent although no two of them are proportional. The example shows that
independence is a property of the whole family, not of its pairs.

::: {#exm-independent-pairwise}
#### Pairwise independent but dependent

In $\mathbb{R}^2$, any two of $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 1)$ are independent, since none is a multiple of another. The
three together are dependent: $(1, 0) + (0, 1) - (1, 1) = 0$.
:::

Independence also depends on the scalars allowed. The last example gives a pair of complex columns that is dependent
over $\mathbb{C}$ and independent over $\mathbb{R}$.

::: {#exm-independent-field}
#### Independence depends on the scalars

In $\mathbb{C}^2$, $u = (1, i)$ and $w = (i, -1)$ satisfy $w = i u$, so they are dependent over $\mathbb{C}$. Over
$\mathbb{R}$ they are independent: $a u + b w = (a + ib, ia - b)$ with real $a, b$ vanishes only if $a = b = 0$.
:::
::::
