z = 0$, so $\mathbf v = (-z, -z, z) = -z(1, 1, -1)$: the kernel is the line. A $1 \times 3$ matrix maps to $\mathbb{R}$, so its
rank is at most $1$ and, by rank-nullity, its nullity at least $3 - 1 = 2$; its kernel is never a line. A $2 \times 3$
matrix has rank at most $2$ and nullity at least $1$, so its kernel is never $\{0\}$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the kernel of the chosen matrix, and the smallest nullity of random rows of the two shapes.

```{.python .sage}
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]])
print("ker B:", B.right_kernel().basis(), "; (1, 1, -1) in it:", vector(QQ, [1, 1, -1]) in B.right_kernel())
set_random_seed(1)
print("least nullity of 1 x 3 matrices:", min(random_matrix(QQ, 1, 3).right_nullity() for _ in range(20)),
      "; of 2 x 3 matrices:", min(random_matrix(QQ, 2, 3).right_nullity() for _ in range(20)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
ker B: [
(1, 1, -1)
] ; (1, 1, -1) in it: True
least nullity of 1 x 3 matrices: 2 ; of 2 x 3 matrices: 1
```
::::
:::

The last exercise uses the reading of @exm-kernel-reactions on real particles. Three conserved quantities, electric
charge, baryon number and lepton number, leave a kernel of dimension one among four particles, and it is beta decay.

::: {#exr-kernel-beta-decay}
#### Beta decay from a kernel

The neutron $n$, proton $p$, electron $e^-$ and electron antineutrino $\bar\nu_e$ have (electric charge, baryon number,
lepton number) equal to $(0, 1, 0)$, $(1, 1, 0)$, $(-1, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 0, -1)$. Let $\mathbf Q$ be the $3 \times 4$ matrix
with these columns. Find $\ker \mathbf Q$, show that it is spanned by the reaction $n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu_e$, and show that
$n \to p + e^-$ violates a conservation law.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A reaction $\mathbf r = (r^n, r^p, r^e, r^\nu)$, counted with sign as in @exm-kernel-reactions, conserves the three charges when
$\mathbf Q \mathbf r = \mathbf 0$: $r^p - r^e = 0$, $r^n + r^p = 0$ and $r^e - r^\nu = 0$. Hence $r^p = r^e = r^\nu = -r^n$ and $\ker \mathbf Q$ is the
line through $(-1, 1, 1, 1)$, the same line as through $(1, -1, -1, -1)$: one neutron consumed, one proton, electron
and antineutrino produced. The rank of $\mathbf Q$ is
$4 - 1 = 3$, so the three conservation laws are independent. For $n \to p + e^-$, $\mathbf r = (-1, 1, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf Q \mathbf r = (0, 0,
1)$: the lepton number is not conserved, which is why the antineutrino has to be there.

## SageMath

Sage computes the kernel and the charges created by the reaction without the antineutrino.

```{.python .sage}
Q = column_matrix(QQ, [(0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0), (-1, 0, 1), (0, 0, -1)])   # columns n, p, e-, anti-nu_e
print("rank Q =", Q.rank(), "; ker Q spanned by", Q.right_kernel().basis())
print("Q (-1, 1, 1, 0) =", Q * vector(QQ, [-1, 1, 1, 0]), " (charge, baryon, lepton number created)")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rank Q = 3 ; ker Q spanned by [
(1, -1, -1, -1)
]
Q (-1, 1, 1, 0) = (0, 0, 1)  (charge, baryon, lepton number created)
```
::::
:::
::::

The dual-basis facts of this section can now be collected: the Kronecker table for the standard basis, and for $f$
the matrix identity that makes its dual basis correct. The proposition states both, with one evaluation of each.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-dual-basis}
#### Dual basis evaluations

$e^2(5, 7, 9) = 7$ and $e^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j$ for the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$; the dual basis of $f$ is
the pair of rows of $\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, which multiplies the matrix of
columns $f_1, f_2$ to the identity and reads off the coordinates $(2, 1)$ of $(5, 4)$.
:::
::::


:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the standard basis the table of values $e^i(e_j)$ has nine entries, one for each pair of indices. The example
lists them and places the single evaluation $e^2(5, 7, 9) = 7$ among them.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-table}
#### The Kronecker table

The nine values $e^i(e_j)$ form the identity matrix: $e^i(e_j) = 1$ for the three pairs with $i = j$ and $0$ for the
six others. The evaluation $e^2(5, 7, 9) = 7$ is the second coordinate functional applied to $5 e_1 + 7 e_2 + 9
e_3$, which by linearity is $5 \cdot 0 + 7 \cdot 1 + 9 \cdot 0$.
:::

The other two standard dual vectors, and combinations of them, are evaluated in the same way. The example shows that a
combination of dual basis vectors returns the same combination of coordinates.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-other-values}
#### Other standard dual vectors

On $v = (5, 7, 9)$, $e^1(v) = 5$ and $e^3(v) = 9$. The covector $e^1 + e^2 + e^3$, the row $(1, 1, 1)$, returns the sum
of the coordinates, $21$, and $e^3 - e^1$ returns $4$: a covector with components $\alpha_i$ in the dual basis gives
$\alpha_i v^i$ (@def-dual-basis).
:::

Behind the dual basis of $f$ stands a $2 \times 2$ matrix product. The example performs it and reads the four entries
as the four values $f^i(f_j)$.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-f-product}
#### The product behind the dual basis

$\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac13
\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf I$: the diagonal entries are $f^1(f_1) = f^2(f_2) = 1$ and the
off-diagonal ones $f^1(f_2) = f^2(f_1) = 0$.
:::

Applying the two dual rows to $(5, 4)$ gives the coordinates of @prp-coordinates-f a second time. The example does the
arithmetic and notes that no system had to be solved.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-coordinates}
#### Coordinates as dual basis values

The two rows applied to $(5, 4)$ give $\tfrac13(10 - 4) = 2$ and $\tfrac13(-5 + 8) = 1$, the
coordinates of @prp-coordinates-f, obtained now without solving a system.
:::

The two dual bases of the plane, the standard one and the one of $f$, are bases of the same space $(\mathbb{R}^2)^*$,
so each can be expanded in the other. The example expands $e^1, e^2$ in $f^1, f^2$ with the rule $\alpha = \alpha(f_j)
f^j$.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-standard-in-f}
#### The standard dual basis in terms of $f^1, f^2$

$e^1(f_1) = 2$ and $e^1(f_2) = 1$, so $e^1 = 2f^1 + f^2$; likewise $e^2 = f^1 + 2f^2$. Indeed $2 \cdot \tfrac13(2, -1) +
\tfrac13(-1, 2) = (1, 0)$. The coefficients are the entries of the matrix with columns $f_1, f_2$, read along its rows.
:::

The covector of @fig-level-sets has components in either dual basis, and the pairing with a vector does not depend on
which basis is used. The example checks this on $(5, 4)$, in the component form $\alpha_i v^i$ of @carroll1997 [Ch. 1].

::: {#exm-dualbasis-level-functional}
#### One covector, two sets of components

The covector $\alpha = 2x + y$ has components $(2, 1)$ in $e^1, e^2$ and $\alpha(f_1) = 5$, $\alpha(f_2) = 4$ in $f^1,
f^2$, so $\alpha = 5f^1 + 4f^2$. The vector $(5, 4)$ has components $(5, 4)$ and $(2, 1)$. Both pairings give the same
number: $2 \cdot 5 + 1 \cdot 4 = 14 = 5 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 1$.
:::

The normal modes of two coupled masses form a basis of the plane, and its dual basis consists of the functionals that
extract the mode amplitudes. The example applies them to the displacement $(5, 4)$ of @exm-coords-normal-modes.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-normal-modes}
#### Mode amplitudes as dual basis values

For the modes $m_1 = (1, 1)$, $m_2 = (1, -1)$ the dual basis is $m^1 = \tfrac12(1, 1)$, $m^2 = \tfrac12(1, -1)$: the
average displacement and half the stretch. They give $m^1(5, 4) = \tfrac92$ and $m^2(5, 4) = \tfrac12$, the mode
coordinates found before. Read in the plane $(t, x)$, the same two functionals $\tfrac12(t \pm x)$ are the light-cone
coordinates of @exm-coords-light-cone.
:::

A crystal is built on a lattice of basis vectors, and diffraction is described by its dual basis, the reciprocal
lattice. The example takes the basis $f$ as the lattice of a two-dimensional crystal (standard material, not from the
sources of this chapter).

::: {#exm-dualbasis-reciprocal-lattice}
#### The reciprocal lattice

A two-dimensional crystal with atoms at $a f_1 + b f_2$, $a, b$ integers, has the reciprocal lattice spanned by $2\pi
f^1$ and $2\pi f^2$. A plane wave $e^{i\kappa(x)}$ with a covector $\kappa$ takes the same value at all atoms exactly when
$\kappa(f_1)$ and $\kappa(f_2)$ are multiples of $2\pi$, that is, when $\kappa = 2\pi(h f^1 + k f^2)$ with integers $h,
k$; the dual basis turns the condition into integer components.
:::

A dual basis vector is not the basis vector written as a row. The example compares $f^1$ with the row $(2, 1)$ that
looks like $f_1$, and shows where the naive guess fails.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-not-transpose}
#### Not the transpose

$f_1 = (2, 1)$, but $f^1 = \tfrac13(2, -1)$. The row $(2, 1)$ gives $5$ on $f_1$ and $4$ on $f_2$, not $1$ and $0$: it is
the covector $\alpha$ of @exm-dualbasis-level-functional. For the standard basis the dual vectors are the transposed
basis vectors, which is why the difference goes unnoticed until the basis is skewed.
:::

The proposition needs a basis. The last example takes two proportional vectors, as in @exm-coords-degenerate, and
shows that no dual basis exists for them.

::: {#exm-dualbasis-degenerate}
#### Without a basis

For $g_1 = (2, 1)$ and $g_2 = (4, 2) = 2g_1$, a functional with $g^1(g_1) = 1$ has $g^1(g_2) = 2g^1(g_1) = 2 \neq 0$, so
no $g^1$ satisfies the Kronecker conditions. In matrix form, the matrix with columns $g_1, g_2$ has proportional
columns and no inverse whose rows could serve as $g^1, g^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise evaluates the standard dual basis and combinations of it on two vectors. It is a direct check of the
first half of the proposition and of the linearity of the dual basis vectors.

::: {#exr-dualbasis-standard-values}
#### Evaluating the standard dual basis

Compute $e^1$, $e^3$ and $e^1 - 2e^3$ on $(5, 7, 9)$ and on $(1, -1, 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$e^i$ returns the $i$-th entry, so on $(5, 7, 9)$ the values are $5$, $9$ and $5 - 18 = -13$, and on $(1, -1, 2)$ they
are $1$, $2$ and $1 - 4 = -3$. The covector $e^1 - 2e^3$ is the row $(1, 0, -2)$.

## SageMath

Sage writes the dual basis as the rows of the identity matrix and applies them.

```{.python .sage}
e = identity_matrix(QQ, 3).rows()
for v in [vector(QQ, [5, 7, 9]), vector(QQ, [1, -1, 2])]:
    print(v, ": e^1 =", e[0] * v, ", e^3 =", e[2] * v, ", e^1 - 2 e^3 =", (e[0] - 2 * e[2]) * v)
print("e^1 - 2 e^3 as a row:", e[0] - 2 * e[2])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(5, 7, 9) : e^1 = 5 , e^3 = 9 , e^1 - 2 e^3 = -13
(1, -1, 2) : e^1 = 1 , e^3 = 2 , e^1 - 2 e^3 = -3
e^1 - 2 e^3 as a row: (1, 0, -2)
```
::::
:::

The four entries of the identity $\mathbf F^{-1} \mathbf F = \mathbf I$ are each a rational computation. The exercise asks the reader to carry
them out by hand, one for each pair of a dual vector and a basis vector.

::: {#exr-dual-f-check}
#### Checking the dual basis by hand

Verify entry by entry that the rows $f^1, f^2$ of @exm-dual-f satisfy $f^i(f_j) = \delta^i_j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$f^1(f_1) = \tfrac13(4 - 1) = 1$, $f^1(f_2) = \tfrac13(2 - 2) = 0$, $f^2(f_1) = \tfrac13(-2 + 2) = 0$, $f^2(f_2) =
\tfrac13(-1 + 4) = 1$. These are the four entries of the product $\mathbf F^{-1} \mathbf F = \mathbf I$ of @exm-dualbasis-f-product.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the four pairings.

```{.python .sage}
f = [vector(QQ, [2, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 2])]
d = [vector(QQ, [2, -1]) / 3, vector(QQ, [-1, 2]) / 3]
print([[d[i] * f[j] for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[[1, 0], [0, 1]]
```
::::
:::

The dual basis of $f$ can be applied to any vector of the plane. The exercise asks for the coordinates of two vectors
already treated by linear systems and compares the two methods.

::: {#exr-dual-f-apply}
#### Applying the dual basis

Use the dual basis of $f$ to find the coordinates of $(1, 5)$ and of $(-1, 1)$, and compare with
@exr-coords-f-other.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$f^1(1, 5) = \tfrac13(2 - 5) = -1$, $f^2(1, 5) = \tfrac13(-1 + 10) = 3$; $f^1(-1, 1) = \tfrac13(-2 - 1) = -1$,
$f^2(-1, 1) = \tfrac13(1 + 2) = 1$. Indeed $-f_1 + 3f_2 = (1, 5)$ and $-f_1 + f_2 = (-1, 1)$. These agree with the
solutions of the linear systems: the dual basis is the inverse matrix applied row by row, so each coordinate costs one
row-times-column product.

## SageMath

Sage applies the inverse matrix and checks the expansions.

```{.python .sage}
F = column_matrix(QQ, [(2, 1), (1, 2)])
for v in [vector(QQ, [1, 5]), vector(QQ, [-1, 1])]:
    c = F.inverse() * v
    print(v, ": coordinates", c, "; c^1 f_1 + c^2 f_2 =", F * c, "; solve_right gives", F.solve_right(v))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(1, 5) : coordinates (-1, 3) ; c^1 f_1 + c^2 f_2 = (1, 5) ; solve_right gives (-1, 3)
(-1, 1) : coordinates (-1, 1) ; c^1 f_1 + c^2 f_2 = (-1, 1) ; solve_right gives (-1, 1)
```
::::
:::

A covector is expanded in a dual basis by evaluating it on the basis vectors. The exercise does this for two covectors
on the plane and checks the expansion on the vector $(5, 4)$ of the proposition.

::: {#exr-dualbasis-expand-functional}
#### Expanding covectors in $f^1, f^2$

Write $\beta = x - y$ and $\gamma = x + y$ in the dual basis $f^1, f^2$, and check both expansions on $(5, 4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @def-dual-basis the components are the values on $f_1, f_2$: $\beta(f_1) = 1$, $\beta(f_2) = -1$, so $\beta = f^1 -
f^2$; $\gamma(f_1) = \gamma(f_2) = 3$, so $\gamma = 3f^1 + 3f^2$. On $(5, 4)$, whose $f$-coordinates are $(2, 1)$:
$\beta(5, 4) = 1 = 1 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1$ and $\gamma(5, 4) = 9 = 3 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 1$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the components as values on $f_1, f_2$ and recombines the dual rows.

```{.python .sage}
f = [vector(QQ, [2, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 2])]
d = [vector(QQ, [2, -1]) / 3, vector(QQ, [-1, 2]) / 3]
v = vector(QQ, [5, 4])
for name, a in [("beta", vector(QQ, [1, -1])), ("gamma", vector(QQ, [1, 1]))]:
    comp = [a * fj for fj in f]
    print(name, ": components", comp, "; recombined row", comp[0] * d[0] + comp[1] * d[1], "; value on (5, 4):", a * v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
beta : components [1, -1] ; recombined row (1, -1) ; value on (5, 4): 1
gamma : components [3, 3] ; recombined row (1, 1) ; value on (5, 4): 9
```
::::
:::

@exm-dualbasis-standard-in-f expanded $e^1, e^2$ in the dual basis of $f$. The exercise proves the general rule behind
it, which follows from the expansion of a covector in a dual basis [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6].

::: {#exr-dualbasis-standard-in-f}
#### The standard dual basis in any dual basis

Let $f_1, \dots, f_n$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbf F$ the matrix with columns $f_j$. Prove that $e^i = F^i{}_j
f^j$, and check it for the basis $f$ of the plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Every covector expands as $\alpha = \alpha(f_j) f^j$ (@def-dual-basis): both sides take the value $\alpha(f_k)$ on
$f_k$, since $f^j(f_k) = \delta^j_k$, and a linear functional is determined by its values on a basis. For $\alpha =
e^i$, $e^i(f_j)$ is the $i$-th entry of $f_j$, which is $F^i{}_j$. So $e^i = F^i{}_j f^j$. For the basis $f$, $\mathbf F =
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, so $e^1 = 2f^1 + f^2$ and $e^2 = f^1 + 2f^2$.

## SageMath

Check on the basis $f$: the rows $F^i{}_j f^j$ are compared with the rows of the identity.

```{.python .sage}
F = column_matrix(QQ, [(2, 1), (1, 2)])
d = F.inverse().rows()                                   # f^1, f^2
print([sum(F[i, j] * d[j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)], "== e^1, e^2:",
      [sum(F[i, j] * d[j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)] == identity_matrix(QQ, 2).rows())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
[(1, 0), (0, 1)] == e^1, e^2: True
```
::::
:::

Coordinates depend on the order and the length of the basis vectors, and so does the dual basis. The exercise finds the
dual bases of the reordered and rescaled bases of @exm-coords-swapped-scaled and uses them to recover the coordinates
found there.

::: {#exr-dualbasis-rescaled}
#### Reordering and rescaling the dual basis

Find the dual bases of $(2f_1, f_2)$ and of $(f_2, f_1)$, and the coordinates of $(5, 4)$ in both bases.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\tfrac12 f^1$ and $f^2$ satisfy $\tfrac12 f^1(2f_1) = 1$, $\tfrac12 f^1(f_2) = 0$, $f^2(2f_1) = 0$, $f^2(f_2) = 1$, so
by uniqueness of the dual basis they are the dual basis of $(2f_1, f_2)$: doubling a basis vector halves its dual
vector. For $(f_2, f_1)$ the dual basis is $(f^2, f^1)$, the same covectors in the other order. On $(5, 4)$:
$(\tfrac12 \cdot 2, 1) = (1, 1)$ and $(f^2, f^1)(5, 4) = (1, 2)$, as in @exm-coords-swapped-scaled.

## SageMath

Sage inverts the two basis matrices and applies the rows to $(5, 4)$.

```{.python .sage}
f1, f2, v = vector(QQ, [2, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 2]), vector(QQ, [5, 4])
for name, b in [("(2 f1, f2)", [2 * f1, f2]), ("(f2, f1)", [f2, f1])]:
    D = column_matrix(QQ, b).inverse()
    print(name, ": dual basis", D.rows(), "; coordinates of (5, 4):", D * v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(2 f1, f2) : dual basis [(1/3, -1/6), (-1/3, 2/3)] ; coordinates of (5, 4): (1, 1)
(f2, f1) : dual basis [(-1/3, 2/3), (2/3, -1/3)] ; coordinates of (5, 4): (1, 2)
```
::::
:::

The rows of the inverse matrix have been used as the dual basis in every computation so far. The exercise proves that
they are the only choice and that they reconstruct each vector from its coordinates [@axler2024linear, Sec. 3F, 3.114
and Exercise 3F.8].

::: {#exr-dualbasis-inverse-proof}
#### The dual basis is the inverse matrix

Let $g_1, \dots, g_n$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathbf G$ the matrix with columns $g_j$, and $\mathbf D$ the matrix whose rows
are the dual basis $g^i$. Prove that $\mathbf D \mathbf G = \mathbf G \mathbf D = \mathbf I$, that $\mathbf D$ is the only matrix with $\mathbf D \mathbf G = \mathbf I$, and that $\mathbf v = g^i(\mathbf v)
g_i$ for every $\mathbf v$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The $(i, j)$ entry of $\mathbf D \mathbf G$ is $g^i(g_j) = \delta^i_j$, so $\mathbf D \mathbf G = \mathbf I$. For a vector $\mathbf v$ with coordinates $\mathbf c$, $\mathbf v = c^j g_j
= \mathbf G \mathbf c$; applying $g^i$ gives $g^i(\mathbf v) = c^j g^i(g_j) = c^i$, so $\mathbf c = \mathbf D \mathbf v$ and $\mathbf v = g^i(\mathbf v) g_i = \mathbf G \mathbf D \mathbf v$. Since this holds for
every $\mathbf v$, $\mathbf G \mathbf D = \mathbf I$. If also $\mathbf D'\mathbf G = \mathbf I$, then $\mathbf D' = \mathbf D'(\mathbf G \mathbf D) = (\mathbf D'\mathbf G)\mathbf D = \mathbf D$. So the dual basis consists of the rows of the
unique inverse of $\mathbf G$.

## SageMath

Check on the basis $b$ of @exr-dual-basis-r3 and the vector $(2, 3, 4)$:

```{.python .sage}
G = column_matrix(QQ, [(1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 1)])
D = G.inverse()
v = vector(QQ, [2, 3, 4])
print("D G == 1:", D * G == 1, "; G D == 1:", G * D == 1)
print("sum g^i(v) g_i =", sum((D.row(i) * v) * G.column(i) for i in range(3)), "== v:", sum((D.row(i) * v) * G.column(i) for i in range(3)) == v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
D G == 1: True ; G D == 1: True
sum g^i(v) g_i = (2, 3, 4) == v: True
```
::::
:::

The dual basis of the normal modes solves the initial value problem of two coupled oscillators in one step. The
exercise starts the masses of @exr-coords-oscillator-modes from rest at a new displacement.

::: {#exr-dualbasis-normal-modes}
#### Starting the coupled oscillators

For the two masses of @exr-coords-oscillator-modes, use the dual basis $m^1, m^2$ of @exm-dualbasis-normal-modes to find
the motion that starts at rest from $(3, -1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The mode amplitudes are $m^1(3, -1) = \tfrac12(3 - 1) = 1$ and $m^2(3, -1) = \tfrac12(3 + 1) = 2$, so $(3, -1) = (1, 1) +
2(1, -1)$. By @exr-coords-oscillator-modes, $(1, 1)\cos\omega_0 t$ and $(1, -1)\cos\sqrt3\,\omega_0 t$ are solutions,
at rest at $t = 0$, and combinations of solutions are solutions. Hence $x(t) = (1, 1)\cos\omega_0 t + 2(1, -1)\cos
\sqrt3\,\omega_0 t$ starts at $(3, -1)$ with velocity $0$, and it is the motion asked for.

## SageMath

Sage computes the amplitudes, then checks the equations of motion and the initial conditions.

```{.python .sage}
t, w0 = var("t omega_0")
m = [vector(QQ, [1, 1]) / 2, vector(QQ, [1, -1]) / 2]
a = [mi * vector(QQ, [3, -1]) for mi in m]
x = a[0] * vector(SR, [1, 1]) * cos(w0 * t) + a[1] * vector(SR, [1, -1]) * cos(sqrt(3) * w0 * t)
K = matrix(QQ, [[2, -1], [-1, 2]])
print("amplitudes:", a, "; residuals:", [r.simplify_full() for r in diff(x, t, 2) + w0^2 * K * x])
print("x(0) =", x.subs(t=0), "; v(0) =", diff(x, t).subs(t=0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
amplitudes: [1, 2] ; residuals: [0, 0]
x(0) = (3, -1) ; v(0) = (0, 0)
```
::::
:::

Everything done for $f$ and for $b$ can be automated. The exercise asks for a Sage function that returns the dual
basis of any basis of $\mathbb{Q}^n$, with the matrix product as the check.

::: {#exr-dual-basis-general}
#### Dual bases in general

Write a Sage function that returns the dual basis of any basis of $\mathbb{Q}^n$, and test it on the standard
basis of $\mathbb{Q}^2$, on $f$, and on the basis $b$ of @exr-dual-basis-r3.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @exr-dualbasis-inverse-proof the dual basis is the list of rows of the inverse of the matrix whose columns are the
basis vectors, and the check $d^i(b_j) = \delta^i_j$ is the product of the two matrices. For the standard basis the
matrix is $\mathbf I$ and the dual basis is $e^1, e^2$; for $f$ it is the pair of rows of @prp-dual-basis; for $b$ it is the
basis found in @exr-dual-basis-r3.

## SageMath

The function inverts the matrix of columns and returns its rows; the loop tests the three bases.

```{.python .sage}
def dual_basis(vectors):
    B = matrix(QQ, vectors).transpose()
    return B.inverse().rows()
for name, b in [("standard", identity_matrix(QQ, 2).rows()), ("f", [vector(QQ, [2, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 2])]),
                ("b", [vector(QQ, [1, 1, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 0, 1])])]:
    d = dual_basis(b)
    print(name, ": dual basis", d, "; d^i(b_j) = delta:", matrix(QQ, d) * matrix(QQ, b).transpose() == 1)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
standard : dual basis [(1, 0), (0, 1)] ; d^i(b_j) = delta: True
f : dual basis [(2/3, -1/3), (-1/3, 2/3)] ; d^i(b_j) = delta: True
b : dual basis [(1/2, 1/2, -1/2), (-1/2, 1/2, 1/2), (1/2, -1/2, 1/2)] ; d^i(b_j) = delta: True
```
::::
:::

The last exercise combines the proposition with the transformation rule of @exr-dual-basis-transform. A new basis is
built from $f$, its dual basis is found from the rule rather than by a new inversion, and the components of a vector
and of a covector are transformed in opposite ways.

::: {#exr-dualbasis-change-rule}
#### A change of basis, vectors and covectors

Let $f'_1 = f_1 + f_2$ and $f'_2 = f_1 - f_2$. Find the dual basis $f'^1, f'^2$ in terms of $f^1, f^2$ and as rows, the
coordinates of $(5, 4)$ in $f'$, and the components of $\alpha = 2x + y$ in $f'^1, f'^2$; check that the pairing
$\alpha(5, 4) = 14$ comes out the same.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

In the notation of @exr-dual-basis-transform, $f'_j = A^i{}_j f_i$ with $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1
\end{pmatrix}$, whose inverse is $\tfrac12 \mathbf A$. Hence $f'^1 = \tfrac12(f^1 + f^2)$ and $f'^2 = \tfrac12(f^1 - f^2)$; as
rows, $f^1 + f^2 = \tfrac13(1, 1)$ and $f^1 - f^2 = (1, -1)$, so $f'^1 = \tfrac16(1, 1)$ and $f'^2 = \tfrac12(1, -1)$.
On $(5, 4)$ they give $\tfrac96 = \tfrac32$ and $\tfrac12$, and indeed $\tfrac32 (3, 3) + \tfrac12(1, -1) = (5, 4)$.
The components of $\alpha$ transform with $\mathbf A$: from $\alpha = 5f^1 + 4f^2$ (@exm-dualbasis-level-functional),
$\alpha'_1 = 5 + 4 = 9$ and $\alpha'_2 = 5 - 4 = 1$, which are $\alpha(3, 3)$ and $\alpha(1, -1)$. The pairing is
$9 \cdot \tfrac32 + 1 \cdot \tfrac12 = 14$.

## SageMath

Sage builds the new basis, its dual basis by inversion and by the rule, and the two sets of components.

```{.python .sage}
F = column_matrix(QQ, [(2, 1), (1, 2)])
A = matrix(QQ, [[1, 1], [1, -1]])
Fp = F * A                                              # columns f'_1, f'_2
Dp = Fp.inverse()                                       # rows f'^1, f'^2
print("f' =", Fp.columns(), "; dual basis rows:", Dp.rows(), "; by the rule A^-1 F^-1:", Dp == A.inverse() * F.inverse())
v, alpha = vector(QQ, [5, 4]), vector(QQ, [2, 1])
c, a = Dp * v, vector(QQ, [alpha * Fp.column(j) for j in range(2)])
print("coordinates of (5, 4):", c, "; components of alpha:", a, "; pairing:", a * c, "=", alpha * v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
f' = [(3, 3), (1, -1)] ; dual basis rows: [(1/6, 1/6), (1/2, -1/2)] ; by the rule A^-1 F^-1: True
coordinates of (5, 4): (3/2, 1/2) ; components of alpha: (9, 1) ; pairing: 14 = 14
```
::::
:::
::::


## Bilinear forms {#sec-bilinear-forms}

A bilinear form assigns a number to two vectors, linearly in each. This section treats bilinear forms on a fixed
vector space, their symmetry, non-degeneracy and signature, with the Euclidean dot product and the Minkowski form
of special relativity as the running examples; the light cone is the picture to keep in mind.
Four definitions and one proposition on the values of the Minkowski form; a degenerate form on the plane serves as
the counterexample throughout.

For more on this topic, see @axler2024linear [Sec. 9A], @knauf2018mathematical [Def. 6.12 and Thm. 6.13, pp. 104-105],
@gourgoulhon2013special [Secs. 1.3 and 1.6.2, pp. 6-12, 23-24] and @lee2013introduction [pp. 341-344].

### Bilinear forms

Two vectors in, one number out, linearly in each slot: this is the structure the rest of the chapter is about. The
definition fixes the component convention $B_{ij} = B(e_i, e_j)$, under which such a map is a square matrix once a
basis is chosen, and every metric tensor in the lectures follows it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bilinear-form}
#### Bilinear form

A **bilinear form** on $V$ is a map $B : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ linear in each argument separately. Its
**components** in a basis are $B_{ij} = B(e_i, e_j)$, and $B(v, w) = B_{ij} v^i w^j$: a bilinear form is an
$n \times n$ matrix once a basis is chosen.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the line a bilinear form has a single component, so it is one number. The first example shows that every
bilinear form on $\mathbb{R}$ is a multiple of the product $xy$ [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.1].

::: {#exm-bilinear-line}
#### Bilinear forms on the line

For $V = \mathbb{R}$ with basis $e_1 = 1$, a bilinear form has the single component $c = B(1, 1)$, and $B(x, y) = xy\,
B(1, 1) = cxy$ by linearity in each slot. So $B(x, y) = 3xy$ is bilinear, and $B(x, y) = xy + 1$ or $x^2 y$ is not.
:::

The first instance everyone meets in more than one dimension is the Euclidean dot product of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Its
components are the Kronecker delta, so in the standard basis its matrix is the identity.

::: {#exm-bilinear-dot}
#### The dot product

$B(v, w) = v^1 w^1 + \dots + v^n w^n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is bilinear with components $\delta_{ij}$, the identity
matrix.
:::

The dot product is $\mathbf v^\top \mathbf I\, \mathbf w$, and nothing stops one from putting another matrix in the middle. The example shows
that every square matrix gives a bilinear form whose components are its entries, so that bilinear forms and matrices
correspond one to one [@axler2024linear, Example 9.2 and result 9.5].

::: {#exm-bilinear-matrix-form}
#### A matrix in the middle

For an $n \times n$ matrix $\mathbf A$, $B_{\mathbf A}(\mathbf v, \mathbf w) = \mathbf v^\top \mathbf A \mathbf w = A_{ij} v^i w^j$ is bilinear on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $B_{\mathbf A}(\mathbf e_i,
\mathbf e_j) = A_{ij}$. For $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B_{\mathbf A}(\mathbf v, \mathbf w) = v^1 w^1 + 2 v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^2$.
Conversely every bilinear form is $B_{\mathbf A}$ for its own matrix of components, so the forms on an $n$-dimensional space
make up a space of dimension $n^2$.
:::

Not every such form is symmetric, and the next example shows two ways to build one that is not. A product of two
covectors has rank one, and the signed area $v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ changes sign when its arguments are swapped.

::: {#exm-bilinear-general}
#### Products of functionals and antisymmetric forms

For covectors $\alpha, \beta$, $B(v, w) = \alpha(v)\beta(w)$ is bilinear with components $\alpha_i \beta_j$; the
signed area $B(v, w) = v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is bilinear with $B(w, v) = -B(v, w)$. Bilinear forms
need not be symmetric.
:::

Bilinear forms live on any vector space, not only on $\mathbb{R}^n$. The example takes a form on polynomials built
from an evaluation and a derivative, and computes its matrix in the monomial basis [@axler2024linear, Example 9.8].

::: {#exm-bilinear-polynomials}
#### Evaluation times derivative

On the polynomials of degree at most $2$, $B(p, q) = p(2)\, q'(3)$ is bilinear, being the product of two linear
functionals. In the basis $1, x, x^2$, the values $p(2)$ are $1, 2, 4$ and the values $q'(3)$ are $0, 1, 6$, so
$$
B_{ij} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 12 \\ 0 & 4 & 24 \end{pmatrix},
$$
a matrix of rank one, as for every product $\alpha(p)\beta(q)$ (@exm-bilinear-general).
:::

An integral of a product is the continuous analogue of the dot product. The example computes the matrix of
$\int_{-1}^1 p q$ on quadratic polynomials, a matrix of integrals of monomials that is no longer the identity.

::: {#exm-bilinear-integral}
#### An integral form

On the polynomials of degree at most $2$, $B(p, q) = \int_{-1}^{1} p(x) q(x)\, dx$ is bilinear by linearity of the
integral. Its components in the basis $1, x, x^2$ are $B_{ij} = \int_{-1}^1 x^{i + j}\, dx$ for $i, j = 0, 1, 2$, which is
$2/(i + j + 1)$ for $i + j$ even and $0$ for $i + j$ odd:
$$
B_{ij} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & \tfrac23 \\ 0 & \tfrac23 & 0 \\ \tfrac23 & 0 & \tfrac25 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
:::

The next instance is the one special relativity is built on, with one positive sign and three negative ones. The
example records two values, one equal to $1$ and one equal to $0$.

::: {#exm-bilinear-minkowski}
#### The Minkowski form

$\eta(v, w) = v^0 w^0 - v^1 w^1 - v^2 w^2 - v^3 w^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$ is bilinear with components
$\eta_{\mu\nu} = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$; $\eta(w, w) = 1$ for $w = (1, 0, 0, 0)$ and $\eta(v, v) = 0$ for
$v = (1, 1, 0, 0)$.
:::

The observables of a spin $\tfrac12$ are the Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices, the real space of @exm-vs-hermitian. The
sum of the diagonal entries of a product pairs two of them, and in the Pauli basis its components are those of the dot product.

::: {#exm-bilinear-trace}
#### Pairing spin observables

On the Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices, $B(\mathbf H, \mathbf K) = \tfrac12 \sum_{a, b} H_{ab} K_{ba}$, half the sum of the
diagonal entries of $\mathbf H \mathbf K$, is real and bilinear over $\mathbb{R}$, since each term is a product of an entry of
$\mathbf H$ and one of $\mathbf K$. In the basis $\sigma_0 = \mathbf I, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ its components are
$\tfrac12\sum_a(\sigma_j \sigma_k)_{aa} = \delta_{jk}$ (@exm-dual-basis-pauli), so in components $B(\mathbf H, \mathbf K) = h^0 k^0 +
h^1 k^1 + h^2 k^2 + h^3 k^3$ [@axler2024linear, Example 9.10].
:::

The phase space of the oscillator of @exm-linear-oscillator-flow carries a bilinear form of its own. It measures
oriented area in the $(x, p)$ plane, and it is the form that Hamiltonian mechanics is built on [@knauf2018mathematical,
Remark 6.15].

::: {#exm-bilinear-symplectic}
#### Phase-space area

On the phase plane with points $u = (x, p)$, $\omega(u, u') = x p' - p x'$ is bilinear, with components
$\omega_{ij} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ in the basis $e_x, e_p$. Its value is the signed area of
the parallelogram spanned by $u$ and $u'$: $\omega(e_x, e_p) = 1$, and $\omega(u, u) = 0$ for every $u$. The time
evolution $U_t$ of the oscillator preserves it.
:::

Some natural ways of producing a number from two vectors fail one of the two linearity conditions. The last example
collects such failures, and notes that a bilinear form is not a linear map on the product space $V \times V$
[@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.3].

::: {#exm-bilinear-not}
#### What is not bilinear

On $\mathbb{R}^2$, $|v \cdot w|$ is not bilinear ($|(-v) \cdot w| = |v \cdot w|$), nor is $(v \cdot w)^2$ (doubling $v$
multiplies it by $4$). The dot product itself is bilinear but not linear on $V \times V$: $(v, w) + (v, w) = (2v, 2w)$
and $2v \cdot 2w = 4\, v \cdot w$, not $2\, v \cdot w$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Bilinearity fails as soon as a constant is added or an absolute value appears. The exercise presents four candidate
expressions on the plane and asks which are bilinear, with a specific counterexample for each one that is not.

::: {#exr-bilinear-check}
#### Which maps are bilinear?

Decide which of the following are bilinear forms on $\mathbb{R}^2$: $v \cdot w + 1$; $v^1 w^2$; $|v|\,|w|$;
$v^1 w^1 - 3 v^2 w^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$v^1 w^2$ and $v^1 w^1 - 3v^2 w^1$ are bilinear: each term is the product of one component of $v$ and one of $w$, and a
component is a linear function of its vector, so each term is linear in $v$ for fixed $w$ and in $w$ for fixed $v$.
$v \cdot w + 1$ is not: a bilinear form vanishes when one argument is $0$, but $B(0, w) = 1$. $|v|\,|w|$ is not:
$B(-v, w) = |v|\,|w|$, while linearity in the first slot would give $-B(v, w)$, and the two differ for $v, w \neq 0$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates each candidate on the counterexamples above, with $v = (3, 4)$ and $w = (5, 0)$.

```{.python .sage}
v, w, z = vector(QQ, [3, 4]), vector(QQ, [5, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 0])
dot1 = lambda a, b: a * b + 1
absprod = lambda a, b: a.norm() * b.norm()
print("v.w + 1 at (0, w):", dot1(z, w), "(a bilinear form gives 0)")
print("|v||w| at (-v, w) and -(|v||w|) at (v, w):", absprod(-v, w), -absprod(v, w))
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, 0], [-3, 0]])      # v1 w1 - 3 v2 w1
print("v1 w1 - 3 v2 w1 is v^T B w with B =", B.rows(), "; at (v, w):", v * B * w, "=", v[0] * w[0] - 3 * v[1] * w[0])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
v.w + 1 at (0, w): 1 (a bilinear form gives 0)
|v||w| at (-v, w) and -(|v||w|) at (v, w): 25 -25
v1 w1 - 3 v2 w1 is v^T B w with B = [(1, 0), (-3, 0)] ; at (v, w): -45 = -45
```
::::
:::

Reading the component matrix off an explicit formula and evaluating the form on two vectors in both orders is the
basic skill. The exercise does this for a non-symmetric form, so that $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w)$ and $B(\mathbf w, \mathbf v)$ come out different.

::: {#exr-bilinear-matrix}
#### Components of a bilinear form

Find the components $B_{ij}$ of $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w) = v^1 w^1 + 2 v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, evaluate $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w)$ and
$B(\mathbf w, \mathbf v)$ for $\mathbf v = (1, 3)$, $\mathbf w = (2, -1)$, and decide whether $B$ is symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$B_{ij} = B(e_i, e_j)$ is the coefficient of $v^i w^j$: $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Then
$B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w) = 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot (-1) - 3 \cdot 2 = -6$ and $B(\mathbf w, \mathbf v) = 2 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 - (-1) \cdot 1 =
15$. The two differ, so $B$ is not symmetric.

## SageMath

Sage builds the matrix, evaluates $\mathbf v^\top \mathbf B \mathbf w$ and $\mathbf w^\top \mathbf B \mathbf v$, and reads the components back from the basis.

```{.python .sage}
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [-1, 0]])
v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 3]), vector(QQ, [2, -1])
print("B =", B.rows())
print("B(v, w) = v^T B w =", v * B * w, "; by the formula v1 w1 + 2 v1 w2 - v2 w1 =", v[0] * w[0] + 2 * v[0] * w[1] - v[1] * w[0])
print("B(w, v) =", w * B * v, "; symmetric:", B.is_symmetric())
E = identity_matrix(QQ, 2).rows()
print("components B(e_i, e_j):", [ei * B * ej for ei in E for ej in E])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B = [(1, 2), (-1, 0)]
B(v, w) = v^T B w = -6 ; by the formula v1 w1 + 2 v1 w2 - v2 w1 = -6
B(w, v) = 15 ; symmetric: False
components B(e_i, e_j): [1, 2, -1, 0]
```
::::
:::

A form on $\mathbb{R}^3$ given by a formula with mixed terms is a first test of the component rule in three
dimensions. The exercise reads off the matrix of a form from Axler's book and evaluates it on a few pairs
[@axler2024linear, Example 9.19].

::: {#exr-bilinear-evaluate-r3}
#### A form on $\mathbb{R}^3$

For $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w) = v^1 w^1 - 4 v^1 w^2 + 8 v^1 w^3 - 3 v^3 w^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, write the matrix $B_{ij}$ and compute
$B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w)$, $B(\mathbf w, \mathbf v)$, $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf v)$ and $B(\mathbf w, \mathbf w)$ for $\mathbf v = (1, 2, 1)$ and $\mathbf w = (2, 0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The coefficient of $v^i w^j$ is $B_{ij}$: $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -4 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$. With
$\mathbf v = (1, 2, 1)$, $\mathbf w = (2, 0, 1)$: $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf w) = 2 - 0 + 8 - 3 = 7$, $B(\mathbf w, \mathbf v) = 2 - 16 + 16 - 3 = -1$, $B(\mathbf v, \mathbf v) = 1 - 8 + 8
- 3 = -2$ and $B(\mathbf w, \mathbf w) = 4 - 0 + 16 - 3 = 17$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the four values as $\mathbf v^\top \mathbf B \mathbf w$.

```{.python .sage}
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, -4, 8], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, -3]])
v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 1]), vector(QQ, [2, 0, 1])
print("B(v, w), B(w, v), B(v, v), B(w, w) =", v * B * w, w * B * v, v * B * v, w * B * w)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B(v, w), B(w, v), B(v, v), B(w, w) = 7 -1 -2 17
```
::::
:::

Components of a bilinear form transform with two factors of the change-of-basis matrix. The exercise derives the rule
$\mathbf B' = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$ and applies it to the dot product in the basis $f$, producing the Gram matrix that the final
exercises return to.

::: {#exr-bilinear-change-basis}
#### Components under a change of basis

Show that under $e'_j = A^i{}_j e_i$ the components become $B'_{ij} = A^k{}_i A^l{}_j B_{kl}$, that is, $\mathbf B' =
\mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$, and compute the components of the dot product of $\mathbb{R}^2$ in the basis $f$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$B'_{ij} = B(e'_i, e'_j) = B(A^k{}_i e_k, A^l{}_j e_l) = A^k{}_i A^l{}_j B_{kl}$ by bilinearity, and $A^k{}_i B_{kl}
A^l{}_j$ is the $(i, j)$ entry of $\mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$. For the dot product, $\mathbf B = \mathbf I$, and $\mathbf A$ is the matrix with columns $f_1 = (2,
1)$, $f_2 = (1, 2)$, so $\mathbf B' = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$, the matrix of dot products $f_i
\cdot f_j$ (the **Gram matrix** of $f$). For $v = (5, 4)$, with $f$-coordinates $(2, 1)$, both bases give $|v|^2 = 25 +
16 = 4 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 + 5 = 41$.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$, compares it with the dot products of the basis vectors, and evaluates $|v|^2$ both ways.

```{.python .sage}
A = matrix(QQ, [[2, 1], [1, 2]]).transpose()      # columns f1, f2
B = identity_matrix(QQ, 2)                         # the dot product
Bp = A.transpose() * B * A
print("B' = A^T B A =", Bp.rows(), "; f_i . f_j:", [[A.column(i) * A.column(j) for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)])
v = vector(QQ, [5, 4]); c = A.inverse() * v       # f-coordinates (2, 1)
print("|v|^2 in the standard basis:", v * B * v, "; with the f-coordinates", c, "and B':", c * Bp * c)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B' = A^T B A = [(5, 4), (4, 5)] ; f_i . f_j: [[5, 4], [4, 5]]
|v|^2 in the standard basis: 41 ; with the f-coordinates (2, 1) and B': 41
```
::::
:::

The change-of-basis rule can be tested on the polynomial form of @exm-bilinear-polynomials. The exercise computes its
matrix in a second basis directly and then checks the rule $\mathbf B' = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$ [@axler2024linear, Example 9.8].

::: {#exr-bilinear-polynomial-matrix}
#### A second basis for the polynomial form

For $B(p, q) = p(2)\, q'(3)$ on the polynomials of degree at most $2$, compute the matrix $\mathbf B'$ in the basis $1, x - 2,
(x - 3)^2$ directly, and check that $\mathbf B' = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$ with $\mathbf B$ the matrix of @exm-bilinear-polynomials and $\mathbf A$ the
matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the new basis in $1, x, x^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The values at $2$ of $1, x - 2, (x - 3)^2$ are $1, 0, 1$, and their derivatives at $3$ are $0, 1, 0$, so $B'_{ij} =
p_i(2)\, p_j'(3)$ is
$$
\mathbf B' = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Since $(x - 3)^2 = 9 - 6x + x^2$, the coordinate columns are $(1, 0, 0)$, $(-2, 1, 0)$ and $(9, -6, 1)$, so $\mathbf A =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. With $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 12 \\
0 & 4 & 24 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf B \mathbf A$ has columns $\mathbf B(1, 0, 0)^\top = (0, 0, 0)$, $\mathbf B(-2, 1, 0)^\top = (1, 2, 4)$ and $\mathbf B(9, -6,
1)^\top = (0, 0, 0)$, and $\mathbf A^\top$ applied to $(1, 2, 4)$ gives $(1, -2 + 2, 9 - 12 + 4) = (1, 0, 1)$: the middle
column of $\mathbf B'$, the other two being zero. So $\mathbf B' = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$ (@exr-bilinear-change-basis).

## SageMath

Sage computes the new matrix from the definition and from the rule.

```{.python .sage}
R.<x> = QQ[]
beta = lambda p, q: p(2) * q.derivative()(3)
old, new = [R(1), x, x^2], [R(1), x - 2, (x - 3)^2]
B = matrix(QQ, 3, 3, lambda i, j: beta(old[i], old[j]))
Bp = matrix(QQ, 3, 3, lambda i, j: beta(new[i], new[j]))
A = matrix(QQ, [p.padded_list(3) for p in new]).transpose()      # columns: coordinates in 1, x, x^2
print("B =", B.rows()); print("B' =", Bp.rows()); print("A =", A.rows())
print("B' == A^T B A:", Bp == A.transpose() * B * A)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B = [(0, 1, 6), (0, 2, 12), (0, 4, 24)]
B' = [(0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)]
A = [(1, -2, 9), (0, 1, -6), (0, 0, 1)]
B' == A^T B A: True
```
::::
:::

On the line the matrix of a bilinear form is a single number, and this number determines the whole form. The
exercise asks for the proof, which is linearity applied once in each slot [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.1].

::: {#exr-bilinear-line-proof}
#### Every form on the line is $cxy$

Prove that every bilinear form on $\mathbb{R}$ is $B(x, y) = cxy$ for a constant $c$, and find $c$ for $B(x, y) = 5xy -
2yx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $c = B(1, 1)$. For real $x, y$, linearity in the first slot gives $B(x, y) = B(x \cdot 1, y) = x B(1, y)$, and
linearity in the second gives $B(1, y) = y B(1, 1) = yc$. So $B(x, y) = cxy$. For $B(x, y) = 5xy - 2yx = 3xy$,
$c = B(1, 1) = 3$.

## SageMath

Check on $B(x, y) = 5xy - 2yx$: Sage compares $B$ with $B(1, 1)\,xy$ symbolically.

```{.python .sage}
x, y = var("x y")
B = lambda a, b: 5 * a * b - 2 * b * a
c = B(1, 1)
print("c = B(1, 1) =", c, "; B(x, y) - c x y =", (B(x, y) - c * x * y).expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
c = B(1, 1) = 3 ; B(x, y) - c x y = 0
```
::::
:::

A bilinear form and a linear map on $V \times V$ both take pairs of vectors to numbers, but they are different
things. The exercise proves that the only map that is both is zero [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.3].

::: {#exr-bilinear-not-linear}
#### Bilinear and linear only for zero

Suppose $B : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ is bilinear and is also linear on the vector space $V \times V$, with
$(v, w) + (v', w') = (v + v', w + w')$ and $\lambda(v, w) = (\lambda v, \lambda w)$. Prove that $B = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

In $V \times V$, $(v, w) = (v, 0) + (0, w)$. Linearity on $V \times V$ gives $B(v, w) = B(v, 0) + B(0, w)$. By
linearity in the second slot $B(v, 0) = B(v, 0 \cdot 0) = 0 \cdot B(v, 0) = 0$, and by linearity in the first slot
$B(0, w) = 0$. So $B(v, w) = 0$ for all $v, w$.

## SageMath

Check on the dot product of $\mathbb{Q}^2$: Sage shows that it fails additivity on $V \times V$ at a concrete pair.

```{.python .sage}
v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2]), vector(QQ, [3, 1])
B = lambda a, b: a * b
print("B((v, 0) + (0, w)) =", B(v, w), "; B(v, 0) + B(0, w) =", B(v, 0 * w) + B(0 * v, w))
print("B(2(v, w)) =", B(2 * v, 2 * w), "; 2 B(v, w) =", 2 * B(v, w))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B((v, 0) + (0, w)) = 5 ; B(v, 0) + B(0, w) = 0
B(2(v, w)) = 20 ; 2 B(v, w) = 10
```
::::
:::

The correspondence between bilinear forms and matrices makes the forms into a vector space with an explicit basis.
The exercise proves that it has dimension $n^2$ and names the basis [@axler2024linear, result 9.5].

::: {#exr-bilinear-space-dim}
#### The space of bilinear forms

Show that the bilinear forms on an $n$-dimensional $V$ form a vector space under pointwise addition and scalar
multiplication, that the $n^2$ forms $E^{kl}(v, w) = v^k w^l$ are a basis, and that the coordinates of $B$ in this basis
are its components $B_{kl}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

A sum of two bilinear forms and a multiple of one are again linear in each slot, so the bilinear forms are a
subspace of the functions $V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ (@def-vector-space). Each $E^{kl}$ is bilinear, being the product of
the coordinate functionals $e^k(v)$ and $e^l(w)$ (@exm-bilinear-general). By @def-bilinear-form, $B(v, w) = B_{kl} v^k w^l
= B_{kl} E^{kl}(v, w)$, so the $E^{kl}$ span. If $\lambda_{kl} E^{kl} = 0$, evaluating at $(e_i, e_j)$ gives
$\lambda_{ij} = 0$, since $E^{kl}(e_i, e_j) = \delta^k_i \delta^l_j$; so they are independent. They form a basis of $n^2$
elements, and the coordinates of $B$ are the $B_{kl}$.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{Q}^2$: Sage expands the form of @exr-bilinear-matrix in the four forms $E^{kl}$ and compares the
two on random vectors.

```{.python .sage}
import random
random.seed(int(3))
Bm = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [-1, 0]])
E = {(k, l): (lambda v, w, k=k, l=l: v[k] * w[l]) for k in range(2) for l in range(2)}
ok = True
for _ in range(10):
    v = vector(QQ, [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(2)]); w = vector(QQ, [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(2)])
    ok = ok and v * Bm * w == sum(Bm[k, l] * E[(k, l)](v, w) for (k, l) in E)
print("B = B_kl E^kl on 10 random pairs:", ok, "; number of basis forms:", len(E))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B = B_kl E^kl on 10 random pairs: True ; number of basis forms: 4
```
::::
:::

A product of two covectors is a bilinear form of rank one, and sums of such products give everything. The exercise
proves that $n$ products always suffice and uses the dual basis to write them down [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.2].

::: {#exr-bilinear-sum-products}
#### Sums of products of covectors

Let $n = \dim V$. Prove that every bilinear form on $V$ is $B(v, w) = \phi_1(v)\tau_1(w) + \dots + \phi_n(v)\tau_n(w)$ for
covectors $\phi_i, \tau_i \in V^*$, and find such covectors for the form of @exr-bilinear-matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Choose a basis $e_i$ with dual basis $e^i$ (@def-dual-basis), so that $v^i = e^i(v)$. Then $B(v, w) = B_{ij} v^i w^j =
\sum_i e^i(v)\, \big(B_{ij} e^j(w)\big)$. Set $\phi_i = e^i$ and $\tau_i = B_{ij} e^j$, a covector whose components are the
$i$-th row of $\mathbf B$; then $B(v, w) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \phi_i(v)\tau_i(w)$. For $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$: $\phi_1 = e^1$, $\tau_1 = e^1 + 2e^2$, $\phi_2 = e^2$, $\tau_2 = -e^1$, that is $B(v, w) = v^1(w^1 + 2w^2)
+ v^2(-w^1)$.

## SageMath

Check on the form of @exr-bilinear-matrix: Sage compares $B(v, w)$ with $\sum_i v^i\,(\text{row}_i \cdot w)$ on random
vectors.

```{.python .sage}
import random
random.seed(int(5))
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [-1, 0]])
ok = True
for _ in range(10):
    v = vector(QQ, [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(2)]); w = vector(QQ, [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(2)])
    ok = ok and v * B * w == sum(v[i] * (B.row(i) * w) for i in range(2))
print("tau_1, tau_2 (rows of B):", B.rows(), "; B(v, w) = sum phi_i(v) tau_i(w) on 10 random pairs:", ok)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
tau_1, tau_2 (rows of B): [(1, 2), (-1, 0)] ; B(v, w) = sum phi_i(v) tau_i(w) on 10 random pairs: True
```
::::
:::

A linear map $T$ can be fed into either slot of a bilinear form, and the result is again a bilinear form whose matrix
is a product. The last exercise derives the two product rules and uses them to show that the time evolution of the
oscillator preserves phase-space area [@axler2024linear, result 9.6], [@knauf2018mathematical, eq. (6.2.2)].

::: {#exr-bilinear-operator}
#### Composing with a linear map

For a bilinear form $B$ and a linear map $T : V \to V$, show that $B(v, Tw)$ and $B(Tv, Tw)$ are bilinear with
matrices $\mathbf B \mathbf T$ and $\mathbf T^\top \mathbf B \mathbf T$. For the form $\omega$ of @exm-bilinear-symplectic and $\mathbf T = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d
\end{pmatrix}$, show that $\mathbf T^\top \omega \mathbf T = (ad - bc)\,\omega$, and deduce that the oscillator's evolution $U_t$ of
@exm-linear-oscillator-flow satisfies $\omega(U_t u, U_t u') = \omega(u, u')$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Both are bilinear, since $T$ is linear and $B$ is linear in each slot. Their components are $B(e_i, T e_j) = B(e_i,
T^k{}_j e_k) = B_{ik} T^k{}_j$, the entries of $\mathbf B \mathbf T$, and $B(Te_i, Te_j) = T^k{}_i B_{kl} T^l{}_j$, the entries of $\mathbf T^\top
\mathbf B \mathbf T$ (@def-linear-map). For $\omega = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$: $\omega \mathbf T = \begin{pmatrix} c & d
\\ -a & -b \end{pmatrix}$, and
$$
\mathbf T^\top \omega \mathbf T = \begin{pmatrix} a & c \\ b & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} c & d \\ -a & -b \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & ad - bc \\ bc - ad & 0 \end{pmatrix} = (ad - bc)\,\omega.
$$
For $\mathbf U_t$, $ad - bc = \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2 \omega t = 1$, so $\mathbf U_t^\top \omega \mathbf U_t = \omega$, which is the statement
$\omega(U_t u, U_t u') = \omega(u, u')$: the evolution preserves oriented phase-space area.

## SageMath

Sage computes $\mathbf T^\top \omega \mathbf T$ for a general $\mathbf T$ and for the oscillator's $\mathbf U_t$.

```{.python .sage}
a, b, c, d, t, w0, m = var("a b c d t omega m")
J = matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [-1, 0]])
T = matrix(SR, [[a, b], [c, d]])
print("T^T J T == (ad - bc) J:", (T.transpose() * J * T - (a * d - b * c) * J).expand() == 0)
U = matrix(SR, [[cos(w0 * t), sin(w0 * t) / (m * w0)], [-m * w0 * sin(w0 * t), cos(w0 * t)]])
print("U_t^T J U_t == J:", (U.transpose() * J * U).simplify_full() == J)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
T^T J T == (ad - bc) J: True
U_t^T J U_t == J: True
```
::::
:::
::::

### Symmetric forms

Most forms in geometry are symmetric, and for them the values on single vectors already determine everything. The
definition states the symmetry condition and the polarisation identity that recovers $B(v, w)$ from the quadratic form
$B(v, v)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-symmetric-form}
#### Symmetric bilinear form

A bilinear form is **symmetric** if $B(v, w) = B(w, v)$, that is, $B_{ij} = B_{ji}$. A symmetric form is
determined by its values $B(v, v)$ on single vectors (its **quadratic form**), by $2B(v, w) = B(v + w, v + w) -
B(v, v) - B(w, w)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In one dimension there is nothing to swap, and in two dimensions the simplest form already fails. The first example
contrasts the two cases on the smallest spaces where the question makes sense.

::: {#exm-symmetric-small}
#### The line and the plane

Every bilinear form $cxy$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (@exm-bilinear-line) is symmetric, since $cxy = cyx$. On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the
form $B(v, w) = v^1 w^2$ is not: $B(e_1, e_2) = 1$ while $B(e_2, e_1) = 0$, and its matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 &
0 \end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric.
:::

Both running forms are symmetric, since their matrices are diagonal. The example records the symmetry $\eta^\top =
\eta$ and the two quadratic forms, the squared length and the Minkowski interval.

::: {#exm-symmetric-dot-minkowski}
#### Dot product and Minkowski form

The dot product and the Minkowski form have diagonal, hence symmetric, matrices; $\eta^\top = \eta$. Their quadratic forms are the squared length $|v|^2 = (v^1)^2 + \dots + (v^n)^2$ and the
interval $\eta(v, v) = (v^0)^2 - (v^1)^2 - (v^2)^2 - (v^3)^2$.
:::

A quadratic polynomial in two variables encodes a symmetric matrix, with half the mixed coefficient off the diagonal.
The example extracts the matrix $\mathbf S$ from $x^2 + 4xy + 4y^2$ and shows that this form never takes a negative value.

::: {#exm-symmetric-quadratic}
#### Reading a form off its quadratic form

The quadratic form $Q(x, y) = x^2 + 4xy + 4y^2$ comes from the symmetric matrix $\mathbf S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4
\end{pmatrix}$: the off-diagonal entry is half the coefficient of $xy$. Since $Q = (x + 2y)^2$, $Q \geq 0$
everywhere, with $Q = 0$ exactly on the line $x = -2y$.
:::

The same quadratic form comes from many bilinear forms, of which exactly one is symmetric. The example takes the
non-symmetric form of @exr-bilinear-evaluate-r3 and finds the symmetric one with the same quadratic form
[@axler2024linear, Examples 9.19 and 9.22].

::: {#exm-symmetric-axler-r3}
#### One quadratic form, two bilinear forms

The form $B(v, w) = v^1 w^1 - 4 v^1 w^2 + 8 v^1 w^3 - 3 v^3 w^3$ is not symmetric, and its quadratic form is $Q(x) =
x_1^2 - 4 x_1 x_2 + 8 x_1 x_3 - 3 x_3^2$. The symmetric form $\tfrac12(B(v, w) + B(w, v))$, with matrix
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$, has the same quadratic form: splitting each mixed
coefficient in half between the two off-diagonal places changes nothing on the diagonal $v = w$.
:::

Symmetry is a property of the form, so it cannot depend on the basis in which the matrix is written. The example
shows that a symmetric matrix stays symmetric under $\mathbf B' = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$, unlike the matrix of a linear map
[@axler2024linear, result 9.12].

::: {#exm-symmetric-matrix-test}
#### Symmetric in every basis

The dot product has the symmetric matrix $\mathbf I$ in the standard basis and the symmetric Gram matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4
\\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ in the basis $f$ (@exr-bilinear-change-basis); in general $(\mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A)^\top = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B^\top
\mathbf A$. A linear map behaves differently: $\mathbf L = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2)$ has, in the basis $f$, the matrix $\mathbf F^{-1} \mathbf L \mathbf F =
\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\mathbf F$ the matrix of columns $f_1, f_2$, and this is not
symmetric.
:::

Matrices themselves carry a symmetric form, built from the diagonal entries of a product. The example computes its quadratic
form on $2 \times 2$ real matrices and finds that it takes both signs [@axler2024linear, Example 9.10].

::: {#exm-symmetric-trace-form}
#### A symmetric form on matrices

On the real $2 \times 2$ matrices, $B(\mathbf X, \mathbf Y) = \sum_i (\mathbf X \mathbf Y)_{ii} = \sum_{i, j} X_{ij} Y_{ji}$ is bilinear and
symmetric, since exchanging $\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf Y$ only renames $i$ and $j$. For $\mathbf X = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d
\end{pmatrix}$ its quadratic form is $B(\mathbf X, \mathbf X) = a^2 + 2bc + d^2$: it is $2$ on the identity and $-2$ on
the rotation generator $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::

Two masses joined to walls and to each other by springs store a potential energy that is a quadratic form in their
displacements. The example writes down its symmetric matrix, which governs the coupled motion.

::: {#exm-symmetric-kinetic}
#### Coupled oscillators

Two equal masses, each tied to a wall by a spring of constant $k$ and to each other by a spring of constant $k'$, have
potential energy $V(x_1, x_2) = \tfrac12 k x_1^2 + \tfrac12 k x_2^2 + \tfrac12 k' (x_1 - x_2)^2$. This is $\tfrac12 \mathbf x^\top
\mathbf K \mathbf x$ with the symmetric matrix $\mathbf K = \begin{pmatrix} k + k' & -k' \\ -k' & k + k' \end{pmatrix}$; the mixed coefficient
$-k' x_1 x_2$ splits into the two off-diagonal entries. The force on mass $i$ is $-(\mathbf K \mathbf x)_i$.
:::

The product of the diagonal entries of a Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrix minus the product of its off-diagonal entries is
a quadratic form, and polarising it produces the Minkowski form. The example works this out in the Pauli basis, which is how a spin $\tfrac12$ sees spacetime.

::: {#exm-symmetric-det-pauli}
#### A quadratic form on spin observables

For $\mathbf H = h^0 + h^1\sigma_1 + h^2\sigma_2 + h^3\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} h^0 + h^3 & h^1 - i h^2 \\ h^1 + i h^2 & h^0 -
h^3 \end{pmatrix}$, $Q(\mathbf H) = H_{11}H_{22} - H_{12}H_{21} = (h^0)^2 - (h^3)^2 - ((h^1)^2 + (h^2)^2)$, that is
$Q(\mathbf H) = (h^0)^2 - (h^1)^2 - (h^2)^2 - (h^3)^2$: a quadratic form on the Hermitian matrices, equal to $\eta(h, h)$ for
the coordinates $h^\mu$ in the basis $\mathbf I, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$. Polarisation gives the symmetric form
$B(\mathbf H, \mathbf K) = \tfrac12(Q(\mathbf H + \mathbf K) - Q(\mathbf H) - Q(\mathbf K))$, whose components in that basis are
$\eta_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

At the opposite extreme stand the forms that change sign when their arguments are exchanged, whose quadratic form
vanishes identically. The example names the instances met so far and the field strength of electromagnetism.

::: {#exm-symmetric-not}
#### Antisymmetric forms

The signed-area form $v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ is antisymmetric, not symmetric, and its quadratic form is identically
zero; so is the phase-space form $\omega$ of @exm-bilinear-symplectic. The field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ of
electromagnetism is an antisymmetric bilinear form on $\mathbb{R}^4$.
:::

Two things a quadratic form cannot do mark the limits of the definition. The last example shows that its zero set is
not a subspace, and that it cannot recover a form that is not symmetric [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.6].

::: {#exm-symmetric-null-not-subspace}
#### What a quadratic form does not tell

For $Q(x, y) = x^2 - y^2$ the zero set is the pair of lines $y = \pm x$, not a subspace: $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ lie on
it, but their sum $(2, 0)$ has $Q = 4$. And the two forms $v^1 w^2$ and $v^2 w^1$ have the same quadratic form $xy$,
so a quadratic form determines only the symmetric part of a bilinear form.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Symmetry is checked by swapping the arguments, or by transposing the matrix. The exercise applies the test to four
forms, two on the plane and two on polynomials.

::: {#exr-symmetric-check}
#### Which forms are symmetric?

Decide which are symmetric: $v^1 w^1 + 2 v^1 w^2 + 2 v^2 w^1$ and $v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$; $p(0) q(1) +
p(1) q(0)$ and $\int_0^1 p(x) q'(x)\, dx$ on the polynomials of degree at most $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The first has matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, symmetric. The second has matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 &
1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and is antisymmetric, not symmetric. The third is unchanged when $p$ and $q$ are swapped, the
two terms exchanging places, so it is symmetric. The fourth is not: for $p = 1$, $q = x$ it gives $\int_0^1 1\, dx = 1$,
and for $p = x$, $q = 1$ it gives $\int_0^1 x \cdot 0\, dx = 0$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the matrices of the two polynomial forms in the basis $1, x$ and tests all four for symmetry.

```{.python .sage}
R.<x> = QQ[]
basis = [R(1), x]
third = lambda p, q: p(0) * q(1) + p(1) * q(0)
fourth = lambda p, q: (p * q.derivative()).integral()(1) - (p * q.derivative()).integral()(0)
mats = {"v1w1 + 2v1w2 + 2v2w1": matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [2, 0]]), "v1w2 - v2w1": matrix(QQ, [[0, 1], [-1, 0]]),
        "p(0)q(1) + p(1)q(0)": matrix(QQ, 2, 2, lambda i, j: third(basis[i], basis[j])),
        "int p q'": matrix(QQ, 2, 2, lambda i, j: fourth(basis[i], basis[j]))}
for name, M in mats.items():
    print(name, ": matrix", M.rows(), "; symmetric:", M.is_symmetric())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
v1w1 + 2v1w2 + 2v2w1 : matrix [(1, 2), (2, 0)] ; symmetric: True
v1w2 - v2w1 : matrix [(0, 1), (-1, 0)] ; symmetric: False
p(0)q(1) + p(1)q(0) : matrix [(2, 1), (1, 0)] ; symmetric: True
int p q' : matrix [(0, 1), (0, 1/2)] ; symmetric: False
```
::::
:::

Extracting a symmetric matrix from a quadratic form in three variables follows the same rule as in two. The exercise
asks for the matrix and for one value of the form, which turns out negative while other values are positive.

::: {#exr-symmetric-quadratic}
#### The symmetric matrix of a quadratic form

Find the symmetric matrix of $Q(x, y, z) = 2x^2 - 3xy + y^2 + 4yz$ and the value $Q(1, 2, -1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Diagonal entries are the coefficients of the squares and off-diagonal entries half the mixed coefficients:
$\mathbf S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -\tfrac32 & 0 \\ -\tfrac32 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, and indeed $\mathbf x^\top \mathbf S \mathbf x = 2x^2 +
2(-\tfrac32)xy + y^2 + 2 \cdot 2\, yz$. $Q(1, 2, -1) = 2 - 6 + 4 - 8 = -8$, while $Q(1, 0, 0) = 2$: the form takes both
signs.

## SageMath

Sage builds $\mathbf S$, checks $\mathbf x^\top \mathbf S \mathbf x = Q$ symbolically and evaluates the two values.

```{.python .sage}
x, y, z = var("x y z")
Q = 2 * x^2 - 3 * x * y + y^2 + 4 * y * z
S = matrix(QQ, [[2, -3/2, 0], [-3/2, 1, 2], [0, 2, 0]])
X = vector(SR, [x, y, z])
print("x^T S x - Q =", (X * S * X - Q).expand(), "; Q(1, 2, -1) =", Q(x=1, y=2, z=-1), "; Q(1, 0, 0) =", Q(x=1, y=0, z=0))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
x^T S x - Q = 0 ; Q(1, 2, -1) = -8 ; Q(1, 0, 0) = 2
```
::::
:::

The polarisation identity of @def-symmetric-form turns values of the quadratic form into values of the bilinear form.
The exercise uses it to recover an off-diagonal component without first writing the matrix.

::: {#exr-symmetric-from-quadratic}
#### From the quadratic form back to the form

For $Q(x, y) = 3x^2 - 2xy + y^2$, compute $B(e_1, e_2)$ for the symmetric form with quadratic form $Q$ from the values
$Q(1, 1)$, $Q(1, 0)$, $Q(0, 1)$, and write its matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$Q(1, 1) = 3 - 2 + 1 = 2$, $Q(1, 0) = 3$, $Q(0, 1) = 1$, so $2B(e_1, e_2) = 2 - 3 - 1 = -2$ and $B(e_1, e_2) = -1$. With
$B(e_1, e_1) = Q(1, 0) = 3$ and $B(e_2, e_2) = Q(0, 1) = 1$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$, whose off-diagonal entry is half the coefficient $-2$ of $xy$, as in @exm-symmetric-quadratic.

## SageMath

Sage polarises $Q$ and compares with the matrix read off the coefficients.

```{.python .sage}
Q = lambda v: 3 * v[0]^2 - 2 * v[0] * v[1] + v[1]^2
e1, e2 = vector(QQ, [1, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1])
B12 = (Q(e1 + e2) - Q(e1) - Q(e2)) / 2
M = matrix(QQ, [[Q(e1), B12], [B12, Q(e2)]])
print("B(e1, e2) =", B12, "; matrix", M.rows(), "; reproduces Q at (2, -5):", vector(QQ, [2, -5]) * M * vector(QQ, [2, -5]) == Q((2, -5)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
B(e1, e2) = -1 ; matrix [(3, -1), (-1, 1)] ; reproduces Q at (2, -5): True
```
::::
:::

Every bilinear form splits uniquely into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part. The exercise asks for the proof and
applies it to the non-symmetric form of @exr-bilinear-matrix, noting which part the quadratic form sees
[@axler2024linear, result 9.17].

::: {#exr-symmetric-decompose}
#### Symmetric plus antisymmetric

Show that every bilinear form is uniquely the sum of a symmetric and an antisymmetric one, and decompose the form
of @exr-bilinear-matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$B = \tfrac12(B + B^\top) + \tfrac12(B - B^\top)$, where $B^\top(v, w) = B(w, v)$; the first part is symmetric and the
second antisymmetric. If $B = S + A$ with $S$ symmetric and $A$ antisymmetric, then $B^\top = S - A$, so $S =
\tfrac12(B + B^\top)$ and $A = \tfrac12(B - B^\top)$ are forced: the splitting is unique. For $\mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 &
2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$: $\mathbf S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12 \\ \tfrac12 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 0
& \tfrac32 \\ -\tfrac32 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Since $A(v, v) = -A(v, v) = 0$, only $S$ contributes to the quadratic form.

## SageMath

Sage splits the matrix and compares the quadratic forms of $B$ and $S$ on a vector.

```{.python .sage}
B = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [-1, 0]])
S, A = (B + B.transpose()) / 2, (B - B.transpose()) / 2
v = vector(QQ, [3, -7])
print("S =", S.rows(), "; A =", A.rows(), "; S + A == B:", S + A == B)
print("B(v, v) =", v * B * v, "; S(v, v) =", v * S * v, "; A(v, v) =", v * A * v)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
S = [(1, 1/2), (1/2, 0)] ; A = [(0, 3/2), (-3/2, 0)] ; S + A == B: True
B(v, v) = -12 ; S(v, v) = -12 ; A(v, v) = 0
```
::::
:::

The identity that recovers $B(v, w)$ from the quadratic form can be tested numerically, and its proof is a two-line
expansion. The exercise checks it on random vectors for the Minkowski form and explains why it says nothing about an
antisymmetric form.

::: {#exr-polarisation}
#### The polarisation identity

Prove the identity $2B(v, w) = B(v + w, v + w) - B(v, v) - B(w, w)$ for a symmetric form, check it for the Minkowski
form on random integer vectors, and show why it fails to recover an antisymmetric form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Expanding by bilinearity, $B(v + w, v + w) = B(v, v) + B(v, w) + B(w, v) + B(w, w)$, and symmetry turns the two
middle terms into $2B(v, w)$. For an antisymmetric form the middle terms cancel instead, and the right-hand side
is $0$ whatever $B(v, w)$ is: for $\mathbf J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $J(e_1, e_2) = 1$ but the formula
gives $0$.

## SageMath

Sage tests the identity for $\eta$ on ten random pairs and evaluates the formula for the antisymmetric $J$.

```{.python .sage}
import random
random.seed(int(7))
eta = diagonal_matrix(QQ, [1, -1, -1, -1])
ok = True
for _ in range(10):
    v = vector(QQ, [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(4)]); w = vector(QQ, [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(4)])
    ok = ok and (2 * (v * eta * w) == (v + w) * eta * (v + w) - v * eta * v - w * eta * w)
print("polarisation identity for eta on 10 random pairs:", ok)
J = matrix(QQ, [[0, 1], [-1, 0]]); v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1])
print("antisymmetric J: J(v, w) =", v * J * w, "but the polarisation formula gives", ((v + w) * J * (v + w) - v * J * v - w * J * w) / 2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
polarisation identity for eta on 10 random pairs: True
antisymmetric J: J(v, w) = 1 but the polarisation formula gives 0
```
::::
:::

A second polarisation formula uses $v + w$ and $v - w$ and no single values. The exercise proves it and uses it on two
null vectors of $\eta$, where both single values vanish [@knauf2018mathematical, proof of Thm. 6.13].

::: {#exr-symmetric-polarisation-four}
#### Polarisation with a difference

For a symmetric form with quadratic form $Q(v) = B(v, v)$, prove that $B(v, w) = \tfrac14\big(Q(v + w) - Q(v - w)\big)$.
Use it to compute $\eta(v, w)$ for the null vectors $v = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ and $w = (1, -1, 0, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By bilinearity and symmetry, $Q(v \pm w) = Q(v) \pm 2B(v, w) + Q(w)$. Subtracting, $Q(v + w) - Q(v - w) = 4B(v, w)$.
For the two null vectors, $v + w = (2, 0, 0, 0)$ with $Q = 4$ and $v - w = (0, 2, 0, 0)$ with $Q = -4$, so $\eta(v, w) =
\tfrac14(4 + 4) = 2$, which is also $1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot (-1) = 2$ from the components.

## SageMath

Check on the two null vectors and on random pairs for $\eta$.

```{.python .sage}
import random
random.seed(int(11))
eta = diagonal_matrix(QQ, [1, -1, -1, -1]); Q = lambda u: u * eta * u
v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [1, -1, 0, 0])
print("Q(v), Q(w) =", Q(v), Q(w), "; (Q(v + w) - Q(v - w))/4 =", (Q(v + w) - Q(v - w)) / 4, "; eta(v, w) =", v * eta * w)
pairs = [(vector(QQ, [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(4)]), vector(QQ, [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(4)])) for _ in range(10)]
print("formula on 10 random pairs:", all(a * eta * b == (Q(a + b) - Q(a - b)) / 4 for a, b in pairs))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
Q(v), Q(w) = 0 0 ; (Q(v + w) - Q(v - w))/4 = 2 ; eta(v, w) = 2
formula on 10 random pairs: True
```
::::
:::

Symmetry was defined as a property of the form, and the definition also states it as a property of the matrix. The
exercise proves that the matrix test in one basis is enough, so that the two statements agree [@axler2024linear,
result 9.12].

::: {#exr-symmetric-basis-independent}
#### One basis is enough

Prove that if the matrix of $B$ in one basis is symmetric, then $B$ is symmetric, and hence its matrix in every basis
is symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Suppose $B_{ij} = B_{ji}$ in the basis $e_i$. For $v = v^i e_i$, $w = w^j e_j$: $B(v, w) = B_{ij} v^i w^j = B_{ji} v^i w^j
= B(w, v)$, the last step renaming the summation indices. So $B$ is symmetric. In any other basis $e'_i$, $B'_{ij} =
B(e'_i, e'_j) = B(e'_j, e'_i) = B'_{ji}$. Equivalently, $(\mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A)^\top = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B^\top \mathbf A = \mathbf A^\top \mathbf B \mathbf A$
(@exr-bilinear-change-basis).

## SageMath

Check on the symmetric matrix $\mathbf S$ of @exm-symmetric-quadratic and a random invertible change of basis.

```{.python .sage}
set_random_seed(2)
S = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2], [2, 4]])
A = random_matrix(ZZ, 2, 2, algorithm="unimodular").change_ring(QQ)
Sp = A.transpose() * S * A
print("A =", A.rows(), "; A^T S A =", Sp.rows(), "; symmetric:", Sp.is_symmetric())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
A = [(1, 2), (-4, -7)] ; A^T S A = [(49, 84), (84, 144)] ; symmetric: True
```
::::
:::

The symmetric and the antisymmetric forms are two subspaces of the space of bilinear forms. The exercise computes
their dimensions and checks that they add up to $n^2$ [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.8].

::: {#exr-symmetric-dimension}
#### Counting symmetric and antisymmetric forms

Show that the symmetric bilinear forms on an $n$-dimensional space form a subspace of dimension $n(n + 1)/2$, and the
antisymmetric ones a subspace of dimension $n(n - 1)/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Sums and multiples of symmetric forms are symmetric, and likewise for antisymmetric ones, so both are subspaces. In a
basis a symmetric form is determined by its entries $B_{ij}$ with $i \leq j$, which can be chosen freely: the forms
$E^{ii}$ and $E^{ij} + E^{ji}$ for $i < j$ (@exr-bilinear-space-dim) are a basis, $n + n(n - 1)/2 = n(n + 1)/2$ of them.
An antisymmetric form has $B_{ii} = -B_{ii} = 0$ and is determined by its entries with $i < j$, with basis $E^{ij} -
E^{ji}$, $n(n - 1)/2$ of them. The sum is $n^2$, as it must be by @exr-symmetric-decompose.

## SageMath

Sage computes the dimensions of the spaces of symmetric and antisymmetric $n \times n$ matrices as kernels of $\mathbf B
\mapsto \mathbf B - \mathbf B^\top$ and $\mathbf B \mapsto \mathbf B + \mathbf B^\top$.

```{.python .sage}
for n in range(1, 6):
    Mn = MatrixSpace(QQ, n)
    basis = Mn.basis().list()
    vec = lambda M: vector(QQ, M.list())
    sym = matrix(QQ, [vec(E - E.transpose()) for E in basis]).left_kernel().dimension()
    alt = matrix(QQ, [vec(E + E.transpose()) for E in basis]).left_kernel().dimension()
    print("n =", n, ": symmetric", sym, "= n(n+1)/2 =", n * (n + 1) // 2, "; antisymmetric", alt, "= n(n-1)/2 =", n * (n - 1) // 2)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n = 1 : symmetric 1 = n(n+1)/2 = 1 ; antisymmetric 0 = n(n-1)/2 = 0
n = 2 : symmetric 3 = n(n+1)/2 = 3 ; antisymmetric 1 = n(n-1)/2 = 1
n = 3 : symmetric 6 = n(n+1)/2 = 6 ; antisymmetric 3 = n(n-1)/2 = 3
n = 4 : symmetric 10 = n(n+1)/2 = 10 ; antisymmetric 6 = n(n-1)/2 = 6
n = 5 : symmetric 15 = n(n+1)/2 = 15 ; antisymmetric 10 = n(n-1)/2 = 10
```
::::
:::

Which functions on $V$ are quadratic forms can be decided without naming a bilinear form. The exercise proves a test
by scaling and polarisation, and applies it to a function that passes the scaling test but fails the other
[@axler2024linear, result 9.21].

::: {#exr-symmetric-quadratic-characterisation}
#### Recognising a quadratic form

Let $Q : V \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $Q(2v) = 4Q(v)$, and suppose that $\beta(u, w) = Q(u + w) - Q(u) - Q(w)$ is a
symmetric bilinear form. Prove that $Q(v) = B(v, v)$ for the symmetric form $B = \tfrac12\beta$. Show that $Q(x, y) =
x^2 + y|y|$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $Q(2v) = 4Q(v)$ but is not a quadratic form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$B(v, v) = \tfrac12\beta(v, v) = \tfrac12(Q(2v) - 2Q(v)) = \tfrac12(4Q(v) - 2Q(v)) = Q(v)$. For $Q(x, y) = x^2 + y|y|$,
$Q(2x, 2y) = 4x^2 + 2y|2y| = 4Q(x, y)$. If $Q$ were the quadratic form of a symmetric $B$, polarisation (@def-symmetric-form)
would make $\beta = 2B$ bilinear, so $\beta(u, -u) = -\beta(u, u)$. For $u = (0, 1)$: $\beta(u, u) = Q(0, 2) - 2Q(0, 1) =
4 - 2 = 2$, but $\beta(u, -u) = Q(0, 0) - Q(0, 1) - Q(0, -1) = 0 - 1 + 1 = 0 \neq -2$. So $Q$ is not a quadratic form.

## SageMath

Sage checks the scaling law of $x^2 + y|y|$ on a few points and evaluates $\beta(u, u)$ and $\beta(u, -u)$.

```{.python .sage}
Q = lambda v: v[0]^2 + v[1] * abs(v[1])
beta = lambda u, w: Q(u + w) - Q(u) - Q(w)
pts = [vector(QQ, p) for p in [(1, 2), (-3, 1), (2, -5)]]
print("Q(2v) == 4 Q(v) at three points:", all(Q(2 * p) == 4 * Q(p) for p in pts))
u = vector(QQ, [0, 1])
print("beta(u, u) =", beta(u, u), "; beta(u, -u) =", beta(u, -u), "(bilinearity needs", -beta(u, u), ")")
```

```{.text .sage-output}
Q(2v) == 4 Q(v) at three points: True
beta(u, u) = 2 ; beta(u, -u) = 0 (bilinearity needs -2 )
```
::::
:::

A form defined by an integral can be symmetric for a reason that is not visible in its formula. The last exercise
combines integration by parts with a subspace defined by boundary conditions, and checks the result on cubic
polynomials [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9A.10].

::: {#exr-symmetric-integral-form}
#### Symmetric thanks to the boundary conditions

Let $V$ be the polynomials $p$ of degree at most $3$ with $p(0) = p(1)$ and $p'(0) = p'(1)$. Show that $V$ is a subspace,
that $\rho(p, q) = \int_0^1 p(x) q''(x)\, dx$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $V$, find a basis of $V$, and compute the
matrix of $\rho$ in it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The two conditions are linear, so $V$ is a subspace, the kernel of a linear map to $\mathbb{R}^2$ (@def-linear-map), and
$\rho$ is bilinear by linearity of the integral and of $q \mapsto q''$. Integrating by parts, $\rho(p, q) = [p q']_0^1 -
\int_0^1 p' q'$, and $[p q']_0^1 = p(1) q'(1) - p(0) q'(0) = p(0)\big(q'(1) - q'(0)\big) = 0$ on $V$. So $\rho(p, q) =
-\int_0^1 p' q'$, which is symmetric in $p$ and $q$. For $p = a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3$ the conditions read $b + c + d = 0$ and
$2c + 3d = 0$, so $d = -\tfrac23 c$, $b = -\tfrac13 c$: $V$ has basis $p_1 = 1$, $p_2 = -x + 3x^2 - 2x^3$. Then $\rho(p_1,
\cdot) = \rho(\cdot, p_1) = 0$ because $p_1' = 0$, and $\rho(p_2, p_2) = -\int_0^1 (-1 + 6x - 6x^2)^2\, dx = -\tfrac15$.
The matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(0, -\tfrac15)$.

## SageMath

Sage solves the two conditions for a basis and computes the matrix of $\rho$ from its definition.

```{.python .sage}
R.<x> = QQ[]
a, b, c, d, t = var("a b c d t")
p = a + b * t + c * t^2 + d * t^3
print("conditions solved:", solve([p.subs(t=1) - p.subs(t=0), diff(p, t).subs(t=1) - diff(p, t).subs(t=0)], b, d))
basis = [R(1), -x + 3 * x^2 - 2 * x^3]
print("basis in V:", all(q(0) == q(1) and q.derivative()(0) == q.derivative()(1) for q in basis))
rho = lambda p, q: (p * q.derivative(x, 2)).integral()(1) - (p * q.derivative(x, 2)).integral()(0)
M = matrix(QQ, 2, 2, lambda i, j: rho(basis[i], basis[j]))
print("matrix of rho:", M.rows(), "; symmetric:", M.is_symmetric())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
conditions solved: [
[b == -1/3*c, d == -2/3*c]
]
basis in V: True
matrix of rho: [(0, 0), (0, -1/5)] ; symmetric: True
```
::::
:::
::::

### Non-degenerate forms

![The Minkowski form $\eta(v, v) = t^2 - x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$: the light cone $\eta = 0$ and the timelike
($\eta > 0$) and spacelike ($\eta < 0$) regions.](figures/minkowski_cone.svg){#fig-minkowski-cone width=45%}

{{< interactive minkowski_cone 520 >}}

A form may have directions that pair to zero with everything, and when it has none it identifies vectors with
covectors. The definition names this property, gives the matrix test, and introduces the lowering and raising of
indices; the light cone above is the picture for the Minkowski form.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-nondegenerate}
#### Non-degenerate bilinear form

A bilinear form is **non-degenerate** if $B(v, w) = 0$ for all $w$ forces $v = 0$; equivalently its matrix
$B_{ij}$ is invertible. A non-degenerate form identifies $V$ with $V^*$ by $v \mapsto B(v, \cdot)$,
which in components is **lowering an index**, $v_i = B_{ij} v^j$; the inverse matrix $B^{ij}$ **raises** it.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the line the matrix is one number, and the matrix test asks only whether it vanishes. The first example
settles non-degeneracy for all the forms of @exm-bilinear-line at once.

::: {#exm-nondegenerate-line}
#### Forms on the line

$B(x, y) = cxy$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is non-degenerate exactly when $c \neq 0$: then $B(x, 1) = cx = 0$ forces $x = 0$. Lowering
the index sends $x$ to the functional $y \mapsto cxy$, the number $cx$, and raising divides by $c$. For $c = 0$ every $x$
pairs to zero with everything.
:::

Both running forms pass the test. The example stresses that non-degeneracy allows null vectors: $\eta$
vanishes on $(1, 1, 0, 0)$ and yet no non-zero vector pairs to zero with everything.

::: {#exm-nondegenerate-minkowski}
