trilinear case and its simplest instance on $\mathbb{R}^3$ [@axler2024linear, Example 9.86].

::: {#exm-multilinear-product}
#### Products of functionals

For covectors $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ on $V$, $(u, v, w) \mapsto \alpha(u)\beta(v)\gamma(w)$ is trilinear; its value
is a product of three linear functions, one of each argument. With the dual basis of @def-dual-basis on
$\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\alpha = e^1$, $\beta = e^2$, $\gamma = e^3$ it is $(u, v, w) \mapsto u^1 v^2 w^3$.
:::

The two products of vector algebra in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are the next familiar cases. The example also shows why the cross
product, although bilinear, is not a multilinear map in the sense of the definition [@lee2013introduction, Example
12.1].

::: {#exm-multilinear-dot-triple}
#### Dot, cross and triple products

The dot product $(u, v) \mapsto u \cdot v$ is bilinear on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the triple product $(u, v, w) \mapsto
u \cdot (v \times w)$ is trilinear on $\mathbb{R}^3$. The cross product $(v, w) \mapsto v \times w$ is linear in each
argument too, but its values are vectors, not numbers; each of its components $e^k(v \times w)$ is a bilinear map
in the sense of @def-multilinear-map.
:::

On the plane, the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by two vectors is bilinear and changes sign when the two
are swapped. The example records both properties and gives the second one its name.

::: {#exm-multilinear-det}
#### Signed area

$\omega(u, v) = u^1 v^2 - u^2 v^1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is bilinear: each term is a product of one coordinate of $u$ and one
of $v$. It is **alternating**: it changes sign when the two arguments are swapped, and $\omega(u, u) = 0$. Its value is
the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by $u$ and $v$; the triple product of @exm-multilinear-dot-triple is the
signed volume on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and it is alternating in the same way.
:::

Multilinear maps need not have vectors of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as arguments; matrices will do. The example multiplies $m$
matrices and takes the sum of the diagonal entries [@axler2024linear, Example 9.26].

::: {#exm-multilinear-trace}
#### The diagonal sum of a product

On the space of $n \times n$ matrices, $(\mathbf X_1, \dots, \mathbf X_m) \mapsto \sum_i (\mathbf X_1 \cdots \mathbf X_m)_{ii}$ is $m$-linear:
the product is linear in each factor when the others are fixed, and taking the sum of the diagonal entries is linear.
For $m = 2$ and the matrix units $\mathbf E_{12}$, $\mathbf E_{21}$ of $2 \times 2$ matrices, $\mathbf E_{12}\mathbf E_{21} = \mathbf E_{11}$ and
$\mathbf E_{21}\mathbf E_{12} = \mathbf E_{22}$ both have diagonal sum $1$, while $\mathbf E_{12}\mathbf E_{12} = \mathbf 0$ has diagonal sum $0$.
:::

Angular momentum gives a first physical multilinear map. The example takes its component along a fixed direction,
which is a triple product, and evaluates it on the orbit of a planar harmonic oscillator.

::: {#exm-multilinear-angular-momentum}
#### Angular momentum of an oscillator

The component of angular momentum along a unit vector $\mathbf n$ of a particle at $\mathbf x$ with momentum
$\mathbf p$ is $L_{\mathbf n} = \mathbf n \cdot (\mathbf x \times \mathbf p)$, trilinear in $(\mathbf n, \mathbf x,
\mathbf p)$. For the planar oscillator $\mathbf x(t) = (A\cos\omega t, B\sin\omega t, 0)$ of mass $m$, $\mathbf p =
m\dot{\mathbf x} = m\omega(-A\sin\omega t, B\cos\omega t, 0)$ and $L_z = m\omega AB(\cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t)
= m\omega AB$, constant in time.
:::

In four dimensions the signed area and the signed volume continue to the Levi-Civita symbol of Minkowski space. The example writes it as a
four-linear map of four-vectors and evaluates it on two lists.

::: {#exm-multilinear-levi-civita}
#### The Levi-Civita symbol on Minkowski space

On $\mathbb{R}^4$ with coordinates $x^\mu$, $\epsilon(u, v, w, z) = \epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} u^\mu v^\nu w^\rho
z^\sigma$ with $\epsilon_{0123} = +1$ is $4$-linear and alternating. It gives $\epsilon(e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3) = 1$ and $\epsilon(e_0, e_1, e_2, e_0 + e_3) = 1$, but
$\epsilon(e_1, e_0, e_2, e_3) = -1$.
:::

The rotational inertia of a rigid body is a multilinear map with much physics in it. The example also shows a
function of one vector, the moment of inertia about an axis, that is not linear, to mark the boundary of the notion.

::: {#exm-multilinear-inertia}
#### Moments of inertia

For point masses $m_k$ at $\mathbf x_k$, $I(\mathbf u, \mathbf v) = \sum_k m_k\big((\mathbf x_k \cdot \mathbf x_k)(\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v) -
(\mathbf x_k \cdot \mathbf u)(\mathbf x_k \cdot \mathbf v)\big)$ is bilinear on $\mathbb{R}^3$, with the components $I_{ij}$ of the
inertia tensor of @exm-dim-inertia. The moment of inertia about the axis of $\mathbf v \neq 0$, $K(\mathbf v) = I(\mathbf v, \mathbf v) /
(\mathbf v \cdot \mathbf v)$, is a ratio of two expressions that are each bilinear in the list $(\mathbf v, \mathbf v)$; it is not
linear, since $K(2\mathbf v) = K(\mathbf v)$: numerator and denominator both pick up a factor $4$.
:::

Linearity in each slot is not linearity on the product space. The example shows that the two notions exclude each
other except for the zero map.

::: {#exm-multilinear-not-linear}
#### Bilinear is not linear

$f(x, y) = xy$ is bilinear on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, but it is not a linear map $\mathbb{R}^2 \to
\mathbb{R}$: $f(2, 2) = 4 \neq 2 = 2 f(1, 1)$. A bilinear map scales as $f(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda^2 f(x,
y)$, quadratically in the pair. Conversely $g(x, y) = x + y$ is linear, but not bilinear, since $x \mapsto x + y$ is
not linear for $y \neq 0$; only the zero map is both.
:::

Alternating maps with more arguments than dimensions have nowhere to go. The last example shows that on $\mathbb{R}^2$
every alternating trilinear map vanishes [@axler2024linear, 9.29].

::: {#exm-multilinear-alternating-zero}
#### Too many arguments

An alternating map vanishes when two arguments coincide, since swapping them changes the sign but not the value. Let
$T$ be alternating and trilinear on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Expanding $u, v, w$ in $e_1, e_2$ writes $T(u, v, w)$ as a sum of
terms $u^i v^j w^k\, T(e_i, e_j, e_k)$, and in each of them two of the three indices are equal, so $T = 0$. In general
an alternating $k$-linear map with $k > \dim V$ is zero.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Trilinearity on $\mathbb{R}^3$ is tested slot by slot. The exercise presents three expressions built from dot and
cross products and asks which are trilinear, naming the slot that fails.

::: {#exr-multilinear-check}
#### Which maps are trilinear?

Decide which of the following maps $\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ are
trilinear: $(u, v, w) \mapsto u \cdot (v \times w)$; $(u, v, w) \mapsto |u|\,(v \cdot w)$; $(u, v, w) \mapsto (u
\cdot v)(v \cdot w)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The triple product $u \cdot (v \times w)$ is trilinear (@exm-multilinear-dot-triple). $|u|\,(v \cdot w)$
is not linear in $u$: $|{-u}| = |u|$, not $-|u|$, so for $v \cdot w \neq 0$ the value does not change sign with $u$.
$(u \cdot v)(v \cdot w)$ is quadratic in $v$: replacing $v$ by $2v$ multiplies it by $4$, not $2$. The first map is
trilinear; the second fails in the first slot and the third in the second slot.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates each map at a sample point after scaling one slot by $2$ and by $-1$, which a linear slot must follow.

```{.python .sage}
u, v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 3]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, -1]), vector(QQ, [2, 0, 1])
maps = {"u.(v x w)": lambda u, v, w: u * v.cross_product(w),
        "|u| (v.w)": lambda u, v, w: u.norm() * (v * w),
        "(u.v)(v.w)": lambda u, v, w: (u * v) * (v * w)}
for name, T in maps.items():
    slots = []
    for k in range(3):
        args = [u, v, w]
        ok = True
        for c in [2, -1]:
            a = list(args); a[k] = c * a[k]
            ok = ok and bool(T(*a) == c * T(*args))
        slots.append(ok)
    print(name, ": homogeneous of degree 1 in slots 1, 2, 3:", slots)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
u.(v x w) : homogeneous of degree 1 in slots 1, 2, 3: [True, True, True]
|u| (v.w) : homogeneous of degree 1 in slots 1, 2, 3: [False, True, True]
(u.v)(v.w) : homogeneous of degree 1 in slots 1, 2, 3: [True, False, True]
```
::::
:::

Two consequences of linearity in each slot are immediate. The exercise asks for them and checks the second on the
triple product, where it says that doubling a box multiplies its volume by eight.

::: {#exr-multilinear-scaling}
#### Zero arguments and scaling

Show that a $k$-linear map $T$ vanishes as soon as one argument is $0$, and that $T(\lambda v_1, \dots, \lambda v_k) =
\lambda^k T(v_1, \dots, v_k)$. What does this give for the triple product and $\lambda = 2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Linearity in the $i$-th slot gives $T(\dots, 0, \dots) = T(\dots, 0 \cdot 0, \dots) = 0 \cdot T(\dots, 0, \dots) =
0$. Pulling $\lambda$ out of each of the $k$ slots in turn gives $\lambda^k$. For the triple product ($k = 3$),
$(2u) \cdot (2v \times 2w) = 8\, u \cdot (v \times w)$: the box spanned by $2u, 2v, 2w$ has eight times the volume.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the triple product at $(2u, 2v, 2w)$ and at $(u, v, 0)$ for a sample triple.

```{.python .sage}
u, v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 3]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, -1]), vector(QQ, [2, 0, 1])
T = lambda u, v, w: u * v.cross_product(w)
print("T(u, v, w) =", T(u, v, w), "; T(2u, 2v, 2w) =", T(2 * u, 2 * v, 2 * w), "= 2^3 T(u, v, w):", T(2 * u, 2 * v, 2 * w) == 8 * T(u, v, w))
print("T(u, v, 0) =", T(u, v, zero_vector(QQ, 3)))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
T(u, v, w) = -9 ; T(2u, 2v, 2w) = -72 = 2^3 T(u, v, w): True
T(u, v, 0) = 0
```
::::
:::

A trilinear map on $\mathbb{R}^3$ is fixed by its $27$ values on triples of basis vectors, most of which may vanish.
The exercise computes them for a simple instance, counts them, and evaluates the map by summing components times
arguments.

::: {#exr-trilinear-components}
#### Components of a trilinear map

For $T(u, v, w) = u^1 v^2 w^3 - u^2 v^1 w^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, find the values $T_{ijk} = T(e_i, e_j, e_k)$,
count how many such values a trilinear map on $\mathbb{R}^3$ has, and evaluate $T$ on $u = (1, 2, 3)$,
$v = (0, 1, -1)$, $w = (2, 0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$T(e_i, e_j, e_k) = \delta^1{}_i \delta^2{}_j \delta^3{}_k - \delta^2{}_i \delta^1{}_j \delta^3{}_k$, so
$T_{123} = 1$, $T_{213} = -1$, and the other $25$ of the $3^3 = 27$ values vanish. By trilinearity
$T(u, v, w) = T_{ijk} u^i v^j w^k = u^1 v^2 w^3 - u^2 v^1 w^3 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 0 \cdot 1 = 1$.

## SageMath

Sage builds $T$ on a free module of rank $3$ (indices from $1$), lists its non-zero values on basis triples and
evaluates it.

```{.python .sage}
V = FiniteRankFreeModule(QQ, 3, name="V", start_index=1)
e = V.basis("e")
T = V.tensor((0, 3), name="T")
T[1, 2, 3] = 1; T[2, 1, 3] = -1
nonzero = [(i, j, k) for i in range(1, 4) for j in range(1, 4) for k in range(1, 4) if T[i, j, k] != 0]
print("non-zero T_ijk at", nonzero, "; number of values: 3^3 =", 3 ^ 3)
u = V([1, 2, 3], basis=e); v = V([0, 1, -1], basis=e); w = V([2, 0, 1], basis=e)
print("T(u, v, w) =", T(u, v, w), "; formula u1 v2 w3 - u2 v1 w3 =", 1 * 1 * 1 - 2 * 0 * 1)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
non-zero T_ijk at [(1, 2, 3), (2, 1, 3)] ; number of values: 3^3 = 27
T(u, v, w) = 1 ; formula u1 v2 w3 - u2 v1 w3 = 1
```
::::
:::

A formula with six signed terms hides an alternating map. The exercise asks for the check that the expression below
is trilinear and vanishes on repeated arguments [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9B.2].

::: {#exr-multilinear-six-terms}
#### An alternating trilinear form

On $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \geq 3$, let $\alpha(x, y, z) = x^1 y^2 z^3 - x^2 y^1 z^3 - x^3 y^2 z^1 - x^1 y^3 z^2 + x^3 y^1
z^2 + x^2 y^3 z^1$. Show that $\alpha$ is trilinear, that it vanishes when two of its arguments are equal, and that it
changes sign when two arguments are swapped.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Each term is a product of one coordinate of $x$, one of $y$ and one of $z$, and coordinates are linear, so $\alpha$
is trilinear (@exm-multilinear-product). For $y = x$ the terms cancel in pairs: $x^1x^2z^3 - x^2x^1z^3 = 0$, $-x^3x^2z^1
+ x^2x^3z^1 = 0$ and $-x^1x^3z^2 + x^3x^1z^2 = 0$; the cases $z = x$ and $z = y$ cancel in the same way. Then
$0 = \alpha(x + y, x + y, z) = \alpha(x, y, z) + \alpha(y, x, z)$ by trilinearity, and likewise for the other pairs
of slots: $\alpha$ changes sign under every swap. It is the triple product $x' \cdot (y' \times z')$ of the vectors
$x', y', z'$ of the first three coordinates of $x, y, z$.

## SageMath

Sage expands $\alpha$ on symbolic vectors of $\mathbb{R}^4$ with two arguments equal, and with two swapped.

```{.python .sage}
X = vector(SR, var("x1 x2 x3 x4")); Y = vector(SR, var("y1 y2 y3 y4")); Z = vector(SR, var("z1 z2 z3 z4"))
def alpha(x, y, z):
    return x[0]*y[1]*z[2] - x[1]*y[0]*z[2] - x[2]*y[1]*z[0] - x[0]*y[2]*z[1] + x[2]*y[0]*z[1] + x[1]*y[2]*z[0]
print("alpha(x, x, z) =", alpha(X, X, Z).expand(), "; alpha(x, y, x) =", alpha(X, Y, X).expand(), "; alpha(x, y, y) =", alpha(X, Y, Y).expand())
print("alpha(y, x, z) + alpha(x, y, z) =", (alpha(Y, X, Z) + alpha(X, Y, Z)).expand(), "; alpha(x, z, y) + alpha(x, y, z) =", (alpha(X, Z, Y) + alpha(X, Y, Z)).expand())
print("equal to the triple product of the first three coordinates:", bool(alpha(X, Y, Z) == X[:3].dot_product(Y[:3].cross_product(Z[:3]))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
alpha(x, x, z) = 0 ; alpha(x, y, x) = 0 ; alpha(x, y, y) = 0
alpha(y, x, z) + alpha(x, y, z) = 0 ; alpha(x, z, y) + alpha(x, y, z) = 0
equal to the triple product of the first three coordinates: True
```
::::
:::

When two arguments of an alternating map coincide its value is zero, and conversely a form that vanishes on the
diagonal is antisymmetric. The exercise asks for both proofs and connects them to matrices with repeated columns.

::: {#exr-multilinear-alternating}
#### Alternating maps vanish on repeated arguments

Show that an alternating bilinear or multilinear map vanishes whenever two of its arguments coincide, and
conversely that a bilinear form with $B(v, v) = 0$ for all $v$ is antisymmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Swapping two equal arguments changes nothing but, by the alternating property, changes the sign: $T(\dots, v,
\dots, v, \dots) = -T(\dots, v, \dots, v, \dots)$, so the value is $0$. Conversely, $0 = B(v + w, v + w) = B(v, v) +
B(v, w) + B(w, v) + B(w, w) = B(v, w) + B(w, v)$, so $B(w, v) = -B(v, w)$. For the triple product this says that
$u \cdot (v \times w)$ vanishes when two of the three vectors are equal.

## SageMath

Check on the triple product of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and on the bilinear form $B(v, w) = v^1 w^2 - v^2 w^1$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$:
Sage evaluates both on repeated and swapped arguments.

```{.python .sage}
u, v = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 3]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, -1])
D = lambda a, b, c: a.dot_product(b.cross_product(c))
print("u.(v x u) =", D(u, v, u), "; u.(u x v) =", D(u, u, v))
B = lambda v, w: v[0] * w[1] - v[1] * w[0]
p, q = vector(QQ, [3, -1]), vector(QQ, [2, 5])
print("B(p, p) =", B(p, p), "; B(p, q) =", B(p, q), "; B(q, p) =", B(q, p))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
u.(v x u) = 0 ; u.(u x v) = 0
B(p, p) = 0 ; B(p, q) = 17 ; B(q, p) = -17
```
::::
:::

Vanishing on equal neighbours is already enough to make a map alternating. The exercise asks for the proof, which moves
two equal arguments next to each other one swap at a time [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9B.3].

::: {#exr-multilinear-adjacent}
#### Equal neighbours suffice

Let $T$ be $k$-linear on $V$ with $T(v_1, \dots, v_k) = 0$ whenever $v_j = v_{j+1}$ for some $j$. Prove that $T$
vanishes whenever any two arguments are equal, and hence that it is alternating.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

First, $T$ changes sign when two neighbouring arguments are swapped: expanding $0 = T(\dots, v + w, v + w, \dots)$ in
the slots $j, j + 1$ leaves $T(\dots, v, w, \dots) + T(\dots, w, v, \dots) = 0$, the two terms with equal neighbours
vanishing. Now let $v_i = v_j$ with $i < j$. Swapping the argument in slot $j$ with its left neighbour $j - i - 1$
times brings it to slot $i + 1$, next to the equal argument in slot $i$; each swap only changes the sign, so
$T(v_1, \dots, v_k) = \pm T(\dots, v_i, v_i, \dots) = 0$. Finally $0 = T(\dots, v + w, \dots, v + w, \dots)$ with the
sums in slots $i$ and $j$ gives, as before, a sign change under the swap of slots $i$ and $j$: $T$ is alternating.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the triple product $T(u, v, w) = u \cdot (v \times w)$, which vanishes on equal neighbours:
Sage evaluates it with equal first and third arguments and with those two arguments swapped.

```{.python .sage}
T = lambda a, b, c: a.dot_product(b.cross_product(c))
u, v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 3]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, -1]), vector(QQ, [2, 0, 1])
print("T(u, v, v) =", T(u, v, v), "; T(u, v, u) =", T(u, v, u), "; T(u, v, w) =", T(u, v, w), "; T(w, v, u) =", T(w, v, u))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
T(u, v, v) = 0 ; T(u, v, u) = 0 ; T(u, v, w) = -9 ; T(w, v, u) = 9
```
::::
:::

An alternating map detects linear dependence. The exercise asks for the proof that it vanishes on every dependent list,
and for the consequence for maps with more arguments than dimensions [@axler2024linear, 9.28-9.29],
[@scott2023problems, Problem 2.36].

::: {#exr-multilinear-dependent}
#### Alternating maps and linear dependence

Let $T$ be an alternating $k$-linear map on $V$. Prove that $T(v_1, \dots, v_k) = 0$ whenever $v_1, \dots, v_k$ are
linearly dependent (@def-linear-independence), and conclude that $T = 0$ when $k > \dim V$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If the list is dependent, some $v_m$ is a combination of the others, $v_m = \sum_{j \neq m} c_j v_j$. Linearity in
slot $m$ gives $T(v_1, \dots, v_k) = \sum_{j \neq m} c_j\, T(v_1, \dots, v_j, \dots, v_k)$ with $v_j$ in slot $m$;
each term has $v_j$ in two slots and vanishes (@exr-multilinear-alternating). If $k > \dim V$, every list of $k$
vectors is dependent (@def-dimension), so $T$ vanishes on every list: $T = 0$.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the triple product $T(u, v, w) = u \cdot (v \times w)$: Sage evaluates it on the dependent
list $(u, v, 2u - 3v)$ and on an independent one.

```{.python .sage}
T = lambda a, b, c: a.dot_product(b.cross_product(c))
u, v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 3]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, -1]), vector(QQ, [2, 0, 1])
print("T(u, v, 2u - 3v) =", T(u, v, 2 * u - 3 * v), "; T(u, v, w) =", T(u, v, w))
print("rank of (u, v, 2u - 3v):", matrix(QQ, [u, v, 2 * u - 3 * v]).rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
T(u, v, 2u - 3v) = 0 ; T(u, v, w) = -9
rank of (u, v, 2u - 3v): 2
```
::::
:::

The values on basis vectors determine a multilinear map completely, and any values may be prescribed. The exercise
asks for both directions, which identify $k$-linear maps on $V$ with arrays of $n^k$ numbers
[@lee2013introduction, Prop. 12.4].

::: {#exr-multilinear-basis-values}
#### Determined by basis values

Let $e_1, \dots, e_n$ be a basis of $V$. Show that a $k$-linear map $T$ on $V$ satisfies $T(v_1, \dots, v_k) =
T(e_{i_1}, \dots, e_{i_k})\, v_1^{i_1} \cdots v_k^{i_k}$, and that for every array of numbers $c_{i_1 \dots i_k}$ the
map $(v_1, \dots, v_k) \mapsto c_{i_1 \dots i_k} v_1^{i_1} \cdots v_k^{i_k}$ is $k$-linear with these values on basis
vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Write $v_m = v_m^{i} e_{i}$ and use linearity in each slot in turn: $T(v_1, \dots, v_k) = v_1^{i_1} T(e_{i_1}, v_2,
\dots, v_k) = \dots = v_1^{i_1} \cdots v_k^{i_k} T(e_{i_1}, \dots, e_{i_k})$. Conversely, each coordinate $v_m^{i}$
is linear in $v_m$ (@def-dual-basis), so each term $c_{i_1 \dots i_k} v_1^{i_1} \cdots v_k^{i_k}$ is linear in each
argument and so is the sum; at $(e_{j_1}, \dots, e_{j_k})$ only the term with $i_m = j_m$ for all $m$ survives, with
value $c_{j_1 \dots j_k}$.

## SageMath

Check on a trilinear map of $\mathbb{R}^2$: Sage fills an array of $8$ numbers, builds the map from it, and compares
its values on basis triples and on a sample triple with the formula.

```{.python .sage}
c = {(i, j, k): (i + 1) * 100 + (j + 1) * 10 + (k + 1) for i in range(2) for j in range(2) for k in range(2)}
T = lambda u, v, w: sum(c[i, j, k] * u[i] * v[j] * w[k] for (i, j, k) in c)
E = identity_matrix(QQ, 2).columns()
print("values on basis triples equal the array:", all(T(E[i], E[j], E[k]) == c[i, j, k] for (i, j, k) in c))
u, v, w = vector(QQ, [1, -1]), vector(QQ, [2, 3]), vector(QQ, [1, 4])
print("T(u, v, w) =", T(u, v, w), "; linear in the first slot:", T(2 * u + w, v, w) == 2 * T(u, v, w) + T(w, v, w))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
values on basis triples equal the array: True
T(u, v, w) = -2500 ; linear in the first slot: True
```
::::
:::

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n = k$ a non-zero alternating map is non-zero on every independent list; for $k < n$ this
fails. The exercise asks for an example on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and contrasts it with the signed area on $\mathbb{R}^2$
[@axler2024linear, Exercise 9B.7].

::: {#exr-multilinear-alternating-r3}
#### Fewer arguments than dimensions

Give a non-zero alternating bilinear form $\alpha$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and a linearly independent pair $v_1, v_2$ with
$\alpha(v_1, v_2) = 0$. Why can this not happen for the signed area $\omega(u, v) = u^1 v^2 - u^2 v^1$ on
$\mathbb{R}^2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\alpha(u, v) = u^1 v^2 - u^2 v^1$ is bilinear, alternating ($\alpha(u, u) = 0$) and non-zero ($\alpha(e_1, e_2) = 1$),
but $\alpha(e_1, e_3) = 0$ although $e_1, e_3$ are independent: $\alpha$ only sees the first two coordinates. On
$\mathbb{R}^2$, an independent pair $v_1, v_2$ is a basis (@def-dimension), so $e_1 = a v_1 + b v_2$, $e_2 = c v_1 +
d v_2$ and $1 = \omega(e_1, e_2) = (ad - bc)\,\omega(v_1, v_2)$ by bilinearity, $\omega(v_i, v_i) = 0$ and $\omega(v_2,
v_1) = -\omega(v_1, v_2)$; hence $\omega(v_1, v_2) \neq 0$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates $\alpha$ on $(e_1, e_2)$ and $(e_1, e_3)$, and the rank of the pair $e_1, e_3$.

```{.python .sage}
alpha = lambda u, v: u[0] * v[1] - u[1] * v[0]
e1, e2, e3 = identity_matrix(QQ, 3).columns()
print("alpha(e1, e2) =", alpha(e1, e2), "; alpha(e1, e3) =", alpha(e1, e3), "; rank of (e1, e3):", matrix(QQ, [e1, e3]).rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
alpha(e1, e2) = 1 ; alpha(e1, e3) = 0 ; rank of (e1, e3): 2
```
::::
:::

Every multilinear map can be turned into an alternating one by summing over permutations of its arguments with signs.
The last exercise proves this and finds the triple product as the result for the simplest trilinear product
[@axler2024linear, Exercise 9B.5].

::: {#exr-multilinear-antisymmetrise}
#### Antisymmetrisation

The sign of a permutation $\sigma$ of $(1, \dots, k)$ is $(-1)^N$, with $N$ the number of pairs that $\sigma$ puts out
of order, and swapping two entries of a permutation changes its sign. For a $k$-linear $\beta$ on $V$ let
$(\operatorname{Alt}\beta)(v_1, \dots, v_k) = \sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, \beta(v_{\sigma(1)}, \dots,
v_{\sigma(k)})$. Prove that $\operatorname{Alt}\beta$ is alternating, and compute it for $\beta(u, v, w) = u^1 v^2
w^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Each term is $k$-linear, so $\operatorname{Alt}\beta$ is. Let $\tau$ swap the slots $i$ and $j$. Then
$(\operatorname{Alt}\beta)(v_{\tau(1)}, \dots, v_{\tau(k)}) = \sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,
\beta(v_{\tau\sigma(1)}, \dots, v_{\tau\sigma(k)})$; as $\sigma$ runs over all permutations so does $\rho =
\tau\sigma$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = -\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)$ because $\rho$ differs from $\sigma$ by a
swap of two entries. The sum is $-(\operatorname{Alt}\beta)(v_1, \dots, v_k)$. For $\beta(u, v, w) = u^1 v^2 w^3$
the six terms are $\pm$ products of one coordinate of each argument, $\sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
x_{\sigma(1)}^1 x_{\sigma(2)}^2 x_{\sigma(3)}^3$ with $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (u, v, w)$: the six terms of the triple
product $u \cdot (v \times w)$, the form of @exr-multilinear-six-terms.

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{R}^3$: Sage sums over the permutations of $(1, 2, 3)$ with their signs and compares with the
triple product on symbolic vectors.

```{.python .sage}
U = [vector(SR, var("u1 u2 u3")), vector(SR, var("v1 v2 v3")), vector(SR, var("w1 w2 w3"))]
beta = lambda a, b, c: a[0] * b[1] * c[2]
alt = sum(s.sign() * beta(*[U[s(i + 1) - 1] for i in range(3)]) for s in Permutations(3))
print("Alt beta =", alt.expand())
print("equals u.(v x w):", bool(alt == U[0].dot_product(U[1].cross_product(U[2]))))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
Alt beta = -u3*v2*w1 + u2*v3*w1 + u3*v1*w2 - u1*v3*w2 - u2*v1*w3 + u1*v2*w3
equals u.(v x w): True
```
::::
:::
::::

### Tensor products

![Tensors as arrays: the components $u^i v^j$ of the elementary tensor $u \otimes v$, a rank-one matrix (left), a
sum of two elementary tensors, of rank two (middle), and a general element of $V \otimes V$ with nine independent
components (right).](figures/tensor_grid.svg){#fig-tensor-grid width=90%}

{{< interactive tensor_grid 360 >}}

Bilinear maps on pairs of covectors form a vector space, and this is the tensor product. The definition gives its
basis and its dimension, the product of the two dimensions; the figure above shows its elements as arrays.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-tensor-product-space}
#### Tensor product space

The **tensor product** $V \otimes W$ of two finite-dimensional vector spaces is the vector space of bilinear maps
$V^* \times W^* \to \mathbb{R}$. If $e_i$ is a basis of $V$ and $f_a$ a basis of $W$, the bilinear maps $e_i \otimes
f_a$ defined by $(e_i \otimes f_a)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(e_i)\beta(f_a)$ form a basis of $V \otimes W$, so
$\dim (V \otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest tensor product is that of the real line with itself. The example shows that it is again a line, spanned
by a single basis tensor.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-line}
#### $\mathbb{R} \otimes \mathbb{R}$

With the basis $e_1 = 1$ of $\mathbb{R}$ and its dual basis $e^1$, $\mathbb{R} \otimes \mathbb{R}$ has the single basis
element $e_1 \otimes e_1$, the bilinear map $(\alpha, \beta) \mapsto \alpha_1 \beta_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^* \times
\mathbb{R}^*$. Every element is $c\, e_1 \otimes e_1$, and $\dim(\mathbb{R} \otimes \mathbb{R}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$.
:::

The tensor square of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the standard case and the one drawn in the figure. The example identifies its
elements with $3 \times 3$ arrays.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-dim}
#### $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$

$\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$ has dimension $9$, with basis $e_i \otimes e_j$, $i, j = 1, 2, 3$; an element
$T = T^{ij} e_i \otimes e_j$ is a $3 \times 3$ array of coefficients $T^{ij} = T(e^i, e^j)$ (@fig-tensor-grid;
hovering a cell of the interactive figure shows its component).
:::

The tensor product multiplies dimensions where the Cartesian product adds them. The example compares the two and finds
the only case in which they agree [@axler2024linear, Sec. 9D, p. 370].

::: {#exm-tensor-space-product-vs-sum}
#### Products multiply, pairs add

$V \times W$, the space of pairs with componentwise operations, has dimension $m + n$ for $\dim V = m$, $\dim W = n$,
while $\dim(V \otimes W) = mn$. For $\mathbb{R}^3$ these are $6$ and $9$. They agree only when $mn = m + n$, that is
$(m - 1)(n - 1) = 1$, so $m = n = 2$ (or $m = n = 0$): even then the two spaces are different constructions of the
same dimension.
:::

Tensoring two copies of the dual recovers the bilinear forms of the previous section. The example records this, with
the Minkowski form as the element to remember.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-dual}
#### $V^* \otimes V^*$ and bilinear forms

$V^* \otimes V^*$ is the space of bilinear maps $V^{**} \times V^{**} \to \mathbb{R}$, and $V^{**}$ is $V$
(@exm-dual-space-dual-dual): it is the space of bilinear forms of @def-bilinear-form, with basis $e^i \otimes e^j$
and $B = B_{ij}\, e^i \otimes e^j$. The Minkowski form is $\eta = e^0 \otimes e^0 - e^1 \otimes e^1 - e^2 \otimes
e^2 - e^3 \otimes e^3$ in $(\mathbb{R}^4)^* \otimes (\mathbb{R}^4)^*$.
:::

Mixing one dual factor with one original factor gives the linear maps of $V$ to itself. The example builds the map
from the bilinear one and finds its matrix among the components.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-mixed}
#### $V^* \otimes V$ and linear maps

An element $T$ of $V^* \otimes V$ is a bilinear map on $V \times V^*$. For fixed $w \in V$, $\beta \mapsto T(w, \beta)$
is a linear functional on $V^*$, hence a vector $L(w)$ of $V$ (@exm-dual-space-dual-dual), and $w \mapsto L(w)$ is
linear: $V^* \otimes V$ is the space of linear maps $V \to V$, whose matrix entries are $L^i{}_j = T(e_j, e^i)$. Its
dimension is $9$ for $\dim V = 3$, the number of entries of a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
:::

Polynomials give a tensor product that one can see. The example identifies the product of two spaces of linear
polynomials with the polynomials of two variables that are linear in each.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-polynomials}
#### Polynomials in two variables

Let $P_1^x$ and $P_1^y$ be the polynomials of degree at most $1$ in $x$ and in $y$, with bases $1, x$ and $1, y$.
Sending the four basis tensors $1 \otimes 1$, $x \otimes 1$, $1 \otimes y$, $x \otimes y$ to $1, x, y, xy$ identifies
$P_1^x \otimes P_1^y$ with the polynomials $a + bx + cy + dxy$, which are of degree at most one in each variable
separately. The polynomials of total degree at most $2$ form a space of dimension $6$: it contains $x^2$, which is not
of this form.
:::

Quantum mechanics builds the states of composite systems as tensor products. The example takes two spins one-half, with
real coefficients for simplicity, and counts the states of $n$ spins [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6.2, eqs.
(3.139) and (3.154)].

::: {#exm-tensor-space-two-spins}
#### Two spins

The states of one spin one-half are combinations of $\lvert 0\rangle$ (up) and $\lvert 1\rangle$ (down), a space of
dimension $2$. Two spins live in $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$, with basis $\lvert ij\rangle = \lvert i\rangle
\otimes \lvert j\rangle$, $i, j \in \{0, 1\}$, and a general state $\sum \psi^{ij}\lvert ij\rangle$ has four
coefficients. Iterating, $n$ spins have a state space of dimension $2^n$: $1024$ for ten spins, against the $2n = 20$
numbers needed to describe ten separate spins.
:::

The two-dimensional harmonic oscillator is two independent one-dimensional ones. The example builds its states as a
tensor product and reads off the degeneracies of its energy levels.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-oscillator}
#### The two-dimensional oscillator

The states of a one-dimensional oscillator are spanned by the states $\lvert n\rangle$, $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, of
definite energy $(n + \tfrac12)\hbar\omega$. Keeping the levels $n < N$ gives a space $V_N$ of dimension $N$, and the
two-dimensional oscillator has the basis $\lvert n_1\rangle \otimes \lvert n_2\rangle$ of $V_N \otimes V_N$, with energy
$(n_1 + n_2 + 1)\hbar\omega$. The level $n_1 + n_2 = n < N$ contains the $n + 1$ states $(n_1, n_2) = (0, n), \dots,
(n, 0)$: degeneracies $1, 2, 3, \dots$.
:::

Continuum mechanics has a two-index object of its own, the stress in a material. The example places it in a tensor
product of duals and counts its components.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-stress}
#### The stress tensor

The Cauchy stress at a point of a body assigns to a unit normal $\mathbf n$ of a small surface element and a direction
$\mathbf m$ the component along $\mathbf m$ of the force per unit area across it, $\sigma(\mathbf n, \mathbf m)$, and
this is bilinear: $\sigma \in (\mathbb{R}^3)^* \otimes (\mathbb{R}^3)^*$ has the $9$ components $\sigma_{ij}$. For a
fluid at rest under pressure $p$, $\sigma_{ij} = -p\,\delta_{ij}$, the same in every orthonormal basis.
:::

Factors of dimension $0$ and $1$ are the degenerate cases of the product formula. The last example looks at them: a
zero factor kills the product and a line changes nothing.

::: {#exm-tensor-space-degenerate}
#### Zero and one

If $W = \{0\}$, then $W^* = \{0\}$ and the only bilinear map on $V^* \times \{0\}$ is zero: $V \otimes \{0\} = \{0\}$,
of dimension $\dim V \cdot 0 = 0$. If $W = \mathbb{R}$, $\dim(V \otimes \mathbb{R}) = \dim V$, and the basis
$e_i \otimes e_1$ corresponds to the basis $e_i$ of $V$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Four tensors $e_i \otimes e_j$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$, and a general tensor is a
combination of them. The exercise asks the reader to evaluate such a tensor on two covectors, which is a sum of
components times the components of the arguments.

::: {#exr-tensor-basis-r2}
#### The basis of $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$

List the basis $e_i \otimes e_j$ of $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$, write a general element with components
$T^{ij}$, and evaluate it as a bilinear map on the covectors $\alpha = (1, 2)$, $\beta = (3, -1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The basis is $e_1 \otimes e_1, e_1 \otimes e_2, e_2 \otimes e_1, e_2 \otimes e_2$, and $T = T^{ij} e_i \otimes e_j$.
Since $(e_i \otimes e_j)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(e_i)\beta(e_j) = \alpha_i \beta_j$, $T(\alpha, \beta) =
T^{ij}\alpha_i\beta_j = 3T^{11} - T^{12} + 6T^{21} - 2T^{22}$: a tensor acts on its arguments by summing its
components against theirs.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the general element on $(\alpha, \beta)$ with symbolic components.

```{.python .sage}
T = matrix(SR, 2, 2, var("T11 T12 T21 T22"))
alpha, beta = vector(SR, [1, 2]), vector(SR, [3, -1])
print("T(alpha, beta) = T^ij alpha_i beta_j =", (alpha * T * beta).expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
T(alpha, beta) = T^ij alpha_i beta_j = 3*T11 - T12 + 6*T21 - 2*T22
```
::::
:::

The difference of two basis tensors is the simplest tensor with a symmetry. The exercise asks for its values on
covectors and checks that it changes sign when its arguments are exchanged.

::: {#exr-tensor-space-antisymmetric}
#### An antisymmetric element

Let $T = e_1 \otimes e_2 - e_2 \otimes e_1 \in \mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$. Compute $T(\alpha, \beta)$, its
component array, and show that $T(\beta, \alpha) = -T(\alpha, \beta)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$T(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha_1\beta_2 - \alpha_2\beta_1$, with components $T^{12} = 1$, $T^{21} = -1$, $T^{11} = T^{22}
= 0$: the array $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Exchanging $\alpha$ and $\beta$ gives $\beta_1\alpha_2
- \beta_2\alpha_1 = -T(\alpha, \beta)$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates $T$ on symbolic covectors in both orders.

```{.python .sage}
a1, a2, b1, b2 = var("a1 a2 b1 b2")
T = matrix(QQ, [[0, 1], [-1, 0]])
al, be = vector(SR, [a1, a2]), vector(SR, [b1, b2])
print("T(alpha, beta) =", al * T * be, "; T(beta, alpha) + T(alpha, beta) =", (be * T * al + al * T * be).expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
T(alpha, beta) = -a2*b1 + a1*b2 ; T(beta, alpha) + T(alpha, beta) = 0
```
::::
:::

Dimensions of tensor products multiply, so products of several factors have dimensions that are products of several
numbers. The exercise asks for two such counts and for the general $n^k$, with $V \otimes W \otimes U$ the trilinear
maps on $V^* \times W^* \times U^*$ [@axler2024linear, 9.88-9.89].

::: {#exr-tensor-dim-general}
#### Dimensions of iterated tensor products

Find $\dim(V \otimes W \otimes U)$ for $\dim V = 2$, $\dim W = 3$, $\dim U = 4$, and $\dim(V^{\otimes k})$ for
$\dim V = n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

As for two factors, the trilinear maps $e_i \otimes f_a \otimes g_b$, $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \mapsto
\alpha(e_i)\beta(f_a)\gamma(g_b)$, with $i, a, b$ ranging independently, form a basis: a trilinear map is determined
by its values on triples of dual basis vectors, which may be prescribed freely (the argument of
@exr-multilinear-basis-values, with a basis in each slot). That
gives $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$ basis elements, and $V^{\otimes k}$ has $n^k$: a tensor with $k$ indices in dimension
$n$ has $n^k$ components.

## SageMath

Sage counts the index triples and the index $k$-tuples for $n = 3$.

```{.python .sage}
print("dim(V (x) W (x) U) =", len(list(cartesian_product([range(2), range(3), range(4)]))))
print("dim of V^(x)k for n = 3, k = 1..4:", [len(list(cartesian_product([range(3)] * k))) for k in range(1, 5)])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
dim(V (x) W (x) U) = 24
dim of V^(x)k for n = 3, k = 1..4: [3, 9, 27, 81]
```
::::
:::

SageManifolds' free modules implement tensors with their components. The exercise builds an element of
$V \otimes V$ from its array, prints the dimensions of $V \otimes V$ and $V^* \otimes V$, and evaluates the element
on two covectors.

::: {#exr-tensor-components}
#### Tensors on a free module

With SageManifolds' `FiniteRankFreeModule` on $\mathbb{Q}^3$, build $T = T^{ij} e_i \otimes e_j$ with
$T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$, print the dimensions of $V \otimes V$ and
$V^* \otimes V$, and check that $T(\alpha, \beta) = T^{ij}\alpha_i\beta_j$ for $\alpha = (1, 0, -1)$,
$\beta = (0, 1, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Both spaces have dimension $3 \cdot 3 = 9$ (@def-tensor-product-space, $\dim V^* = \dim V$). By bilinearity
$T(\alpha, \beta) = T^{ij}(e_i \otimes e_j)(\alpha, \beta) = T^{ij}\alpha_i\beta_j$, here
$\alpha_i T^{ij} = (1, 2, -5)$ and then $(1, 2, -5) \cdot (0, 1, 1) = -3$.

## SageMath

Sage builds the free module, the tensor and the covectors, and compares the two values.

```{.python .sage}
V = FiniteRankFreeModule(QQ, 3, name="V", start_index=1)
e = V.basis("e")
T = V.tensor((2, 0), name="T"); T[:] = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 3, 1], [0, 0, 5]]
print("dimension of V (x) V:", V.tensor_module(2, 0).rank(), "; of V* (x) V:", V.tensor_module(1, 1).rank())
alpha = V.linear_form(name="alpha"); alpha[:] = [1, 0, -1]
beta = V.linear_form(name="beta"); beta[:] = [0, 1, 1]
print("T(alpha, beta) =", T(alpha, beta), "; T^ij alpha_i beta_j =", vector(QQ, [1, 0, -1]) * matrix(QQ, T[:]) * vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1]))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
dimension of V (x) V: 9 ; of V* (x) V: 9
T(alpha, beta) = -3 ; T^ij alpha_i beta_j = -3
```
::::
:::

The definition claims that the $e_i \otimes f_a$ form a basis, and linear independence is the first half. The
exercise proves it by evaluating a vanishing combination on pairs of dual basis covectors [@axler2024linear, 9.74(a)].

::: {#exr-tensor-space-independent}
#### The basis tensors are independent

Let $e^i$ and $f^a$ be the dual bases (@def-dual-basis). Show that $(e_i \otimes f_a)(e^j, f^b) = \delta^j{}_i\,
\delta^b{}_a$, and deduce that $c^{ia}\, e_i \otimes f_a = 0$ forces every $c^{ia} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$(e_i \otimes f_a)(e^j, f^b) = e^j(e_i) f^b(f_a) = \delta^j{}_i \delta^b{}_a$. Applying $c^{ia}\, e_i \otimes f_a = 0$
to $(e^j, f^b)$ gives $0 = c^{ia}\delta^j{}_i\delta^b{}_a = c^{jb}$ for every $j, b$, so the family is linearly
independent (@def-linear-independence).

## SageMath

Check on $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$: Sage flattens the six basis tensors into their component vectors and
computes the rank of the family.

```{.python .sage}
basis = [matrix(QQ, 2, 3, {(i, a): 1}) for i in range(2) for a in range(3)]
M = matrix(QQ, [b.list() for b in basis])
print("number of tensors e_i (x) f_a:", len(basis), "; rank of their component vectors:", M.rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
number of tensors e_i (x) f_a: 6 ; rank of their component vectors: 6
```
::::
:::

The second half of the basis claim is that the $e_i \otimes f_a$ span. The exercise expands an arbitrary bilinear map
on $V^* \times W^*$ in them, with its values on dual basis pairs as coefficients [@lee2013introduction, Prop. 12.4],
[@axler2024linear, 9.70].

::: {#exr-tensor-space-spanning}
#### The basis tensors span

Show that every $T \in V \otimes W$ equals $T(e^i, f^a)\, e_i \otimes f_a$, and conclude that
$\dim(V \otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $S = T(e^i, f^a)\, e_i \otimes f_a$. For covectors $\alpha = \alpha_j e^j$, $\beta = \beta_b f^b$, bilinearity gives
$T(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha_i\beta_a T(e^i, f^a)$, and $S(\alpha, \beta) = T(e^i, f^a)\alpha(e_i)\beta(f_a) =
T(e^i, f^a)\alpha_i\beta_a$: the same number, so $S = T$. With @exr-tensor-space-independent the $e_i \otimes f_a$
form a basis of $\dim V \cdot \dim W$ elements (@def-basis, @def-dimension).

## SageMath

Check on $V = W = \mathbb{Q}^2$: Sage takes the bilinear map $T(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha_1\beta_1 + 3\alpha_1\beta_2 -
\alpha_2\beta_2$, rebuilds it from its four values on dual basis pairs, and compares on symbolic covectors.

```{.python .sage}
T = lambda a, b: a[0] * b[0] + 3 * a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[1]
E = identity_matrix(QQ, 2).rows()
vals = {(i, j): T(E[i], E[j]) for i in range(2) for j in range(2)}
S = lambda a, b: sum(vals[i, j] * a[i] * b[j] for (i, j) in vals)
al, be = vector(SR, var("a1 a2")), vector(SR, var("b1 b2"))
print("values T(e^i, f^a):", vals, "; S - T on symbolic covectors:", (S(al, be) - T(al, be)).expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
values T(e^i, f^a): {(0, 0): 1, (0, 1): 3, (1, 0): 0, (1, 1): -1} ; S - T on symbolic covectors: 0
```
::::
:::

$V \otimes W$ and $W \otimes V$ are different spaces of the same dimension, and exchanging the arguments identifies
them. The exercise asks for the proof and for the effect on the component array
[@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6.2, p. 84].

::: {#exr-tensor-space-swap}
#### Swapping the factors

For $T \in V \otimes W$ define $(\tau T)(\beta, \alpha) = T(\alpha, \beta)$ for $\beta \in W^*$, $\alpha \in V^*$.
Show that $\tau : V \otimes W \to W \otimes V$ is a linear bijection, and that it transposes the component array.
Compute it for the element of $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$ with components $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & -1
& 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\tau T$ is bilinear on $W^* \times V^*$ because $T$ is bilinear, and $\tau(T + \lambda S) = \tau T + \lambda\tau S$
pointwise. The same construction in the other direction is an inverse, so $\tau$ is bijective. Its components are
$(\tau T)(f^a, e^i) = T(e^i, f^a)$: the $a i$ entry of the new array is the $i a$ entry of the old one. Here $\tau T$
has the $3 \times 2$ array $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates both tensors on covectors in the two orders and prints the transposed array.

```{.python .sage}
T = matrix(QQ, [[1, 0, 2], [0, -1, 3]])
tauT = T.transpose()
al, be = vector(SR, var("a1 a2")), vector(SR, var("b1 b2 b3"))
print("tau T has components", tauT.rows(), "; (tau T)(beta, alpha) - T(alpha, beta) =", (be * tauT * al - al * T * be).expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
tau T has components [(1, 0), (0, -1), (2, 3)] ; (tau T)(beta, alpha) - T(alpha, beta) = 0
```
::::
:::

A tensor with one dual factor is a linear map, which makes the tensor product a home for matrices of every shape. The
exercise asks for the identification of $V \otimes W^*$ with the linear maps $W \to V$
[@lee2013introduction, Problem 12-4], [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6.2, eq. (3.148)].

::: {#exr-tensor-space-linear-maps}
#### Tensors as linear maps

An element $T \in V \otimes W^*$ is a bilinear map on $V^* \times W$. Show that for each $w \in W$ there is a unique
$L_T(w) \in V$ with $\alpha(L_T(w)) = T(\alpha, w)$ for all $\alpha$, that $L_T : W \to V$ is linear, and that
$T \mapsto L_T$ is a linear bijection onto the linear maps $W \to V$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\alpha \mapsto T(\alpha, w)$ is a linear functional on $V^*$, so it is evaluation at a unique vector $L_T(w) \in V$
(@exm-dual-space-dual-dual), namely $L_T(w) = T(e^i, w)\, e_i$. Linearity of $T$ in $w$ makes $L_T$ linear, and
$T \mapsto L_T$ is linear. It is injective: $L_T = 0$ means $T(\alpha, w) = \alpha(L_T(w)) = 0$ for all
$\alpha, w$. Both spaces have dimension $\dim V \cdot \dim W$ (the linear maps $W \to V$ are the matrices of that size,
@def-linear-map), so by rank-nullity the injective map is a bijection. The matrix of $L_T$ is $L^i{}_a = T(e^i, f_a)$.

## SageMath

Check on $V = \mathbb{Q}^2$, $W = \mathbb{Q}^3$: Sage takes components $T(e^i, f_a)$, forms $L_T$, and compares
$\alpha(L_T(w))$ with $T(\alpha, w)$ on symbolic arguments.

```{.python .sage}
C = matrix(QQ, [[1, 0, 2], [0, -1, 3]])          # C[i, a] = T(e^i, f_a)
T = lambda al, w: al * C * w
L = lambda w: C * w
al, w = vector(SR, var("a1 a2")), vector(SR, var("w1 w2 w3"))
print("L_T(w) =", L(w), "; alpha(L_T(w)) - T(alpha, w) =", (al * L(w) - T(al, w)).expand())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
L_T(w) = (w1 + 2*w3, -w2 + 3*w3) ; alpha(L_T(w)) - T(alpha, w) = 0
```
::::
:::

The degeneracies of the two-dimensional oscillator can be read off a table of basis tensors. The exercise asks for that
table for the truncated space of @exm-tensor-space-oscillator and for the reason the highest levels come out wrong.

::: {#exr-tensor-space-oscillator-levels}
#### Counting oscillator states

For $V_3 \otimes V_3$ (one-dimensional levels $n = 0, 1, 2$), list the basis states $\lvert n_1\rangle \otimes \lvert
n_2\rangle$ by total $n = n_1 + n_2$, give the number of states at each $n$, and explain why the counts for $n = 3, 4$
differ from those of the full oscillator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The nine basis states give $n = 0$: $(0, 0)$; $n = 1$: $(0, 1), (1, 0)$; $n = 2$: $(0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 0)$; $n = 3$:
$(1, 2), (2, 1)$; $n = 4$: $(2, 2)$. The counts $1, 2, 3, 2, 1$ add up to $9 = 3 \cdot 3$. The full oscillator has
$n + 1$ states at level $n$, so $4$ and $5$ at $n = 3, 4$; the truncation removed the states with $n_1 \geq 3$ or
$n_2 \geq 3$, such as $(0, 3)$, so only the levels $n \leq 2$ are complete.

## SageMath

Sage lists the pairs $(n_1, n_2)$ and counts them by total.

```{.python .sage}
pairs = [(n1, n2) for n1 in range(3) for n2 in range(3)]
for n in range(5):
    lev = [p for p in pairs if sum(p) == n]
    print("n =", n, ":", len(lev), "states", lev, "; full oscillator:", n + 1)
```

```{.text .sage-output}
n = 0 : 1 states [(0, 0)] ; full oscillator: 1
n = 1 : 2 states [(0, 1), (1, 0)] ; full oscillator: 2
n = 2 : 3 states [(0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 0)] ; full oscillator: 3
n = 3 : 2 states [(1, 2), (2, 1)] ; full oscillator: 4
n = 4 : 1 states [(2, 2)] ; full oscillator: 5
```
::::
:::

Bilinear forms and $V^* \otimes V^*$ are the same thing, which the last exercise makes precise. It combines the
definition with the double dual and the components of a bilinear form, and expands the Minkowski form.

::: {#exr-tensor-space-bilinear-forms}
#### Bilinear forms as tensors

Using $V^{**} = V$ (@exm-dual-space-dual-dual), show that the components $B_{ij}$ of a bilinear form
(@def-bilinear-form) are its coordinates in the basis $e^i \otimes e^j$ of $V^* \otimes V^*$, that $B$ is symmetric
(@def-symmetric-form) exactly when $B_{ij} = B_{ji}$, and expand $\eta$ in this basis.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The basis tensor $e^i \otimes e^j$ acts on $(v, w) \in V \times V$ by $v(e^i)\, w(e^j) = e^i(v)\, e^j(w) = v^i w^j$.
Hence $B_{ij}\, e^i \otimes e^j$ sends $(v, w)$ to $B_{ij}v^iw^j = B(v, w)$, so it is $B$, with coordinates $B_{ij}$
(@exr-tensor-space-spanning). $B(w, v) = B_{ij}w^iv^j = B_{ji}v^iw^j$, which equals $B(v, w)$ for all $v, w$ exactly
when $B_{ij} = B_{ji}$ (take $v, w$ basis vectors). For $\eta$, $\eta_{\mu\nu} = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$
gives $\eta = e^0 \otimes e^0 - \sum_{i = 1}^3 e^i \otimes e^i$.

## SageMath

Sage builds $\eta$ as a type $(0, 2)$ tensor on a rank-$4$ module (indices from $0$), prints its expansion and checks
its symmetry on two sample vectors.

```{.python .sage}
M = FiniteRankFreeModule(QQ, 4, name="M", start_index=0)
e = M.basis("e")
eta = M.tensor((0, 2), name="eta"); eta[0, 0] = 1; eta[1, 1] = -1; eta[2, 2] = -1; eta[3, 3] = -1
print(eta.display())
v = M([1, 2, 0, -1], basis=e); w = M([3, 0, 1, 1], basis=e)
print("eta(v, w) =", eta(v, w), "; eta(w, v) =", eta(w, v))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
eta = e^0⊗e^0 - e^1⊗e^1 - e^2⊗e^2 - e^3⊗e^3
eta(v, w) = 4 ; eta(w, v) = 4
```
::::
:::
::::

### Elementary tensors

The tensor product of two vectors is the simplest element of the tensor product space. The definition gives its
components, the products $v^i w^a$, and names the tensors of this form elementary; a general tensor is a sum of
elementary ones.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-elementary-tensor}
#### Elementary tensor

The **tensor product of vectors** $v \in V$, $w \in W$ is the element $v \otimes w \in V \otimes W$ with
$(v \otimes w)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(v)\beta(w)$; it is bilinear in $(v, w)$, and its components are the products
$v^i w^a$. Tensors of the form $v \otimes w$ are **elementary** (or **decomposable**); a general tensor is a sum
of them.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The basis tensors of the previous definition are the first elementary tensors. The example checks that the new
definition gives them back, and writes one as an array.

::: {#exm-elementary-basis}
#### Basis tensors are elementary

For basis vectors, $(e_i \otimes f_a)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(e_i)\beta(f_a)$ is exactly the basis tensor of
@def-tensor-product-space, so every basis tensor is elementary. In $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$, $e_1 \otimes
e_2$ has the single non-zero component $(e_1 \otimes e_2)^{12} = 1$: the array $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$.
:::

The outer product of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a rank-one matrix. The example gives the one of the figure and
notes that a sum of two elementary tensors can have a larger rank.

::: {#exm-elementary-outer}
#### An outer product

For $u = (1, 2, 3)$ and $v = (1, 0, -1)$, the components $(u \otimes v)^{ij} = u^i v^j$ form the rank-one matrix
of @fig-tensor-grid, $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$, whose columns are all
multiples of $u$. The middle panel of the figure shows a sum of two elementary tensors with rank two.
:::

Bilinearity in $(v, w)$ means that scalars and sums move freely between the factors. The example lists the rules and
draws the consequence that an elementary tensor has many expressions as $v \otimes w$ [@axler2024linear, 9.73].

::: {#exm-elementary-bilinearity}
#### Moving scalars and sums

$(\lambda v) \otimes w = v \otimes (\lambda w) = \lambda (v \otimes w)$, $(v_1 + v_2) \otimes w = v_1 \otimes w + v_2
\otimes w$ and $v \otimes (w_1 + w_2) = v \otimes w_1 + v \otimes w_2$, since both sides take the same value on every
$(\alpha, \beta)$. Thus $(2e_1) \otimes e_2 = e_1 \otimes (2e_2)$, and $e_1 \otimes e_1 + e_1 \otimes e_2 = e_1
\otimes (e_1 + e_2)$ is elementary although written as a sum.
:::

The same construction with covectors gives elementary elements of $V^* \otimes V^*$, that is, bilinear forms. The
example evaluates the simplest one on $\mathbb{R}^2$ [@lee2013introduction, Example 12.2].

::: {#exm-elementary-covectors}
#### Products of covectors

For covectors $\alpha, \beta$, $\alpha \otimes \beta$ is the bilinear form $(v, w) \mapsto \alpha(v)\beta(w)$. With the
dual basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $(e^1 \otimes e^2)\big((w, x), (y, z)\big) = wz$: it reads the first coordinate of the
first argument and the second coordinate of the second.
:::

Elementary tensors in $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$ are exactly the matrices of rank at most one. The example
notes that the identity needs three elementary terms, matching the rank-three array of the figure.

::: {#exm-elementary-matrix}
#### Rank-one matrices

A $3 \times 3$ matrix is elementary in $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$ exactly when it has rank at most one
the identity matrix is a sum $e_1 \otimes e_1 + e_2 \otimes e_2 + e_3 \otimes e_3$
of three and no fewer (@fig-tensor-grid, rank three).
:::

The metrics of physics are sums of elementary tensors of covectors. The example writes the Euclidean form and the
Minkowski form this way and splits the second into a time part and a space part.

::: {#exm-elementary-metric}
#### Metrics as sums of squares

The dot product of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is $e^1 \otimes e^1 + e^2 \otimes e^2 + e^3 \otimes e^3$, and the Minkowski form is
$\eta = e^0 \otimes e^0 - (e^1 \otimes e^1 + e^2 \otimes e^2 + e^3 \otimes e^3)$: an elementary tensor for time minus
the Euclidean form of space. Each term $e^\mu \otimes e^\mu$ is elementary; $\eta$, with a component matrix of rank
four, is not [@lee2013introduction, Example 13.2].
:::

In quantum mechanics an elementary tensor of two states is a product state, and the other states are entangled. The
example shows that the simplest Bell state is not elementary [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6.2, eqs.
(3.140)-(3.143)].

::: {#exm-elementary-product-state}
#### Product states and entanglement

$(a\lvert 0\rangle + b\lvert 1\rangle) \otimes (c\lvert 0\rangle + d\lvert 1\rangle) = ac\lvert 00\rangle + ad\lvert
01\rangle + bc\lvert 10\rangle + bd\lvert 11\rangle$. The Bell state $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert 00\rangle + \lvert
11\rangle)$ would need $ac = bd = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}$ and $ad = bc = 0$; the first two make $a, b, c, d$ all non-zero,
contradicting the last two. It is entangled: no state of the first spin and state of the second produce it.
:::

Adding orbital and spin angular momentum in the hydrogen atom produces states of both kinds. The example takes a $2p$
electron with its spin and reads off which combined states are elementary.

::: {#exm-elementary-hydrogen}
#### Spin and orbit in hydrogen

The $2p$ states of hydrogen with $m_l = 1, 0, -1$ span a space of dimension $3$, and the spin states $\lvert
\uparrow\rangle, \lvert \downarrow\rangle$ one of dimension $2$. The state $\lvert 1\rangle \otimes \lvert
\uparrow\rangle$ of total $j = m_j = \tfrac32$ is elementary. The state of total $j = m_j = \tfrac12$,
$\sqrt{\tfrac23}\, \lvert 1\rangle \otimes \lvert \downarrow\rangle - \sqrt{\tfrac13}\, \lvert 0\rangle \otimes \lvert
\uparrow\rangle$, has a $3 \times 2$ component array of rank two: it is not elementary.
:::

The elementary tensors are not closed under addition. The example shows that they do not form a subspace as soon as
both factors have dimension at least two [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9D.4].

::: {#exm-elementary-not-subspace}
#### Not a subspace

$e_1 \otimes e_1$ and $e_2 \otimes e_2$ are elementary, but their sum has the component array $\operatorname{diag}(1,
1)$ of rank two and is not. So the elementary tensors of $V \otimes W$, with $\dim V, \dim W \geq 2$, are not a
subspace: they are a cone through the origin (closed under scaling), and their span is all of $V \otimes W$.
:::

The zero tensor is the degenerate elementary tensor. The last example records when $v \otimes w$ vanishes and how much
freedom there is in writing a non-zero elementary tensor [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9D.1].

::: {#exm-elementary-zero}
#### When the product vanishes

$v \otimes w = 0$ exactly when $v = 0$ or $w = 0$: $0 \otimes w = 0$ by bilinearity, and
$v \otimes 0 = 0$ likewise. A non-zero elementary tensor determines its factors up to a scalar: $v \otimes w = v'
\otimes w' \neq 0$ exactly when $v' = \lambda v$ and $w' = \lambda^{-1} w$ for some $\lambda \neq 0$, since the
columns of the array $(v^i w^a)$ span the line of $v$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The rank criterion for elementary tensors can be tested on two matrices. The exercise asks whether a given rank-one
matrix and the identity are elementary, and the ranks decide.

::: {#exr-rank-one}
#### Which matrices are elementary?

Decide whether $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$ and the $3 \times 3$ identity
are elementary tensors in $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The first is $u \otimes v$ with $u = (1, 2, 3)$, $v = (1, 0, -1)$: its $ij$ entry is $u^i v^j$, so it is elementary.
An elementary tensor $u \otimes v$ has columns $v^j u$, all multiples of $u$, so its rank is at most one. The identity
has rank three, so it is not elementary; it needs the three terms $e_i \otimes e_i$.

## SageMath

Sage computes both ranks and rebuilds the first matrix as an outer product.

```{.python .sage}
M = matrix(QQ, [[1, 0, -1], [2, 0, -2], [3, 0, -3]])
u, v = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 3]), vector(QQ, [1, 0, -1])
print("rank of M:", M.rank(), "; M == u (x) v:", M == u.outer_product(v), "; rank of the identity:", identity_matrix(QQ, 3).rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rank of M: 1 ; M == u (x) v: True ; rank of the identity: 3
```
::::
:::

An elementary tensor evaluated on two covectors is the product of their values. The exercise computes this both
directly and by summing components, and finds the rank of the component matrix.

::: {#exr-elementary-evaluate}
#### An elementary tensor as a bilinear map

Evaluate $u \otimes v$, for $u = (1, 2, 3)$, $v = (1, 0, -1)$, on the covectors $a = (1, 0, -1)$ and $b = (0, 1,
1)$, both directly and as $a(u) b(v)$, and find the rank of its component matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$a(u) = 1 - 3 = -2$ and $b(v) = 0 - 1 = -1$, so $(u \otimes v)(a, b) = a(u)b(v) = 2$. The same number is
$a_i b_j u^i v^j$ summed over the nine components, and the component matrix has rank $1$ (@exr-rank-one).

## SageMath

Sage builds $u \otimes v$ on a free module and evaluates it.

```{.python .sage}
V = FiniteRankFreeModule(QQ, 3, name="V", start_index=1)
e = V.basis("e")
u = V([1, 2, 3], basis=e, name="u"); v = V([1, 0, -1], basis=e, name="v")
a = V.linear_form(name="a"); a[:] = [1, 0, -1]
b = V.linear_form(name="b"); b[:] = [0, 1, 1]
t = u * v
print("(u (x) v)(a, b) =", t(a, b), "; a(u) b(v) =", a(u) * b(v))
print("components u^i v^j:", t[:], "; rank:", matrix(QQ, t[:]).rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
(u (x) v)(a, b) = 2 ; a(u) b(v) = 2
components u^i v^j: [ 1  0 -1]
[ 2  0 -2]
[ 3  0 -3] ; rank: 1
```
::::
:::

Bilinearity expands a product of two sums into four terms. The exercise does this for two vectors of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and
reads off the component array.

::: {#exr-elementary-expand}
#### Expanding a product

Expand $(e_1 + 2e_2) \otimes (e_1 - e_2)$ in the basis $e_i \otimes e_j$ of $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$ and give
its component array and rank.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By bilinearity (@exm-elementary-bilinearity), $(e_1 + 2e_2) \otimes (e_1 - e_2) = e_1 \otimes e_1 - e_1 \otimes e_2 +
2e_2 \otimes e_1 - 2e_2 \otimes e_2$. The array is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, the products
$u^i v^j$ with $u = (1, 2)$, $v = (1, -1)$; its second row is twice the first, so its rank is $1$.

## SageMath

Sage computes the outer product and its rank.

```{.python .sage}
M = vector(QQ, [1, 2]).outer_product(vector(QQ, [1, -1]))
print("components:", M.rows(), "; rank:", M.rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
components: [(1, -1), (2, -2)] ; rank: 1
```
::::
:::

In $\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$ one polynomial equation in the four components decides whether a tensor is
elementary. The exercise proves the criterion and applies it to two states of two spins.

::: {#exr-elementary-two-by-two}
#### A test for two spins

Show that $\psi = \psi^{ij}\lvert ij\rangle \in \mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^2$ is elementary exactly when
$\psi^{00}\psi^{11} - \psi^{01}\psi^{10} = 0$. Apply it to the Bell state $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert 00\rangle + \lvert
11\rangle)$ and to $\tfrac12(\lvert 00\rangle + \lvert 01\rangle + \lvert 10\rangle + \lvert 11\rangle)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $\psi = u \otimes v$, then $\psi^{00}\psi^{11} - \psi^{01}\psi^{10} = u^0v^0u^1v^1 - u^0v^1u^1v^0 = 0$. Conversely,
suppose the expression vanishes. If the row $(\psi^{00}, \psi^{01})$ is zero, $\psi = \lvert 1\rangle \otimes
(\psi^{10}\lvert 0\rangle + \psi^{11}\lvert 1\rangle)$. Otherwise the second row is $\lambda$ times the first: for
$\psi^{00} \neq 0$ take $\lambda = \psi^{10}/\psi^{00}$, so $\psi^{11} = \psi^{01}\psi^{10}/\psi^{00} =
\lambda\psi^{01}$; for $\psi^{00} = 0$ the equation gives $\psi^{10} = 0$ (as $\psi^{01} \neq 0$), and $\lambda =
\psi^{11}/\psi^{01}$. Then $\psi = (\lvert 0\rangle + \lambda\lvert 1\rangle) \otimes (\psi^{00}\lvert 0\rangle +
\psi^{01}\lvert 1\rangle)$. The Bell state gives $\tfrac12 - 0 \neq 0$: entangled. The second gives $\tfrac14 -
\tfrac14 = 0$: it is $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert 0\rangle + \lvert 1\rangle) \otimes \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert 0\rangle +
\lvert 1\rangle)$.

## SageMath

Sage evaluates the test for both states and checks the factorisation of the second.

```{.python .sage}
test = lambda P: P[0, 0] * P[1, 1] - P[0, 1] * P[1, 0]
bell = matrix(SR, [[1, 0], [0, 1]]) / sqrt(2)
plus = matrix(SR, [[1, 1], [1, 1]]) / 2
h = vector(SR, [1, 1]) / sqrt(2)
print("Bell state:", test(bell), "; second state:", test(plus), "; second = h (x) h:", plus == h.outer_product(h))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
Bell state: 1/2 ; second state: 0 ; second = h (x) h: True
```
::::
:::

A sum of two elementary tensors is elementary only under a proportionality condition. The exercise asks for the proof
and for a counterexample, and identifies the rank of the component matrix with the minimal number of elementary terms.

::: {#exr-elementary-sum}
#### When is a sum of two elementary tensors elementary?

Show that $u \otimes v + w \otimes z$ is elementary if $w$ is a multiple of $u$ or $z$ a multiple of $v$, and that
$e_1 \otimes e_1 + e_2 \otimes e_2$ is not elementary in $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $w = \lambda u$, bilinearity gives $u \otimes v + \lambda u \otimes z = u \otimes (v + \lambda z)$; if $z = \mu v$,
it gives $(u + \mu w) \otimes v$. The component matrix of $e_1 \otimes e_1 + e_2 \otimes e_2$ is $\operatorname{diag}(1,
1, 0)$, of rank $2$, while an elementary tensor has rank at most $1$ (@exr-rank-one), so it is not elementary.

## SageMath

Check on $u = (1, 2, 0)$, $v = (0, 1, 1)$, $z = (1, 0, 3)$ and $w = 2u$: Sage computes the ranks of the sum and of
$\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 0)$.

```{.python .sage}
u, v, z = vector(QQ, [1, 2, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 1]), vector(QQ, [1, 0, 3])
w = 2 * u
S = u.outer_product(v) + w.outer_product(z)
print("rank of u(x)v + 2u(x)z:", S.rank(), "; equals u (x) (v + 2z):", S == u.outer_product(v + 2 * z))
print("rank of e1(x)e1 + e2(x)e2:", diagonal_matrix(QQ, [1, 1, 0]).rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rank of u(x)v + 2u(x)z: 1 ; equals u (x) (v + 2z): True
rank of e1(x)e1 + e2(x)e2: 2
```
::::
:::

An elementary tensor vanishes only if one of its factors does. The exercise asks for the proof, which uses a covector
that takes the value one on a given non-zero vector [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9D.1].

::: {#exr-elementary-zero-proof}
#### Zero products

Prove that $v \otimes w = 0$ if and only if $v = 0$ or $w = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $v = 0$, $(v \otimes w)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(0)\beta(w) = 0$; likewise for $w = 0$. Conversely let $v \otimes
w = 0$ and $v \neq 0$. Extend $v$ to a basis $v = e_1, e_2, \dots, e_n$ of $V$ (@def-basis) and let $\alpha = e^1$,
so $\alpha(v) = 1$ (@def-dual-basis). Then $0 = (v \otimes w)(\alpha, \beta) = \beta(w)$ for every $\beta \in W^*$,
and a vector on which every covector vanishes is $0$ (its coordinates $f^a(w)$ vanish), so $w = 0$.

## SageMath

Check on $v = (1, 2)$, $w = (3, -1, 0)$: Sage computes $v \otimes w$, $v \otimes 0$ and $0 \otimes w$.

```{.python .sage}
v, w = vector(QQ, [1, 2]), vector(QQ, [3, -1, 0])
print("v (x) w is zero:", v.outer_product(w).is_zero(), "; v (x) 0:", v.outer_product(zero_vector(QQ, 3)).is_zero(), "; 0 (x) w:", zero_vector(QQ, 2).outer_product(w).is_zero())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
v (x) w is zero: False ; v (x) 0: True ; 0 (x) w: True
```
::::
:::

The previous exercise has a version with many terms. The exercise shows that a vanishing sum of elementary tensors with
independent first factors has all second factors zero [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9D.3].

::: {#exr-elementary-independent}
#### Independent first factors

Let $v_1, \dots, v_m \in V$ be linearly independent and $w_1, \dots, w_m \in W$ with $v_1 \otimes w_1 + \dots + v_m
\otimes w_m = 0$. Prove that $w_1 = \dots = w_m = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Extend $v_1, \dots, v_m$ to a basis of $V$ and let $\alpha^1, \dots, \alpha^m$ be the first $m$ elements of its dual
basis, so that $\alpha^j(v_k) = \delta^j{}_k$ (@def-dual-basis). Applying the sum to $(\alpha^j, \beta)$ gives $0 =
\sum_k \alpha^j(v_k)\beta(w_k) = \beta(w_j)$ for every $\beta \in W^*$. Hence $w_j = 0$, as in
@exr-elementary-zero-proof, for each $j$.

## SageMath

Check on $v_1 = (1, 0, 1)$, $v_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and unknown $w_1, w_2 \in \mathbb{R}^2$: Sage solves
$v_1 \otimes w_1 + v_2 \otimes w_2 = 0$ for the four unknown components.

```{.python .sage}
p, q, r, s = var("p q r s")
v1, v2 = vector(SR, [1, 0, 1]), vector(SR, [0, 1, 1])
S = v1.outer_product(vector(SR, [p, q])) + v2.outer_product(vector(SR, [r, s]))
print("solutions:", solve(S.list(), [p, q, r, s]))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
solutions: [
[p == 0, q == 0, r == 0, s == 0]
]
```
::::
:::

The rank criterion for elementary tensors in $\mathbb{R}^m \otimes \mathbb{R}^n$ holds in general. The exercise asks
for its proof in both directions [@axler2024linear, Exercise 9D.5].

::: {#exr-elementary-rank-criterion}
#### Elementary means rank at most one

Identify $T \in \mathbb{R}^m \otimes \mathbb{R}^n$ with its $m \times n$ array of components. Prove that $T$ is
elementary if and only if the array has rank at most one, the rank being the dimension of the span of its columns.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

If $T = u \otimes v$, the $j$-th column is $v^j u$, so all columns lie in the span of $u$ and the rank is at most one.
Conversely, if the rank is $0$, $T = 0 = 0 \otimes 0$. If it is $1$, the columns span a line $\operatorname{span}(u)$,
so the $j$-th column is $v^j u$ for some numbers $v^j$; then $T^{ij} = u^i v^j$, which are the components of $u \otimes
v$, so $T = u \otimes v$.

## SageMath

Check on a rank-one $3 \times 4$ array: Sage factors it as a column times a row and compares.

```{.python .sage}
T = matrix(QQ, [[2, -4, 0, 6], [1, -2, 0, 3], [-3, 6, 0, -9]])
u = T.column(0)
v = vector(QQ, [T[0, j] / u[0] for j in range(4)])
print("rank:", T.rank(), "; T == u (x) v with u =", u, "and v =", v, ":", T == u.outer_product(v))
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rank: 1 ; T == u (x) v with u = (2, 1, -3) and v = (1, -2, 0, 3) : True
```
::::
:::

A vanishing sum of elementary tensors need not come from cancelling pairs. The exercise asks for three non-proportional
elementary tensors in $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$, built from six distinct vectors, that add up to zero
[@axler2024linear, Exercise 9D.2].

::: {#exr-elementary-cancel}
#### Three terms that cancel

Find six distinct vectors $v_1, v_2, v_3, w_1, w_2, w_3 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $v_1 \otimes w_1 + v_2 \otimes w_2 + v_3
\otimes w_3 = 0$ such that none of the three terms is a multiple of another.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Take all $w_k$ along $e_3$: $w_1 = e_3$, $w_2 = 2e_3$, $w_3 = -3e_3$. Then the sum is $(v_1 + 2v_2 - 3v_3) \otimes e_3$,
which vanishes when $v_3 = \tfrac13(v_1 + 2v_2)$; take $v_1 = e_1$, $v_2 = e_2$, $v_3 = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, 0)$. The six
vectors are distinct. The array of $v_k \otimes w_k$ has its non-zero column (the third) equal to a multiple of $v_k$,
and the $v_k$ are pairwise non-proportional, so no term is a multiple of another. By @exr-elementary-independent such
an example needs dependent $v_k$, as here.

## SageMath

Sage adds the three outer products and checks that the columns of different terms are not proportional.

```{.python .sage}
v = [vector(QQ, [1, 0, 0]), vector(QQ, [0, 1, 0]), vector(QQ, [1/3, 2/3, 0])]
w = [vector(QQ, [0, 0, 1]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, 2]), vector(QQ, [0, 0, -3])]
terms = [v[k].outer_product(w[k]) for k in range(3)]
print("sum is zero:", sum(terms).is_zero(), "; six distinct vectors:", len(set(tuple(x) for x in v + w)) == 6)
print("pairs of terms that are proportional:", [(j, k) for j in range(3) for k in range(j + 1, 3) if matrix(QQ, [terms[j].list(), terms[k].list()]).rank() < 2])
```

```{.text .sage-output}
sum is zero: True ; six distinct vectors: True
pairs of terms that are proportional: []
```
::::
:::

Rank counts elementary terms beyond the first: a rank-two array is a sum of two of them and no fewer. The last exercise
proves this and shows that the identity of $\mathbb{R}^3 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3$ is not a sum of two elementary tensors
[@axler2024linear, Exercises 9D.6-9D.7].

::: {#exr-elementary-rank-two}
#### Sums of two elementary tensors

Prove that an array in $\mathbb{R}^m \otimes \mathbb{R}^n$ is a sum of two elementary tensors exactly when its rank is at
most two, and conclude that the $3 \times 3$ identity is not such a sum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The columns of $u_1 \otimes v_1 + u_2 \otimes v_2$ are $v_1^j u_1 + v_2^j u_2$, all in $\operatorname{span}(u_1, u_2)$,
so the rank is at most two. Conversely, if the columns lie in a space spanned by $u_1, u_2$ (a basis of the column span,
completed by any vectors if the rank is smaller), the $j$-th column is $v_1^j u_1 + v_2^j u_2$ for some numbers, and
$T^{ij} = u_1^i v_1^j + u_2^i v_2^j$: $T = u_1 \otimes v_1 + u_2 \otimes v_2$. The identity has rank three, so it needs
three terms, as in @exm-elementary-matrix.

## SageMath

Check on a $3 \times 3$ array of rank two: Sage writes it with two column vectors and the coordinates of every column
in them.

```{.python .sage}
T = matrix(QQ, [[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 1], [1, 3, 4]])
u1, u2 = T.column(0), T.column(1)
B = matrix(QQ, [u1, u2]).transpose()
coords = [B.solve_right(T.column(j)) for j in range(3)]
v1, v2 = vector(QQ, [c[0] for c in coords]), vector(QQ, [c[1] for c in coords])
print("rank:", T.rank(), "; T == u1 (x) v1 + u2 (x) v2:", T == u1.outer_product(v1) + u2.outer_product(v2), "; v1 =", v1, ", v2 =", v2)
print("rank of the identity:", identity_matrix(QQ, 3).rank())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
rank: 2 ; T == u1 (x) v1 + u2 (x) v2: True ; v1 = (1, 0, 1) , v2 = (0, 1, 1)
rank of the identity: 3
```
::::
:::
::::

### Tensors of mixed type

Tensors can mix original and dual factors, and the number of each is the type. The definition names the contravariant
and covariant ranks and lists the types of vectors, covectors, bilinear forms and linear maps.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-tensor-type}
#### Mixed tensor

A **tensor of type $(r, s)$** (a **mixed tensor** when both $r, s > 0$) on $V$ is an element of $V^{\otimes r} \otimes (V^*)^{\otimes s}$, equivalently a
multilinear map of $r$ covectors and $s$ vectors. It is **contravariant** of rank $r$ and **covariant** of rank
$s$; vectors are of type $(1, 0)$, covectors $(0, 1)$, bilinear forms $(0, 2)$, linear maps $(1, 1)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest types are the objects met before: numbers, vectors and covectors. The example reads each as a
multilinear map of the right number of arguments [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6, p. 79].

::: {#exm-type-small}
#### Types $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$

A tensor of type $(0, 0)$ takes no arguments: it is a number. A tensor of type $(0, 1)$ is a linear map $V \to
\mathbb{R}$, a covector. A tensor of type $(1, 0)$ is a linear map $V^* \to \mathbb{R}$, which is evaluation
$\alpha \mapsto \alpha(v)$ at a vector $v$ (@exm-dual-space-dual-dual): a vector.
:::

The metric and its inverse are of opposite types. The example records them and identifies the Kronecker delta as the
type $(1, 1)$ identity map.

::: {#exm-type-metric}
#### Metric and inverse metric

$g_{ij}$ is of type $(0, 2)$ and its inverse $g^{ij}$ of type $(2, 0)$; the Kronecker delta $\delta^i{}_j$ is of type
$(1, 1)$, the identity map, and as a multilinear map it is the pairing $(\alpha, v) \mapsto \alpha(v)$.
:::

A type $(1, 1)$ tensor eats a covector and a vector, and in components this is a row times a matrix times a column.
The example writes this out [@carroll1997, Ch. 1, eq. (1.54)].

::: {#exm-type-linear-map}
#### A matrix as a type $(1, 1)$ tensor

A matrix $M^i{}_j$ defines the type $(1, 1)$ tensor $M(\omega, v) = \omega_i M^i{}_j v^j$: the row $\omega$, times $\mathbf M$,
times the column $v$. For $\mathbf M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $\omega = (1, 0)$ and $v = (0, 1)$,
$M(\omega, v) = M^1{}_2 = 2$.
:::

Tensors of any types can be multiplied, and the types add. The example states the product and the convention that
puts the vector slots before the covector slots [@keskivakkuri2022mathematical, Sec. 3.6, eqs. (3.119) and
(3.168)], [@carroll1997, Ch. 1, eq. (1.46)].

::: {#exm-type-product}
#### Products of tensors

For $R$ of type $(r, s)$ and $S$ of type $(r', s')$, $R \otimes S$ of type $(r + r', s + s')$ feeds the first $r$
covectors and $s$ vectors to $R$, the remaining ones to $S$, and multiplies the values. In components, $(R \otimes
S)^{i_1 \dots i_r k_1 \dots k_{r'}}{}_{j_1 \dots j_s l_1 \dots l_{s'}} = R^{i_1 \dots i_r}{}_{j_1 \dots j_s}\, S^{k_1
\dots k_{r'}}{}_{l_1 \dots l_{s'}}$. For instance $T^i{}_j$ times $v^k$ gives the type $(2, 1)$ tensor $T^i{}_j v^k$,
with the two upper indices first in its slot order.
:::

A tensor need not be given all its arguments at once. The example feeds a type $(1, 1)$ tensor a vector only, and
reads the result as a vector [@carroll1997, Ch. 1, eqs. (1.52)-(1.53)].

::: {#exm-type-partial}
#### Feeding some of the arguments

A type $(1, 1)$ tensor with only its vector slot filled, $\alpha \mapsto T(\alpha, v)$, is a linear map on covectors,
a vector, with components $T^i{}_j v^j$: this is how a type $(1, 1)$ tensor acts as a linear map $V \to V$. Filling one
slot of a type $(r, s)$ tensor with a vector leaves a tensor of type $(r, s - 1)$; filling a covector slot leaves type
$(r - 1, s)$.
:::

SageManifolds records the type of every tensor it builds. The example shows how the type is read off and how a tensor
of prescribed type is created.

::: {#exm-type-sage}
#### Types in Sage

In SageManifolds' `FiniteRankFreeModule` the product of two vectors has type $(2, 0)$, a linear form has type $(0, 1)$,
and `V.tensor((1, 1))` creates a type $(1, 1)$ tensor:

```{.python .sage}
V = FiniteRankFreeModule(QQ, 3, name="V", start_index=1)
e = V.basis("e")
u = V([1, 2, 3], basis=e); v = V([1, 0, -1], basis=e)
a = V.linear_form(); a[:] = [1, 0, -1]
print("u * v:", (u * v).tensor_type(), "; a:", a.tensor_type(), "; v * a:", (v * a).tensor_type(), "; V.tensor((1, 1)):", V.tensor((1, 1)).tensor_type())
```

```{.text .sage-output}
u * v: (2, 0) ; a: (0, 1) ; v * a: (1, 1) ; V.tensor((1, 1)): (1, 1)
```
:::

The tensors of mechanics, relativity and electromagnetism each have a definite type. The example lists them, from the
type $(0, 4)$ Levi-Civita symbol down to a type $(0, 0)$ number.

::: {#exm-type-physics}
#### Tensors of physics

The Levi-Civita symbol $\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ of @exm-multilinear-levi-civita is of type $(0, 4)$, the inertia
tensor $I_{ij}$ of @exm-multilinear-inertia of type $(0, 2)$, a four-velocity $u^\mu$ of type $(1, 0)$ and a mass of type
$(0, 0)$ (a number); the field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ is of type $(0, 2)$ and the energy-momentum tensor $T^{\mu\nu}$ of
type $(2, 0)$.
:::

On Minkowski space a vector and a covector with the same physical content have different components. The example lowers
the index of a four-momentum and shows the signs that appear [@carroll1997, Ch. 1, eqs. (1.62)-(1.63)].

::: {#exm-type-minkowski-lowering}
#### Upper and lower four-momentum

The four-momentum $p^\mu = (E, \mathbf p)$ is of type $(1, 0)$. Lowering its index with $\eta$ (@def-nondegenerate)
gives the covector $p_\mu = \eta_{\mu\nu}p^\nu = (E, -\mathbf p)$ of type $(0, 1)$, and $p_\mu p^\mu = E^2 -
|\mathbf p|^2 = m^2$. In Euclidean space with the dot product the two arrays coincide, which is why the distinction is
easy to miss there.
:::

The inertia tensor of a rigid body is a type $(0, 2)$ tensor of mechanics. The example gives its components and the
kinetic energy it computes from the angular velocity.

::: {#exm-type-inertia}
#### The inertia tensor

For point masses $m_a$ at positions $\mathbf x_a$, $I_{ij} = \sum_a m_a(|\mathbf x_a|^2\delta_{ij} - x_a^i x_a^j)$ is a
symmetric type $(0, 2)$ tensor on the space of angular velocities, and the kinetic energy of the rotation with angular
velocity $\omega$ is $\tfrac12 I_{ij}\omega^i\omega^j$. A single mass $m$ at $(1, 0, 0)$ has $I = m\,\operatorname{diag}(0,
1, 1)$: no energy for rotation about the axis through it.
:::

Not every rule that assigns an array to each basis defines a tensor. The last example shows that "the identity array in
every basis" defines a tensor of type $(1, 1)$ but none of type $(0, 2)$ [@carroll1997, Ch. 1, p. 16].

::: {#exm-type-not-tensor}
#### An array that is not a tensor

A type $(0, 2)$ tensor $B$ with $B(e_i, e_j) = \delta_{ij}$ in every basis cannot exist: in the basis $2e_1, e_2,
\dots$ it would give $B(2e_1, 2e_1) = 1$, while bilinearity gives $B(2e_1, 2e_1) = 4B(e_1, e_1) = 4$. The type
$(1, 1)$ tensor $\delta^i{}_j$ has the identity array in every basis, since $e'^i(e'_j) = \delta^i{}_j$ for every basis
and its dual (@def-dual-basis).
:::
::::
